Avoid the common mistake of letting your body twist toward the supinated side; keep your shoulders and hips square throughout.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, then on your next set switch the grip so the hand that was supinated is now pronated and vice versa, ensuring balanced development.

name: Monster Walk
instructions: Loop one resistance band around both ankles and a second band around both legs just above the knees. Choose a band tension that stays taut when your feet are at shoulder width.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointing straight ahead, and push your knees out slightly so there is constant tension in both bands and your knees do not cave inward.
Sit into a quarter-squat: hinge at the hips, push the glutes back, bend the knees slightly, and keep your chest up, back flat, and core braced. This athletic stance is your starting position.
Keep your hips low and level throughout; do not let your torso bob up and down as you walk.

Take a short, controlled step forward and slightly out with one foot, maintaining tension and width, then step the other foot forward to match. Continue stepping forward in this manner for the prescribed number of steps.
Drive each step from the glutes and keep your toes pointing forward; resist the band's pull rather than letting it snap your feet together.
After your forward steps, reverse direction and walk backward with the same short, controlled steps until you return to the start.
Keep breathing steadily and avoid the common mistakes of standing up tall, letting the knees collapse in, or taking steps so large the band goes slack.

name: Mountain Climbers
instructions: Begin in a high plank (top of a push-up) position with hands planted directly under your shoulders, fingers spread, and arms straight.
Extend your legs behind you and support your weight on the balls of your feet, creating a straight line from your head through your hips to your heels.
Brace your core hard, squeeze your glutes, and keep your hips level and low; do not let them pike up or sag down.
Drive one knee forward toward your chest until it is roughly under your hip, keeping the foot off the floor. This is your starting position.
Keeping your shoulders stacked over your hands, explosively switch leg positions: extend the bent leg straight back while simultaneously driving the opposite knee forward.
Land lightly on the balls of your feet and continue alternating legs in a quick, rhythmic running motion.
Breathe in a steady rhythm and keep your upper body still; the movement should come from the hips and legs, not from rocking the shoulders.
Avoid the common mistakes of bouncing the hips up, letting the lower back sag, or letting your hands drift forward of your shoulders.
Continue the alternating drive for the prescribed time, typically 20 to 30 seconds, then rest.

name: Moving Claw Series
instructions: Stand tall on a flat, open running surface with feet hip-width apart, chest up, and core braced. This is a dynamic running drill to groove sprint mechanics.
Begin moving forward at an easy jog, staying tall through the torso with a slight forward lean from the ankles, not the waist.
As you drive one leg back, flex the knee and snap the heel up toward your glute as the hip extends, then cycle the knee forward and up.

As the leg comes forward, load the quad and prepare to strike, then 'claw' the ground by pulling the foot down and back underneath your hips in an active pawing motion, landing on the ball of the foot.
Reload the same quad as the leg recovers forward so you can attack the ground again on the next step, keeping ground contacts quick and light.
Drive the arms in a rapid, piston-like one-two motion, hands relaxed, elbows bent about 90 degrees, swinging from the shoulder without crossing the midline of the body.
Keep your hips tall and avoid sitting back; the power comes from active hip extension and the downward clawing action of the foot.
Avoid the common mistakes of overstriding (reaching the foot out in front of the hips) and letting the torso collapse forward.
Continue for the prescribed distance or duration, then walk back to recover and repeat.

name: Muscle Snatch
instructions: Load a barbell and stand with feet directly below your hips, toes turned out slightly for comfort.
Take a wide (snatch-width) grip on the bar, typically so the bar sits in the crease of the hips when standing tall; a hook grip (thumb wrapped under the fingers) is recommended for security.
Set up with the bar at mid-thigh: lower the hips, lift the chest, keep the back flat, head looking forward, and position your shoulders just in front of the bar with arms long and elbows rotated out.
Take a breath and brace your core; this is your starting position.
Begin the pull by driving through the front of your heels and raising the bar smoothly while keeping it close to your body and your shoulders over the bar.
As the bar passes the upper thigh, explosively extend through the hips, knees, and ankles in one violent triple extension, shrugging the traps to accelerate the bar upward.
Continue pulling with high elbows leading, then turn the arms over and punch the bar straight to the overhead lockout in one continuous motion WITHOUT re-bending the knees to drop under it.
Receive the bar overhead with arms locked, head pushed through, and the bar stacked over the mid-foot; stand fully erect and stable.
Exhale at lockout, then lower the bar under control back to the mid-thigh hang to begin the next rep.
Avoid the common mistakes of letting the bar swing away from the body, bending the arms early, and dipping under the bar instead of muscling it overhead.

name: Muscle Up
instructions: Set up a pair of gymnastic rings (or a bar) at a height that lets you hang with arms fully extended and feet off the floor.

Grip the rings using a false grip: rotate your wrists so the base of your palms sits on top of the rings and your wrists wrap over them, which shortens the transition later. Keep the thumbs around the rings.
Hang with arms straight, shoulders engaged (not loose in the sockets), core braced tight, and a slight hollow-body position with legs together and toes pointed.
Initiate an explosive pull-up by driving your elbows down and back toward your sides, pulling the rings toward your lower chest rather than your chin.

As you reach the top of the pull and the rings approach your sternum, aggressively roll your shoulders forward and lean your chest over the rings, pulling the rings into your armpits while your elbows shoot straight back behind you.
This forward roll transitions you from the pull into the support position at the bottom of a dip; keep the rings tight to your body throughout the turnover.
From this catch position, press hard through your hands and extend the elbows fully to push up into a locked-out support at the top, ribs down and core tight.
Pause briefly at the top in full support, then reverse the motion under control: bend the elbows to lower into the dip, roll back through the transition, and lower into the dead hang.
Use care when descending and avoid the common mistakes of losing the false grip, kipping wildly, or pulling the rings only to the chin instead of high enough to roll the shoulders over.

name: Narrow Stance Hack Squats
instructions: Step into the hack squat machine and place your back flat against the back pad with your shoulders tucked snugly under the shoulder pads.

Position your feet on the platform in a narrow stance, closer than shoulder width with about three inches or less between your heels, and turn the toes out slightly. This narrow stance emphasizes the outer quadriceps (sweep).
Keep your head up, your entire back pressed against the pad, and your core braced throughout the movement.
Grip the side handles and disengage the safety stops, usually by rotating the handles from a forward-facing to a diagonal position.
Press the platform up by straightening your legs WITHOUT locking the knees; this is your starting position.
Inhale and slowly lower the carriage by bending the knees, keeping your back flat against the pad and your knees tracking in line over your toes.
Descend under control until the angle between your thigh and calf is slightly less than 90 degrees, meaning your thighs drop just below parallel to the platform.
Exhale and drive the platform back up by pushing primarily through your heels, straightening the legs to return to the start without locking the knees.
Avoid the common mistakes of letting the heels lift, rounding the lower back off the pad, or letting the knees cave inward.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, then re-engage the safety stops before stepping out.

name: Narrow Stance Leg Press
instructions: Sit down in the leg press machine with your back and head resting flat against the padded support and your hips settled into the seat.

Place your feet flat on the platform directly in front of you in a narrow stance, with about three inches or less between your heels and the toes pointed slightly outward. This narrow placement targets the outer quadriceps.
Keep your head against the pad, your lower back in contact with the seat, and your core braced.

Release the safety bars holding the sled and press the platform up until your legs are nearly fully extended, keeping a slight bend so you do NOT lock out the knees. Your torso and legs should form roughly a 90-degree angle; this is your starting position.
Inhale and slowly lower the platform by bending the knees, keeping them tracking in line with your toes, until your upper and lower legs reach about a 90-degree angle.
Do not let the descent push your hips up off the seat or round your lower back off the pad.
Exhale and press the platform back up by driving mainly through your heels and using the quadriceps, returning to the starting position without locking the knees.
Avoid the common mistakes of bringing the knees down toward your chest so far that the pelvis tucks, and of letting the knees buckle inward under load.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, then re-engage the safety stops securely before relaxing your legs.

name: Narrow Stance Squats
instructions: Set the barbell in a squat rack at roughly mid-chest height and load it. Step under the bar and position it across the meaty part of your upper back (the traps, slightly below the base of the neck), not on the bony spine.
Grip the bar with both hands evenly spaced outside your shoulders, pull your elbows down and your shoulder blades together to create a solid shelf, and brace your core.
Lift the bar off the rack by pushing through your legs and straightening your torso, then take one or two steps back to clear the rack.
Set your feet in a narrow stance, less than shoulder width with the heels about three to six inches apart, and turn your toes out slightly.
Keep your head up looking forward, your chest tall, and a neutral, flat back; take a deep breath into your belly and brace. This is your starting position.
Inhale and begin lowering by simultaneously bending the knees and hips, pushing the knees out over the toes while keeping your torso upright and back flat.
Descend under control until your thighs drop just below parallel, so the angle between your thigh and calf is slightly less than 90 degrees.
Keep your weight over your mid-foot and heels; if performed correctly your knees track in line with your toes and do not collapse inward.
Exhale and drive back up by pushing through your heels and the whole foot, extending the knees and hips together until you return to standing.
Avoid the common mistakes of letting the heels rise, rounding the lower back at the bottom, or letting the knees shoot far past the toes.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, then step forward and re-rack the bar securely.

name: Natural Glute Ham Raise
instructions: Anchor your ankles securely under a fixed pad, such as the leg-restraint pad of a lat pulldown machine or a loaded preacher bench, with your knees resting on a padded surface for comfort.
Kneel facing away from the anchor with your ankles pinned, knees down, hips fully extended, and your body upright in a tall, straight line from knees to head.
Squeeze your glutes, brace your core, and tuck your chin slightly so your spine stays neutral; this is your starting position.
Keeping your hips fully extended and your torso rigid (do not bend at the waist), lower your body forward toward the floor as slowly as you can by resisting with your hamstrings.
Control the descent for as long as possible until your hamstrings can no longer hold you, then catch yourself with your hands as your chest nears the floor, ending in a push-up position.
From the catch, push off the floor with your hands just enough to assist your hamstrings, then contract the hamstrings hard to pull your body back up to the tall kneeling start.
Breathe in on the way down and out as you raise yourself, keeping the movement smooth and avoiding any jerking.
Keep the hips extended throughout; the common mistake is breaking at the hips and turning it into a back extension instead of a true hamstring curl.
If you cannot complete a rep under your own power, loop a band for assistance, have a partner spot, or push more firmly off a box or the floor to help. Repeat for the prescribed reps.

name: Neck Press
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a flat bench with the barbell racked above you, your eyes roughly under the bar, and your feet planted firmly on the floor.
Set a stable base: plant your feet, keep a slight natural arch in the lower back, and pull your shoulder blades down and together against the bench.
Grip the bar with a medium width that produces about a 90-degree angle between your forearms and upper arms at the bottom of the movement.
Unrack the bar and hold it straight over your neck/upper sternum with arms locked out. This higher bar path is what shifts emphasis onto the upper chest. This is your starting position.
Inhale and lower the bar slowly and under control until it lightly touches the base of your neck or very top of the chest, keeping the elbows flared at roughly 90 degrees.
Pause for a second at the bottom without bouncing the bar off your body.
Exhale and press the bar back up to the starting position by driving with the chest, locking out the arms and squeezing the chest at the top.
Lower roughly twice as slowly as you press to maximize control and tension.
Use lighter loads than a standard bench press and consider a spotter, because lowering to the neck is a higher-risk position; never lose control of the bar.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, then carefully rack the bar.

name: Neck Side Stretch
instructions: Sit or stand tall with your spine straight, shoulders relaxed and pulled down away from your ears, and your gaze forward.
Let your arms hang at your sides and keep both shoulders level; do not let the shoulder on the stretching side hike up.
Slowly tilt your head to one side, bringing your ear toward that shoulder until you feel a gentle stretch along the opposite side of your neck.
For a deeper stretch, gently rest the hand on the same side as the tilt over the top of your head and apply light downward pressure; never pull hard.
Keep your face pointing forward and avoid rotating or dropping the chin; the movement is a pure sideways tilt.
Breathe slowly and relax into the stretch, holding for about 20 to 30 seconds without bouncing.
Release gently, return your head to center, then repeat on the opposite side for an equal hold.

name: Neck-SMR
instructions: Sit or lie comfortably and take a firm muscle roller or rolling pin. This is a self-myofascial release drill for the neck muscles.
Place the roller behind your head against the base of your neck, positioning it slightly off-center so it presses on the muscles to either side of the spine, NOT directly on the spine itself.
Tilt the roller so its pressure stays on the soft muscle tissue (the upper traps and neck extensors) rather than on the bony vertebrae. This is your starting position.
Keeping the pressure gentle and controlled, slowly roll downward from the top of your neck along the muscle on one side of the spine.
When you reach a tender or tight spot, pause and hold steady pressure on it for 10 to 30 seconds, breathing slowly to let the muscle release.
Avoid rolling directly on the spine, on the front of the throat, or near the carotid arteries on the sides of the neck.
Repeat down the muscles on the other side of the spine, keeping the pressure light enough to stay comfortable throughout.

name: Nordic Hamstring Curl
instructions: Kneel on a soft pad or mat with your knees roughly hip-width apart and your ankles anchored securely under a sturdy support, a partner's hands, or a loaded barbell so your heels cannot lift.

Position your torso, hips, and thighs in one straight vertical line, squeeze your glutes, brace your core hard, and tuck your chin slightly so your spine stays neutral. This is your starting position.
Keeping your hips fully extended (do not bend at the waist), slowly lower your torso forward toward the floor by resisting with your hamstrings, controlling the descent as slowly as you possibly can.
Maintain the rigid straight line from knees to head the entire way down; the only thing moving should be the angle at your knees.
Lower under control as far as your hamstrings can hold you, then place your hands out in front to catch yourself softly as your chest nears the floor.
From the bottom, push off the floor with your hands just enough to help, then drive your hamstrings hard to pull your body back up to the tall kneeling start.
Breathe in as you lower and out as you raise, and keep the motion smooth without jerking or snapping the hips.
Avoid the common mistake of breaking at the hips, which turns the exercise into a forward bow instead of a hamstring curl; keep glutes squeezed and hips locked out.
Repeat for the prescribed reps.

name: Oblique Crunches
instructions: Lie flat on your back on the floor with your lower back pressed gently into the ground.
Place one hand lightly behind your head (do not lace the fingers or pull on the neck) and rest the other arm out to the side flat against the floor for balance.
Bring your feet up and rest them on a flat elevated surface, such as a bench, so your hips and knees are bent at about 90 degrees.
Brace your core and keep the elbow of the hand behind your head wide; this is your starting position.

Exhale and lift the shoulder of the supporting hand off the floor, twisting your torso diagonally to bring that elbow toward the opposite knee. For example, with your right hand behind your head, curl up and rotate until your right elbow travels toward your left knee.
Drive the movement from the obliques and the abdominal wall, not by yanking on your neck or jerking the head forward.
Squeeze the obliques at the top of the contraction for a moment.
Inhale and slowly lower your shoulder and torso back down under control to the starting position.
Keep your lower back from arching excessively and keep the chin off the chest with the neck relaxed.
Continue alternating sides, completing the prescribed reps for each side.

name: Oblique Crunches - On The Floor
instructions: Lie down on your right side on a mat with your legs stacked on top of each other and your knees bent slightly for stability.
Let your right (bottom) arm rest comfortably on the floor in front of you or across your torso for support.
Place your left hand lightly behind your head with the elbow pointed up and out; do not lace the fingers or pull on your neck.
Brace your core and keep your hips stacked; this is your starting position.
Exhale and crunch your top (left) elbow and shoulder upward toward your hip, contracting the obliques on your right side to lift your torso laterally.
Crunch up as high as you comfortably can, focusing on squeezing the side of your waist rather than swinging the arm.
Hold the peak contraction for a second to maximize tension on the obliques.
Inhale and slowly lower your torso back down under control to the starting position without flopping back to the floor.
Avoid pulling on your head and keep the movement coming from the waist, not the neck or momentum.
Complete the prescribed reps on this side, then roll over and repeat lying on your left side for the other set of obliques.

name: Olympic Squat
instructions: Set the barbell in a squat rack at roughly mid-chest height. Step under the bar and place it across the meat of your upper traps (high-bar position), not on the bony spine of your neck. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width, drive your elbows down and forward, and pull your shoulder blades together to create a solid shelf of muscle for the bar.
Brace your core, lift the bar out of the rack by extending your hips and knees, and take two or three small controlled steps back. Avoid walking too far out.

Set your feet about hip to shoulder width apart with the toes turned out roughly 10 to 30 degrees. Screw your feet into the floor to create torque in the hips. Keep the chest tall and the head facing forward with a neutral neck.
Take a big breath into your belly and brace your abs as if bracing for a punch. Hold this intra-abdominal pressure throughout the rep.

Begin the descent by breaking at the knees first, letting them travel forward over the toes while keeping the torso as upright as possible. Unlike a powerlifting squat, you deliberately minimize how far the hips travel back.
Keep your knees tracking in line with your feet (do not let them cave inward) and keep your weight balanced over the middle of the foot toward the front of the heel, never rolling onto the toes.

Descend all the way down until the backs of your thighs meet your calves (full depth), keeping the heels flat on the floor and the spine neutral. Avoid letting the lower back round at the bottom (no buttwink).
At the bottom, reverse the motion smoothly by driving through the whole foot, keeping the chest up and the elbows from dropping, and stand the weight back up to the start.
Exhale near the top or after completing the rep, then re-brace before the next repetition. Move at a controlled tempo, roughly two to three seconds down and a strong drive up.
After your final rep, step forward and carefully rack the bar by guiding it back onto the hooks.

name: On Your Side Quad Stretch
instructions: Lie down on your right side on a comfortable surface, stacking your hips and shoulders so your body forms a straight line.
Bend your bottom (right) knee to about 90 degrees and rest it on the floor in front of your hips. This bent bottom leg anchors and stabilizes your torso so you do not roll forward.
Bend your top (left) knee behind you and reach back with your left hand to grasp the top of your left foot or ankle.
Gently draw the heel toward your glute until you feel a mild stretch along the front of the left thigh. Keep your lower back from arching by drawing your navel toward your spine.
To intensify and add a hip-flexor stretch, press your left hip forward while pushing your left foot back into your hand, creating a gentle isometric tension.
Hold the stretch for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing slowly and keeping the knee pointing down rather than flaring out to the side.
Release, roll over to the other side, and repeat with the right leg.

name: On-Your-Back Quad Stretch
instructions: Lie on your back along the length of a flat bench or step so that one side of your body is at the edge of the bench.
Let one leg and the same-side arm hang off the side of the bench toward the floor.
Engage your core by pulling your navel toward your spine to keep your pelvis in a neutral position. This prevents your lower back from arching as you stretch.
Bend the hanging knee and reach down with the same-side hand to grasp the top of that foot.
Gently draw the heel toward your glute, feeling the stretch along the front of the thigh. Keep the knee pointing down toward the floor rather than letting it flare outward.
For a deeper combined hip-flexor and quad stretch, gently press the foot down into your hand and lift the hip of the stretching leg up toward the ceiling.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds while breathing steadily and keeping the lower back flat, never arched.
Release slowly, then switch sides and repeat with the other leg.

name: One Arm Against Wall
instructions: Stand upright an arm's length away from a wall or the frame of a doorway, side-on to the wall.
Raise the arm nearest the wall and place the forearm or a bent elbow against the wall at roughly head height so the arm forms an L shape overhead.
Set your feet about hip width apart with a slight stagger for balance, and keep your core lightly braced.
Slowly lean your torso away from the arm and toward the wall, sinking your hip outward, until you feel a stretch along the side of your back beneath the armpit (the lat).
Keep the stretch gentle and controlled; avoid bouncing or yanking. Breathe slowly and deeply to let the muscle relax.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds, then ease out of the stretch, switch sides, and repeat with the other arm.

name: One Arm Chin-Up
instructions: Loop a sturdy towel over a chin-up bar next to where you will grip with your working hand. The towel gives your assisting hand something to hold so you can offload part of your bodyweight.
Reach up and grip the bar with your working hand using a supinated grip (palm facing toward you), and grasp the hanging towel with your other hand.
Hang with both arms, then set your starting position by leaning the torso back roughly 30 degrees, arching the lower back slightly, and pushing the chest out.
Brace your core and pull your shoulder blade down and back on the working side before you bend the elbow, initiating the pull from the back rather than the arm.
Pull your torso upward until the bar reaches the level of your upper chest, drawing the shoulder and upper arm down and back. Exhale as you pull. Use only as much help from the towel hand as needed.
Squeeze the back and biceps hard at the top while keeping the upper torso stationary, letting only the arm move through space.
After a brief pause at the top, inhale and lower yourself slowly and under control until the working arm is fully extended and the lat is fully stretched.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, then switch the working hand and towel hand and repeat on the other side.
As you get stronger, grip the towel lower down (or use fewer fingers) to reduce assistance and progress toward an unassisted one-arm chin-up.

name: One Arm Dumbbell Bench Press
instructions: Sit on the end of a flat bench holding a dumbbell in one hand, resting it on top of your thigh on that side.

Lie back onto the bench while using your thigh to kick the dumbbell up, then bring it up so you are holding it at shoulder level with the elbow bent. Use your free hand to help guide and balance the weight into position.

Plant your feet flat on the floor, set your shoulder blades back and down against the bench, and keep a slight natural arch in your lower back. Brace your core to keep your torso from twisting toward the loaded side.
Rotate the wrist so the palm faces away from you (toward your feet). This is your starting position with the arm extended and the dumbbell over your shoulder.

Inhale and lower the dumbbell slowly and under full control toward the side of your chest, allowing the elbow to travel down at roughly a 45 to 75 degree angle from your torso. Keep your free hand ready to assist with balance only if needed.
Lower until you feel a comfortable stretch across the chest, keeping your wrist stacked over your elbow and avoiding letting the torso rotate.
Exhale and press the dumbbell back up over your shoulder by driving through the chest, stopping just short of locking the elbow to keep tension on the muscle.
Squeeze the chest briefly at the top, then lower again, taking about twice as long to descend as to press up.
Complete the prescribed repetitions, then switch the dumbbell to the other hand and repeat. Keeping your non-working side braced makes this a strong anti-rotation core challenge as well.

name: One Arm Dumbbell Preacher Curl
instructions: Set up at a preacher bench (or use the angled side of an incline bench) and select a dumbbell you can control through a full range of motion.

Sit so the top of the preacher pad fits snugly under your armpit. Drape your working upper arm flat against the pad with the elbow firmly supported, and grip the dumbbell with an underhand (supinated) grip, palm facing up.
Plant your feet flat, sit tall, and brace your core so your body stays still and the back of the upper arm stays pressed into the pad throughout.
Start with the arm extended so the biceps is lengthened, but keep a slight bend in the elbow at the bottom rather than fully locking out, to protect the joint and keep tension on the muscle.
Inhale and lower the dumbbell slowly until the upper arm is extended and the biceps is fully stretched, keeping the elbow planted on the pad.

Exhale and curl the dumbbell up by contracting the biceps until the forearm is near vertical and the muscle is fully contracted at shoulder height. Slightly turning the pinky upward at the top maximizes the contraction.
Squeeze the biceps hard for a count of one at the top, keeping the upper arm glued to the pad the whole time.
Lower under control for the next rep, resisting the weight on the way down. Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.
Switch the dumbbell to the other arm, reposition on the pad, and repeat.

name: One Arm Floor Press
instructions: Lie on your back on the floor or an exercise mat with your knees bent and feet flat, pressing your spine and shoulder blades into the ground.

Have a partner hand you a barbell into one hand, or carefully set it up yourself. Position the working hand so the bar is balanced and your arm is nearly fully extended over your shoulder, similar to the top of a bench press.
Use a neutral-style grip with the wrist firm and stacked under the bar, and rest your non-working hand flat on the floor by your side for stability.
Brace your core and squeeze the working-side shoulder blade down into the floor to create a stable base. This guards against the torso rotating toward the loaded side.
Inhale and lower the bar slowly by bending the elbow until the back of your upper arm and elbow lightly touch the floor. The floor naturally limits the range and protects the shoulder.
Pause briefly with the elbow resting on the floor without bouncing or relaxing the tension.
Exhale and press the bar back up to the starting position by driving primarily through the triceps, extending the elbow until the arm is straight again.
Keep the wrist straight and the bar path vertical over the shoulder throughout. Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.
Carefully hand off or lower the bar, then switch it to the other arm and repeat.

name: One Arm Lat Pulldown
instructions: At a lat pulldown station, attach a single-grip (D-handle) to the cable and select a manageable weight. Adjust the thigh pad so it holds your legs firmly down and keeps you anchored to the seat.
Sit facing the machine with your feet flat on the floor and your thighs locked under the pad. Reach up and grasp the handle with a pronated grip (palm facing forward) using one hand.
Sit tall with the chest up, shoulders set, and core braced. Allow the working arm to extend fully overhead so the lat is stretched. This is your starting position.
Initiate the pull by depressing your shoulder blade down, then drive the elbow down and into your side, flexing the elbow as the handle comes toward your shoulder.
Exhale through the pull and focus on squeezing the lat. Keep your torso facing forward and resist the urge to rotate or lean toward the working side.
Pause briefly at the bottom of the motion with the lat fully contracted and the elbow pulled to your ribs.
Inhale and return the handle slowly and under control back overhead, resisting the cable the whole way.
For multiple repetitions, stop just short of letting the weight stack rest to keep continuous tension on the lat.
Complete the prescribed reps, then switch the handle to the other hand and repeat.

name: One Arm Pronated Dumbbell Triceps Extension
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a bench with your feet planted firmly on the floor and your shoulder blades and head supported.
Hold a dumbbell in your working hand and press it straight up so the arm is fully extended and perpendicular to your body, directly over your shoulder.
Set the wrist in a pronated grip so the palm faces toward your feet, and keep the wrist firm and neutral so it does not bend back.
Place your non-working hand against the working-side biceps or under the elbow to support and steady the upper arm so it stays vertical throughout.

Inhale and slowly lower the dumbbell by bending only at the elbow, bringing the weight down toward your shoulder or the side of your head while keeping the upper arm fixed in place and pointing at the ceiling.
Lower until you feel a stretch in the triceps, keeping the descent controlled and never letting the elbow drift or flare.
Exhale and extend the elbow to drive the dumbbell back up to the starting position, contracting the triceps hard at the top without locking out aggressively.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, keeping the upper arm motionless throughout.
Switch the dumbbell to the other arm and repeat.

name: One Arm Supinated Dumbbell Triceps Extension
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a bench with your feet planted on the floor and your head and shoulders fully supported.
Press a dumbbell up in your working hand so the arm is fully extended and perpendicular to your body, directly above your shoulder.
Rotate the wrist into a supinated grip so the palm faces back toward your face, and keep the wrist firm so it does not collapse backward.
Rest your non-working hand on the working-side biceps or beneath the elbow to brace the upper arm and keep it vertical and stable.
Inhale and lower the dumbbell slowly by bending only at the elbow, bringing the weight down toward your forehead or the side of your head while the upper arm stays pointing straight up.
Descend until you feel a stretch in the triceps, keeping the movement smooth and the elbow from flaring outward.
Exhale and contract the triceps to extend the elbow and press the dumbbell back to the starting position over your shoulder.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, keeping the upper arm fixed the entire time. The supinated grip places extra emphasis on the inner (medial) head of the triceps.
Switch the dumbbell to the other arm and repeat.

name: One Half Locust
instructions: Lie facedown on the floor on a mat with your legs extended and the tops of your feet resting on the ground.
Slide your left hand, palm down, underneath your left hipbone to pad and protect the hip and pubic bone against the floor.
Bend your right knee and reach back with your right hand to take hold of the top of your right foot or ankle.
Press your hips and lower belly gently into the floor and brace your core to support your lower back before you lift.
Simultaneously lift the right foot up into your hand (drawing it away from your glute) and raise your shoulders and chest off the floor, creating a gentle backbend.
Feel the combined stretch across the front of the right thigh and hip flexor, the chest, and the front of the shoulders. Keep your gaze slightly forward without crunching the back of the neck.
Hold for 15 to 30 seconds, breathing steadily, and stop if you feel any pinching in the lower back.
Lower down with control, then switch sides and repeat with the left leg. If your back tolerates it, you can progress to lifting both arms and legs at once.

name: One Handed Hang
instructions: Stand beneath a chin-up bar and reach up to grip it firmly with one hand using a pronated grip (palm facing away from you).
Keep your feet on the floor or a step so you can control how much of your bodyweight loads the hanging arm.
Engage the grip, let the working shoulder relax into the hang, and allow the majority of your bodyweight to pull down through that arm while your feet lightly support you.
Keep your core gently braced and your body still, feeling a decompressing stretch through the lat, shoulder, and forearm.
Breathe slowly and hold for 10 to 20 seconds. Do not let yourself drop or swing abruptly.
Step up to unload the arm, release the bar, then switch hands and repeat on the other side.

name: One Knee To Chest
instructions: Lie flat on your back on the floor or a mat with both legs extended.
Keep one leg straight and resting on the floor, pressing the back of that thigh down to feel a stretch through its hip flexor.
Bend the opposite knee and draw it up toward your chest, clasping your hands underneath the knee joint rather than over the kneecap to protect the joint.
Gently pull the bent knee toward your nose, feeling the stretch deepen in the glute and lower back of that side.
Keep your head, shoulders, and the straight leg relaxed on the floor, and avoid lifting your hips or rounding hard off the mat.
Breathe slowly and hold for 20 to 30 seconds, easing into the stretch rather than forcing it.
Release the leg back to the floor, then switch sides and repeat with the other knee.

name: One Leg Barbell Squat
instructions: Set up about two to three feet in front of a flat bench with your back facing it, and place a barbell on the floor in front of you. Stand with your feet roughly shoulder width apart.

Bend your knees and grip the barbell with a pronated grip slightly wider than shoulder width, then lift it to your chest, and from there press and rest it across the base of your neck and upper traps as in a back squat.
Reach one foot back and rest the top of that toe or the laces on the bench behind you, keeping the front foot planted firmly and flat on the floor a comfortable stride ahead.
Stand tall with your chest out, head up, and a straight, neutral back. Brace your core and find your balance before descending. Looking down will throw off your balance.

Inhale and slowly lower into the squat by bending the front knee until the front thigh is about parallel to the floor. At the bottom, the front knee should track over the toes and your chest should be positioned directly above the middle of the front thigh.
Keep your weight in the front heel and mid-foot and avoid letting the front knee cave inward.
Exhale and drive up through the front foot, leading with the chest and hips and contracting the quadriceps, to return to the standing start position.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, then carefully step the rear foot off the bench, switch legs, and repeat on the other side.
When finished, lower the barbell back to your chest and then to the floor under control.

name: One-Arm Dumbbell Row
instructions: Place a dumbbell on the floor on each side of a flat bench, or just on the side you will work first.

Put your right knee on the end of the bench and bend forward at the hips until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor, then place your right hand on the bench ahead of you for support. Keep the supporting arm firm.

Reach down with your left hand and pick up the dumbbell, letting it hang at arm's length with the palm facing your torso (neutral grip). Set your back flat and neutral, not rounded, with your shoulders square. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your hips level so the spine stays neutral throughout. Do not let the working shoulder drop or the back twist open.
Exhale and pull the dumbbell straight up to the side of your chest, leading with the elbow and keeping the upper arm close to your side. Drive the movement with the back muscles, not the forearm.
Squeeze the back and lat hard at the top of the pull, keeping the torso stationary and only the arm moving.
Inhale and lower the dumbbell slowly and under control straight back down to the fully extended starting position, feeling the lat stretch at the bottom.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, keeping the forearm passive and avoiding any jerking or torso rotation.
Switch your stance to put the left knee and hand on the bench, take the dumbbell in your right hand, and repeat on the other side.

name: One-Arm Flat Bench Dumbbell Flye
instructions: Select a moderate dumbbell and sit on the end of a flat bench with the dumbbell resting on top of the thigh on your working side, held with a neutral grip (palm facing in).
Lie back onto the bench, using your thigh to kick the dumbbell up as you go, until you are flat with feet planted firmly on the floor about shoulder-width apart for a stable base.
Press the dumbbell up so your working arm is extended straight over your chest with a neutral grip, and grip the side or underside of the bench with your free hand to anchor your torso.
Brace your core, keep your shoulder blades pulled back and down into the bench, and set a slight, fixed bend in your working elbow to protect the biceps tendon and shoulder.

Inhale and lower the dumbbell out to the side in a wide arc, keeping the elbow angle fixed, until you feel a deep stretch across your chest, stopping when your upper arm is roughly level with your torso.
Keep the movement at the shoulder joint only; do not bend or straighten the elbow, and do not let the weight drift toward your face or hips.
Exhale and squeeze your chest to bring the dumbbell back up along the same arc to the start, as if hugging a large barrel.
Pause and squeeze the pec at the top for one second without letting the arm flop straight inward.
Complete all reps without rotating your torso toward the working side, then switch the dumbbell to the other hand and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm High-Pulley Cable Side Bends
instructions: Attach a single D-handle to the cable and set the pulley to the highest position on the tower.
Stand sideways to the machine, close enough that the cable stays taut, with your feet hip-width apart and weight evenly balanced.
Reach up with the hand nearest the machine and grab the handle with an underhand grip (palm up), then pull the cable down until your elbow is pinned to your side and the handle sits by your shoulder.
Place your free hand on the opposite hip to feel the pivot point and to gauge the bend, and stand tall with your chest up and core braced.
Keep your working arm locked in static position against your side throughout; all the work must come from your obliques, not your arm.
Exhale and contract the oblique on the working side to crunch your torso down sideways, pulling the weight down toward your hip in a controlled side bend.
Bend only laterally; do not rotate, lean forward, or push with the hip, and keep your hips facing forward and stationary.
Inhale and slowly resist the weight back up to the start, stopping before the stack touches down so tension stays constant on the muscle.
Repeat for the prescribed reps or to failure, then reposition with the other side toward the machine and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Incline Lateral Raise
instructions: Set an incline bench to roughly 45 to 60 degrees and select a light dumbbell, since this is a strict isolation movement.
Lie sideways on the bench so the side of your torso and your bottom shoulder press against the back pad, with your bottom arm wrapped across your body or holding the bench for support.
Hold the dumbbell in your top hand and extend that arm down in front of you so it hangs parallel to the floor, palm facing down. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your top shoulder blade set, keeping a very slight bend in the elbow that stays fixed throughout.
Exhale and raise the dumbbell straight up in an arc, leading with the elbow, until your arm points toward the ceiling directly above your shoulder.
Keep the dumbbell traveling roughly parallel to the floor and avoid shrugging the trap or swinging your torso to cheat the weight up.
Pause at the top and feel the contraction in the side delt for a one-count.
Inhale and lower the dumbbell slowly back across your body to the starting position under full control.
Complete all reps, then turn over to lie on the other side and repeat with the opposite arm for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Clean
instructions: Place a kettlebell on the floor between your feet, which should be roughly shoulder-width apart with toes pointed slightly out.
Hinge at the hips, pushing your butt back and bending the knees, keeping your chest up, spine neutral, and eyes looking forward to reach down and grip the handle with one hand.
Set your shoulders back and down, brace your core, and take the slack out of the arm so the weight is loaded onto your hips and hamstrings. This is your starting position.
Drive explosively through your legs and hips, extending the knees and snapping the hips forward to accelerate the kettlebell up the front of your body, keeping it close to your torso.
As the kettlebell rises, pull your elbow in tight and rotate your wrist around the bell so it settles on the back of your forearm rather than slamming into it.
Receive the kettlebell in the rack position: bell resting on the back of the forearm and against the shoulder, elbow tucked down, wrist straight, with a soft punch up to absorb the weight.
Stand fully tall with hips and knees extended and the bell racked, keeping your core and glutes tight.
Lower the kettlebell back down by guiding it off the shoulder and hinging at the hips to return it to the floor or to a swing back between the legs, then repeat.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Clean and Jerk
instructions: Stand with feet about shoulder-width apart and a kettlebell on the floor between or just in front of your feet, hinging down to grip the handle with one hand.

Clean the kettlebell to the rack position by extending through the legs and hips, pulling the bell up close to the body and rotating your wrist so the bell settles on the back of the forearm against your shoulder with the palm facing forward. This is your starting position.
Keep the bell racked, your core braced, torso upright, and feet flat as you set up to jerk.
Dip by bending the knees a few inches straight down, keeping your torso vertical and not leaning forward.
Immediately reverse and drive hard through your heels, extending the legs explosively as if jumping, to launch the kettlebell upward off your shoulder.
As the bell travels up, punch your arm to full lockout overhead, dropping slightly under the weight rather than pressing it the whole way with the shoulder.
Receive the weight overhead by re-bending the knees into a partial squat directly under the locked-out arm, then stand fully erect with the bell stacked over your shoulder and hips.
Hold the lockout momentarily with the elbow straight and the bicep near the ear, then lower the bell back to the rack and down to the floor or a backswing for the next rep.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Floor Press
instructions: Lie flat on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet planted, holding a kettlebell in one hand racked against the shoulder with the palm facing in (neutral grip).
Position your working upper arm flat on the floor at roughly a 45-degree angle to your torso, so your triceps rests down and the forearm is vertical with the bell over your wrist.
Drive your free hand and feet into the floor for stability, brace your core, and keep the wrist straight so the bell sits on the back of the forearm.
Exhale and press the kettlebell straight up toward the ceiling, extending the arm fully and allowing a slight natural rotation so the palm finishes facing your feet or stays neutral.
Lock out the elbow at the top with the bell stacked directly over the shoulder, keeping the shoulder packed down, not shrugged.
Inhale and lower the kettlebell under control until the back of your upper arm lightly touches the floor; the floor limits your range and protects the shoulder.
Pause briefly when the triceps touches down, keeping tension, then press again for the next rep.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Jerk
instructions: Stand with feet about shoulder-width apart and clean a kettlebell into the rack position, extending through the legs and hips and rotating the wrist so the bell rests on the back of the forearm against the shoulder with the palm facing forward. This is your starting position.
Stand tall with the bell racked, torso upright, core and glutes braced, and weight balanced over the middle of your feet.
Dip straight down by bending the knees a few inches, keeping your chest up and torso vertical so the bell stays over your shoulder.
Immediately reverse direction and drive explosively through your heels, extending the legs like a jump to send the kettlebell upward.
As the bell rises off the shoulder, punch your arm to full lockout overhead, dropping under the weight by re-bending the knees into a partial squat rather than grinding it up with the shoulder.
Receive the weight overhead with the arm locked, then extend the legs to stand fully erect with the kettlebell stacked over your shoulder and hip.
Hold the overhead lockout for a moment with the elbow straight and shoulder packed, then lower the bell back to the rack under control for the next rep.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Military Press To The Side
instructions: Stand with feet hip- to shoulder-width apart and clean a kettlebell to the rack position, extending through the legs and hips and rotating the wrist so the bell rests on the back of the forearm with the palm facing inward. This is your starting position.
Brace hard: squeeze your glutes, tighten your abs, and contract the lat on the working side to create a stable base, keeping your torso upright with no leaning back.
Keep your forearm vertical and wrist straight, with the bell resting on the back of the forearm and your eyes tracking up toward the kettlebell.
Exhale and press the kettlebell up and slightly out to the side in an arc, driving it overhead rather than straight in front of your face.
Continue pressing until the arm is locked out overhead, with the bell settling onto the back of the forearm and the palm facing forward at the top.
Keep your core and glutes tight throughout so your spine does not arch or your torso does not bend sideways to assist the press.
Inhale and lower the kettlebell back down to the rack position at your shoulder under full control.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Para Press
instructions: Stand with feet hip- to shoulder-width apart and clean a kettlebell to the rack position, extending through the legs and hips and rotating the wrist so the bell rests on the back of the forearm with the palm facing forward. This is your starting position.
Open your working elbow out to the side so the upper arm is roughly parallel to the floor and the forearm is vertical, with the bell resting on the back of the forearm.
Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and contract the lat for stability, standing tall with your torso upright.
Exhale and press the kettlebell up and out from this elbow-out position until the arm is locked out overhead.
Keep the wrist straight and the bell tracking onto the back of the forearm as you reach full lockout, shoulder packed and not shrugged.
Do not lean back or bend sideways; keep the abs, glutes, and lat tight to keep the spine neutral.
Inhale and lower the kettlebell under control back to the elbow-out rack starting position.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Push Press
instructions: Stand with feet about shoulder-width apart and clean a kettlebell to the rack position, extending through the legs and hips and rotating the wrist so the bell rests on the back of the forearm against the shoulder with the palm facing forward. This is your starting position.
Stand tall with the bell racked, torso upright, core braced, and weight over the middle of your feet.
Dip straight down by bending the knees a few inches, keeping your chest up and torso vertical so the bell stays loaded over your shoulder.
Immediately reverse and drive explosively through your heels, extending the legs to transfer momentum up into the kettlebell.
As the leg drive launches the bell, press your arm the rest of the way to full lockout overhead, finishing the lift with the triceps and shoulder.
Lock the arm out overhead with the bell on the back of the forearm, shoulder packed, and the bicep near your ear, standing fully erect.
Lower the kettlebell back to the rack position under control to begin the next rep, re-bracing before each dip.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Row
instructions: Place a kettlebell on the floor just in front of and between your feet, standing with feet roughly hip- to shoulder-width apart.
Hinge at the hips, pushing your butt back as far as possible and bending the knees slightly, until your torso is close to parallel with the floor with a flat, neutral back and chest up.
Reach down and grip the kettlebell handle with one hand, letting that arm hang straight down; you may brace the free hand on your thigh or knee for support.
Set your shoulders back, brace your core, and keep your hips square and back flat throughout. This is your starting position.
Exhale and pull the kettlebell up toward your stomach or lower ribs, leading with the elbow and retracting your shoulder blade as you flex the elbow.
Keep the elbow tracking close to your body and avoid twisting your torso, jerking the weight, or rounding your spine to cheat it up.
Squeeze your back at the top for a brief pause, then inhale and lower the kettlebell back down under control until the arm is fully extended.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Snatch
instructions: Place a kettlebell on the floor between your feet, which should be roughly shoulder-width apart with toes slightly out.
Hinge at the hips and push your butt back, bending the knees and keeping a flat back, chest up, and eyes forward, then grip the handle with one hand.
Brace your core, set your shoulder back, and hike the kettlebell back between your legs like a hike pass to load the hips and hamstrings.
Immediately reverse direction and drive explosively through your hips and knees, snapping the hips forward to accelerate the bell upward close to your body.

As the kettlebell rises past chest height, pull your elbow high and back, then punch your hand straight up and rotate it around the bell so the kettlebell settles smoothly onto the back of the forearm.
Catch the weight locked out directly overhead in one fluid motion, arm straight, wrist neutral, shoulder packed, and bicep near your ear, avoiding any bang of the bell onto the wrist.
Stand tall and stable for a beat with the bell overhead.
Lower the kettlebell back down in a controlled arc, hinging the hips to send it back between your legs for the next rep.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Split Jerk
instructions: Stand with feet about shoulder-width apart and clean a kettlebell to the rack position, extending through the legs and hips and rotating the wrist so the bell rests on the back of the forearm against the shoulder with the palm facing forward. This is your starting position.
Stand tall with the bell racked, torso upright, and core, glutes, and lat braced.
Dip straight down by bending the knees a few inches, keeping your torso vertical so the bell stays over your shoulder.
Immediately reverse and drive explosively through your heels, extending the legs like a jump to launch the kettlebell upward off the shoulder.
As the bell rises, punch your arm to full lockout overhead while simultaneously splitting your feet, one leg striding forward and the other sliding back, to drop your body under the weight.
Receive the kettlebell locked out overhead in the split stance, with the front shin roughly vertical, back knee soft, and the bell stacked over your shoulder and midline.
Recover by stepping the front foot back partway, then the back foot forward, to bring your feet together while keeping the weight locked out overhead.
Lower the kettlebell back to the rack position under control to begin the next rep.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Split Snatch
instructions: Stand with feet about shoulder-width apart, holding a kettlebell in one hand by the handle, letting it hang between or just in front of your legs.
Hinge slightly or dip into a partial squat, keeping a flat back, chest up, and core braced to load the hips. This is your starting position.
Reverse the motion explosively, extending the hips, then the knees, and finally rising onto the ankles to accelerate the kettlebell upward close to your body in one uninterrupted pull.
As the bell rises overhead, punch your hand up and rotate it around the bell so the kettlebell settles onto the back of the forearm without banging the wrist.
At the same moment, drop under the weight by splitting your feet into a lunge, one leg forward and one leg back, to receive the kettlebell locked out overhead.
Catch the bell with the arm fully locked, shoulder packed and stacked over your midline, front shin vertical and back knee soft, in a stable split position.
Recover by stepping the front foot back partway, then the rear foot forward, to bring your feet together while keeping the weight locked out overhead.
Lower the kettlebell back to the starting position under control for the next rep.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Swings
instructions: Place a kettlebell on the floor about a foot in front of you and stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointed slightly out.
Hinge at the hips, pushing your butt back and bending the knees slightly, keeping a flat back and chest up, then grip the handle with one hand and let the free arm hang relaxed at your side.

Set your shoulder back and down, brace your core, and hike the kettlebell back between your legs to load the hamstrings and glutes; keep the arm long and the bell high in the groin, not down by the knees.
Drive explosively through your heels and snap your hips forward, squeezing your glutes hard, to propel the kettlebell up and forward in an arc to about chest or eye height.
Let the bell float on momentum from the hips, keeping the working arm relaxed and straight; do not lift the weight with your shoulder or arm.
Keep your core braced and spine neutral at the top, with a tall standing position and no leaning back.
Let the kettlebell swing back down, hinging at the hips again and loading the hamstrings as it passes between your legs for the next rep.
Maintain a smooth, continuous rhythm, breathing out sharply at the top of each swing and in as it descends.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Long Bar Row
instructions: Wedge one end of a barbell into a landmine attachment or securely into a corner so it cannot slide, then load an appropriate plate onto the free end.
Stand alongside the loaded end and position yourself so you can grip the bar just behind the collar with one hand.
Using your hips and legs, lift the loaded end off the floor and rise to a standing bent-over position.
Assume a staggered or athletic bent-knee stance with your hips pushed back, chest up, flat back, and the working arm hanging extended down toward the bar. This is your starting position.
Brace your core, set the working shoulder back, and keep your torso angle fixed throughout.
Exhale and pull the loaded end of the bar up toward your side and lower ribs, retracting the shoulder blade and flexing the elbow as you drive the elbow back.
Keep the movement strict; do not jerk the weight, twist the torso, or use the legs to cheat the bar up.
Squeeze the back at the top for a brief pause, then inhale and lower the bar under control back to the fully extended starting position.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch hands and repeat for equal reps.

name: One-Arm Medicine Ball Slam
instructions: Choose a non-bouncing (dead-ball) or lightly bouncing medicine ball you can throw explosively, typically 6 to 15 pounds, and clear a few feet of open floor in front of you.
Stand in a staggered athletic stance with feet roughly hip-to-shoulder width, one foot slightly ahead of the other, knees soft, and weight balanced over the midfoot.
Hold the ball in one hand on the same side as your rear foot, cradling it against your palm and fingers, and let your other arm stay relaxed at your side or out for balance.
Brace your core, keep your spine long, and set your shoulders down and back so the slam comes from your trunk and lat, not just the arm.
Wind up by reaching the ball up and behind you overhead as you extend through the ankles, knees, and hips, rising onto the balls of your feet for maximum stretch and load.
Inhale during the wind-up, then forcefully exhale as you initiate the slam by snapping the hips and spine into flexion and driving the lat down.

Throw the ball hard straight down into the floor about a foot in front of your lead foot, following through so your hand finishes near knee height, keeping the elbow only slightly bent to transmit power.
Hinge at the hips and bend the knees to absorb and catch the ball on the bounce, or pick it up from a dead stop, keeping your back flat as you reload.
Reset the wind-up and repeat for the prescribed reps, then switch the ball to the other hand and repeat to balance both sides.
Common mistakes: slamming with only the arm instead of the whole body, rounding the lower back to reach the ball, and slamming too far forward so you chase the ball.

name: One-Arm Open Palm Kettlebell Clean
instructions: Set a single kettlebell on the floor centered between your feet, standing with feet slightly wider than shoulder width and toes turned out a few degrees.
Hinge at the hips and bend the knees to reach down with one hand, keeping your chest up, back flat, and shoulders pulled down away from your ears.
Grip the handle with a loose, open hook of the fingers so the bell can rotate freely, with your free arm out to the side for balance.
Brace your core, take a breath, and drive explosively through your legs and hips, extending the knees, hips, and ankles to launch the bell upward in a straight vertical path close to your body.

As the kettlebell rises to chest height and becomes nearly weightless, relax and open your palm and let the bell flip so the ball rotates up and settles into your open palm against the back of your forearm, without banging your wrist.
Absorb the catch by softening the knees slightly and keeping the elbow tucked close to your ribs, with the bell resting balanced on the open palm.
To return, toss the kettlebell out and slightly forward, letting the handle rotate back down so you can catch the handle in your hand as it descends.
Hinge at the hips and guide the bell back down between your feet to the floor under control, resetting your flat-back start position.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, then switch hands and perform the same number on the other side to balance both sides.
Common mistakes: letting the bell swing out in a wide arc instead of rising vertically, catching with a clenched fist so the bell bangs the wrist, and rounding the back on the way down.

name: One-Arm Overhead Kettlebell Squats
instructions: Stand with a kettlebell on the floor beside one foot, setting your feet shoulder-width to slightly wider with toes turned out about 15 to 30 degrees.

Clean the kettlebell to the rack position by hinging, gripping the handle, driving through the legs and hips, and pulling the bell to your shoulder while rotating your wrist so the bell settles on the back of the forearm.

Press the kettlebell straight overhead by extending the elbow until the arm is fully locked out, the bicep near your ear, and the bell stacked directly over your shoulder and midfoot; this is your starting position.
Keep your free arm out to the side for counterbalance, brace your core hard, and fix your gaze straight ahead to help stabilize the overhead load.
Keeping the kettlebell locked out and the shoulder packed, take a breath and begin the descent by pushing your hips back and bending the knees, tracking the knees over the toes.

Lower your torso between your legs as upright as possible, keeping the chest up and the loaded arm vertical, descending until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor or as deep as your mobility allows.
Pause for one second at the bottom while keeping the bell directly overhead and the core tight, not letting the weight drift forward or back.
Drive back up through the heels and midfoot, extending the hips and knees together, and exhale as you stand fully tall with the bell still locked overhead.
Complete the prescribed reps, then carefully lower the bell to the rack and to the floor, switch arms, and repeat for the same number on the other side.
Common mistakes: letting the overhead arm bend or drift forward, the chest collapsing forward in the squat, and the heels lifting off the floor.

name: One-Arm Side Deadlift
instructions: Position a loaded barbell on the floor and stand beside it so its center is alongside the middle of your foot, with the bar running front-to-back next to your leg.
Set your feet shoulder-width apart with toes pointing straight ahead, standing close enough that you can grip the bar at its balance point without leaning.
Push your hips back and bend your knees to lower into a squat-deadlift position, keeping your chest up, spine neutral, and core braced.
Reach down and grasp the bar at its center with one hand as if holding a briefcase, palm facing in toward your leg (a suitcase grip), using a wrist wrap if the load is heavy.
Set your shoulders down and back, take a breath into your belly, and take the slack out of the bar so it is balanced and not tipping forward or back.
Drive through your heels and extend your knees and hips together to stand the weight up, keeping the bar close to your leg and your gripping arm fully straight, exhaling as you rise.
Finish standing tall with shoulders level and hips fully extended, resisting the tendency to lean or rotate toward the loaded side and keeping your torso square.
Inhale, then lower the bar under control by hinging at the hips and bending the knees, keeping a flat back the entire way down until the bar touches the floor.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, then set the bar down, walk to the other side, and perform the same number with the opposite hand to balance both sides.
Common mistakes: rounding the lower back to reach the bar, letting the torso tilt sideways toward the weight, and yanking with the arm instead of driving with the legs.

name: One-Arm Side Laterals
instructions: Select a moderate dumbbell and hold it in one hand, standing beside a sturdy upright such as a power rack or the frame of an incline bench.
Grab the support with your free hand at about waist-to-chest height, then lean your torso away from the support so your working-side shoulder is the high point and the dumbbell hangs freely.
Set your feet about hip-width for a stable base, keep a slight bend in the knees, and brace your core so your torso stays fixed throughout.
Let the dumbbell hang at arm's length with a slight bend in the elbow and the palm facing in toward your body; this is your starting position.
Keeping the torso completely still with no swinging, raise the dumbbell out to the side, leading with the elbow and keeping the elbow slightly higher than the hand.
Tilt the hand slightly forward as if pouring water from a pitcher to bias the side delt, and lift until the upper arm is parallel to the floor, exhaling through the lift.
Pause for one second at the top with the deltoid fully contracted, avoiding any shrug of the trap.
Lower the dumbbell slowly and under control back to the starting position as you inhale, resisting gravity on the way down.
Complete the prescribed reps, then switch the dumbbell to the other hand, reposition, and repeat for the same number on the other side.
Common mistakes: swinging the body or using momentum, shrugging the trap to raise the weight, and lifting the hand higher than the elbow.

name: One-Legged Cable Kickback
instructions: Attach a leather ankle cuff to the low pulley of a cable machine and set the pulley to its lowest position, selecting a light to moderate weight.
Strap the cuff snugly around one ankle, then stand facing the weight stack about two feet away, close enough that there is tension on the cable in the start position.
Grasp the machine frame with both hands at chest height for support and stability, and keep your standing leg's knee slightly bent.
Hinge forward very slightly at the hips, brace your abs, and keep your spine neutral, with the working leg starting slightly in front and a soft bend in the knee.
Keeping the working leg fairly straight, contract your glute to sweep the leg back and up in a smooth semicircular arc, leading with the heel.
Drive the leg back only as far as you can without arching your lower back or rotating your hips, exhaling as you kick and keeping the motion controlled rather than swinging.
Squeeze the glute hard for a one-second peak contraction at the top of the arc.
Slowly return the working leg forward, resisting the pull of the cable, until you reach the starting position without letting the weight stack rest.
Complete the prescribed reps on that leg, then detach and switch the cuff to the other ankle and repeat for the same number.
Common mistakes: arching the lower back to gain height, using momentum to swing the leg, and bending the knee so the hamstring takes over instead of the glute.

name: Open Palm Kettlebell Clean
instructions: Place a single kettlebell on the floor centered between your feet, standing with feet slightly wider than shoulder width and toes turned out a few degrees.
Hinge at the hips and bend the knees to grip the handle with both hands, keeping your chest up, spine flat, and shoulders packed down.
Brace your core, take a breath, and explosively extend through the legs and hips, driving the knees, hips, and ankles to launch the kettlebell straight up close to your body.
As the bell reaches chest height and becomes momentarily weightless, release your grip and open both palms, letting the bell flip so the ball rotates up and lands cradled in your open palms.
Absorb the catch by softening the knees, keeping the elbows close to the body and the bell balanced against the backs of the forearms.
To return the bell, toss it out and slightly forward so the handle rotates back down, and catch the handle with both hands as it descends.
Hinge at the hips with a flat back and guide the kettlebell back down between your feet to the floor under control, resetting your start position.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, keeping each rep explosive on the way up and controlled on the way down.
Common mistakes: letting the bell swing out in a wide forward arc rather than rising vertically, catching with clenched fists so the bell jars the wrists, and rounding the back when lowering.

name: Otis-Up
instructions: Sit on the floor and anchor your feet under a heavy object or a loaded barbell, or have a partner hold them, bending your knees to roughly 90 degrees.
Lie back on the floor with your knees bent and feet flat and secured.
Hold a weight plate or dumbbell with both hands against your chest, elbows tucked; this is your starting position.
Brace your core and take a breath, then initiate the movement by flexing the spine and hips to curl and raise your torso up off the floor toward your knees.
As your torso rises through the top portion, press the weight up and out so it travels overhead at full sit-up, arms extending toward the ceiling.
Exhale as you press, finishing with your torso upright and the weight locked out above your head.
Reverse the motion by pulling the weight back to your chest, then lower your torso under control toward the floor.
Stop just short of your shoulders touching down so tension stays on the abs, then begin the next rep.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, keeping the movement smooth and avoiding jerking the weight to gain momentum.
Common mistakes: using the arm press to yank yourself up rather than the abs, relaxing fully at the bottom and losing tension, and straining the neck instead of curling the torso.

name: Overhead Cable Curl
instructions: Set the two high pulleys of a dual cable column to a height above your shoulders, attach a single handle to each side, and load the same moderate weight on both stacks.
Stand in the exact center between the two columns with your feet shoulder-width apart and your body squarely aligned between the handles.
Grab one handle in each hand with an underhand (supinated) grip, palms facing up toward the ceiling.
Step into position so your arms are extended out to the sides and roughly parallel to the floor, with tension on both cables, keeping your chest up and core braced.
Keep your upper arms fixed in this raised, parallel position throughout so that only the forearms move.
Exhale and curl both hands toward the sides of your head by flexing the elbows, squeezing the biceps until your forearms approach your biceps.
Pause and squeeze the biceps hard at peak contraction with the cables drawing your hands inward.
Inhale and slowly straighten your arms back to the fully extended starting position, resisting the cables throughout.
Keep the rest of your body completely stationary, not letting the upper arms drop or the torso sway.
Repeat for the prescribed reps. Common mistakes: letting the elbows drift down or forward, leaning side to side, and rushing the eccentric instead of controlling it.

name: Overhead Lat
instructions: Sit upright on the floor with good posture and your partner kneeling or standing behind you.
Raise one arm straight up overhead, then bend the elbow so your hand reaches down behind your head toward the middle of your upper back.
Have your partner support the arm by holding your triceps with one hand and your wrist with the other; this is your starting position.

Keeping your spine tall and not arching the lower back, gently attempt to pull your upper arm down to your side while your partner resists, holding the arm in place so nothing moves, in an isometric contraction.
Hold this gentle contraction for 10 to 20 seconds while breathing steadily.
Relax the arm fully and exhale, then let your partner apply slow, gentle pressure to the triceps to ease the elbow further back and deepen the stretch along the lat and side of the torso.
Hold the deepened stretch for 10 to 20 seconds, staying relaxed and never forcing past mild tension.
Lower the arm, then switch and repeat the same sequence on the other side.
Common mistakes: arching the lower back to gain range, pushing into pain rather than a mild stretch, and the partner moving too fast or too forcefully.

name: Overhead Slam
instructions: Choose a non-bouncing or dead-ball medicine ball you can slam explosively, and clear open floor directly in front of you.
Stand tall with your feet about shoulder-width apart, knees soft, and weight balanced over the midfoot.
Hold the ball with both hands at chest height, fingers spread around the sides, and brace your core; this is your starting position.
Begin the countermovement by reaching the ball straight overhead, fully extending your arms and body and rising onto the balls of your feet for maximum stretch.
Inhale during the wind-up to fill and brace your trunk.
Forcefully exhale and reverse the motion, driving the lats and snapping the hips and spine into flexion to throw the ball straight down into the floor a foot in front of you as hard as possible.
Follow through so your hands finish low near knee height, keeping the back flat rather than rounding to reach down.
Catch the ball on the bounce with both hands, or pick it up if using a dead ball, hinging at the hips to absorb it, and immediately reset.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, keeping every slam maximally explosive.
Common mistakes: slamming with the arms only instead of the lats and trunk, rounding the lower back to follow through, and throwing too far forward so you chase the ball.

name: Overhead Squat
instructions: Start with an empty or lightly loaded barbell, since this lift demands shoulder and ankle mobility; build load slowly. Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder width and toes turned out about 20 to 30 degrees.
Grip the bar with a wide (snatch-width) overhand grip, hands well outside the shoulders so that with arms overhead the bar sits comfortably back over your head.

Bring the bar to your front rack or press it from the floor, then press and lock it directly overhead with arms fully extended, elbows locked, and the bar stacked over the midfoot and slightly behind the head.
Pull your shoulder blades together, keep your head neutral with eyes forward, set a tall braced torso, and feel the bar pressing up while the shoulders stay packed; this is your starting position.
Take a deep breath into your belly and brace your core hard to support the spine under the overhead load.
Begin the descent by pushing your hips back and bending the knees, keeping the knees tracking over the toes and the torso as upright as possible.
Descend until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor, or deeper if mobility allows, keeping the bar locked out directly over the midfoot the entire time and the chest up.
Drive back up through the heels and midfoot, extending the hips and knees together while keeping the bar pinned overhead, exhaling as you pass the hardest part and stand fully tall.
Reset your breath and brace at the top, then repeat for the prescribed reps.
Common mistakes: the bar drifting forward of the midfoot, the chest collapsing forward, the heels lifting, and the elbows bending and losing the overhead lockout.

name: Overhead Stretch
instructions: Stand tall with your feet about hip-width apart, weight evenly balanced, and your posture upright.
Lace your fingers together in front of you, then rotate your palms to face away and turn them up toward the ceiling.
Keeping your shoulders pressed down away from your ears, extend both arms straight overhead until you feel a stretch through the sides, chest, lats, and forearms.
Gently draw your tailbone down and brace your torso so you lengthen the spine rather than arching the lower back.
Reach a little higher through the fingertips to elongate the front and back of the torso, breathing slowly and steadily.
Hold the stretch for 20 to 30 seconds, staying at a mild, comfortable tension.
Lower the arms under control and relax. Common mistakes: shrugging the shoulders up to the ears, and over-arching the lower back instead of stabilizing the trunk.

name: Overhead Triceps
instructions: Sit upright on the floor with good posture and your partner kneeling or standing behind you.
Raise one arm straight up overhead, then bend the elbow so your hand drops down behind your head toward your upper back.
Have your partner support your arm by holding your elbow with one hand and your wrist with the other; this is your starting position.
