Take a breath and brace, then lower the bar under control to your lower chest or upper stomach, keeping the bar, wrist, and elbow stacked in a vertical line and your elbows tucked rather than flared.
Pause briefly when the bar touches your torso, then drive it up explosively against the easing band assistance, keeping the elbows tucked until lockout.
Lock out fully at the top while maintaining your arch and tight upper back, then repeat for reps before carefully racking the bar.

name: Reverse Band Box Squat
instructions: Set up inside a power rack with a box positioned behind you at a height that puts your hip crease at or just below knee level when you sit on it.

Anchor bands to the band pegs or the top of the rack so they hang directly above the bar, then attach the lower ends to the bar; the bands should de-load the bar most at the bottom and least at the top.

Step under the bar and place it across your upper back on the rear delts and traps, squeezing your shoulder blades together and rotating your elbows forward as if trying to bend the bar across your shoulders.

Unrack the bar by standing it up, create a tight arch in your lower back, and step back into position over the box. Set your feet wide for more back, glute, adductor, and hamstring emphasis, or closer for more quad emphasis, with toes turned out slightly. Keep your head facing forward.
Brace your core hard and take a breath. Initiate by pushing your knees out and sitting your hips back, descending under control against the band tension.
Sit back until you are fully seated on the box with your shins roughly perpendicular to the ground, pausing momentarily and relaxing the hip flexors without rocking or bouncing off the box.
Keep the weight on your heels, your feet and knees pushed out, and your whole body tight while seated.
Drive explosively up off the box, leading with your head and chest, pushing the floor away as the bands add resistance near the top.
Stand to full lockout maintaining head-to-toe tightness, then repeat, taking care to re-rack the bar safely when finished.

name: Reverse Band Deadlift
instructions: Set a barbell on the floor inside a power rack and attach bands to the top of the rack using band pegs or the frame, then connect the lower ends to the bar so the bands assist the lift most off the floor and least at lockout.
Step up so the bar is centered over your midfoot, with your feet about hip-width apart.
Hinge at the hips and bend down to grip the bar just outside your legs at about shoulder width, letting your shoulder blades protract; use a double-overhand grip, or a mixed grip on heavier sets.
With your grip and feet set, take a big breath, lower your hips, and bend your knees until your shins touch the bar.
Set your back flat and arched, chest up, and head looking forward, taking the slack out of the bar so it is loaded against your body.
Drive through your heels and push the floor away, extending the hips and knees together to move the weight upward while keeping the bar dragging close to your legs.
Once the bar passes your knees, aggressively pull it back by driving your hips forward into the bar and pulling your shoulder blades together to reach a tall lockout.
Finish standing fully upright with glutes squeezed, without leaning back or overextending the lower back.
Lower the bar by hinging at the hips first, then bending the knees, guiding it back down to the floor under control against the band tension, then reset and repeat.

name: Reverse Band Power Squat
instructions: Set up inside a power rack with the bar and safety pins at the appropriate height and the bar loaded.

Attach bands to the top of the rack via pegs or the frame so they hang directly above the bar, then connect the lower ends to the bar; the bands will de-load the bar most at the bottom of the squat and least at the top.
Step under the bar and place it across your upper back, squeezing your shoulder blades together and rotating your elbows forward as if to bend the bar across your shoulders.

Unrack the bar by standing it up, create a tight arch in your lower back, and step back into position. Set your feet wide for more emphasis on the back, glutes, adductors, and hamstrings, with toes turned out. Keep your head facing forward.
Brace your core and back hard, take a breath, then begin the descent by pushing your knees out and sitting your hips back as far as possible against the band tension.
Keep the bar tracking over your heels; with a lower bar placement, allow a greater forward torso lean to stay balanced, and keep shins as vertical as you can.
Descend until you break parallel, meaning the crease of your hip drops below the top of your knee, without letting your knees cave or your lower back round.
Drive upward out of the hole, keeping the weight on your heels and pushing your feet and knees out while leading the movement with your head and chest.
Continue up to full standing lockout, maintaining head-to-toe tightness, then repeat and re-rack carefully when done.

name: Reverse Band Sumo Deadlift
instructions: Set a loaded barbell on the floor inside a power rack and attach bands to the top of the rack using pegs or the frame, then connect the lower ends to the bar so the bands give the most assistance off the floor.
Approach the bar so it intersects the middle of your feet, then set a very wide sumo stance with your feet pointed out and nearly reaching the collars.
Hinge straight down at the hips and grip the bar inside your legs with arms hanging directly below your shoulders; use a double-overhand, mixed, or hook grip.
Relax and lengthen your arms by letting the shoulders drop, keep your chest up, back flat and arched, and your head looking forward.
Take a breath and brace, lower your hips into position, and pull the slack out of the bar so it is loaded against your weight.
Drive through the floor by spreading your feet apart and pushing the ground away, keeping your weight on the back half of your feet as you extend the hips and knees together.
As the bar passes your knees, lean back and drive your hips forward into the bar while pulling your shoulder blades together to reach a tall lockout.
Stand fully upright with glutes squeezed and knees and hips locked, without overextending the lower back.
Return the weight to the ground by hinging at the hips and controlling the descent against the band tension, then reset your stance and repeat.

name: Reverse Barbell Curl
instructions: Stand tall with your feet about shoulder-width apart, knees soft, core braced, and a neutral upright spine.
Grip a barbell with a pronated (overhand) grip, palms facing down, hands about shoulder-width apart.
Let the bar hang at thigh level with your arms extended and your elbows pinned close to your sides. This is your starting position.
Keeping your upper arms stationary and elbows fixed against your torso, exhale and curl the bar upward by flexing the elbows, moving only the forearms.
Continue until the bar reaches shoulder level and your biceps and forearm extensors are fully contracted, keeping the wrists firm and straight rather than letting them drop.
Hold the top position for a moment and squeeze the muscles, avoiding any swinging of the body or torso to heave the weight up.
Inhale and slowly lower the bar back to the starting position under control, fully extending the arms.
Use a lighter load than a standard curl since the pronated grip is weaker, and repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Reverse Barbell Preacher Curls
instructions: Set the preacher bench so the top of the pad sits at about armpit height when you are seated; sit down with your chest pressed lightly against the back of the pad and your feet flat on the floor for stability.
Take an EZ-curl bar with a pronated (palms-down) grip on the angled inner sections, hands about shoulder-width apart so your wrists sit in a comfortable, slightly angled position.
Rest the backs of your upper arms flat along the slanted pad, armpits near the top edge, so the arms cannot drift up or off the pad during the set.
Lower the bar until your elbows are nearly fully extended and you feel a stretch in the biceps and forearm flexors; keep a slight soft bend to protect the elbow joint. This is your starting position.
Brace your core, keep your shoulders down, and exhale as you curl the bar upward using the biceps and forearm extensors, keeping the wrists firm and straight rather than letting them flop back.
Curl until your forearms are roughly vertical and the bar reaches about shoulder height; squeeze the biceps hard at the top for a one-second pause.
Inhale and lower the bar slowly under control over about two to three seconds back to the fully stretched starting position, resisting the weight the whole way.
Keep the upper arms glued to the pad and avoid swinging the torso or shrugging the shoulders to heave the weight up.
Common mistake: going too heavy and letting the wrists collapse or the elbows lift off the pad. Use a weight lighter than a normal curl since the pronated grip is weaker.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, then set the bar down or rack it carefully without jerking your arms straight.

name: Reverse Cable Curl
instructions: Attach a straight or EZ bar to the low pulley of a cable machine and set the pulley to its lowest position.
Stand facing the machine, feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly soft, and grip the bar with a pronated (palms-down) grip at about shoulder width.
Step back just enough so the cable has tension at the bottom, stand tall with your chest up, shoulders back, and core braced.
Pin your elbows close to your sides and keep your upper arms locked against your torso; let your arms hang so the bar rests near your thighs. This is the starting position.
Keeping the wrists straight and firm, exhale and curl the bar upward by contracting the biceps and forearm extensors, moving only the forearms.
Continue until the bar reaches roughly chest or shoulder level and the biceps are fully contracted; hold and squeeze for a one-second count.
Inhale and slowly lower the bar back to the starting position over about two seconds, controlling the cable's pull and keeping tension on the muscle.
Do not swing your torso, lean back, or let your elbows drift forward or out; the upper arms stay stationary throughout.
Common mistake: letting the wrists bend backward under load. Keep the knuckles pointing up and wrists neutral to protect the forearm tendons.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Reverse Crunch
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your legs extended and your arms resting alongside your torso, palms flat on the floor for stability.
Press your lower back gently into the floor and brace your abdominals; your arms and hands stay planted throughout to anchor your upper body.
Lift your legs and bend your knees to about 90 degrees so your thighs are perpendicular to the floor and your shins are roughly parallel to it. This is the starting position.
Exhale and curl your knees toward your chest by rolling your pelvis backward and lifting your hips off the floor, using your lower abdominals rather than momentum.
Continue until your knees travel toward your chest and your hips are clearly off the mat; pause and squeeze the abs for a one-second count at the top.
Inhale and slowly lower your hips and legs back to the starting position under control, stopping before your lower back arches off the floor.
Keep the movement controlled and driven by the abs; do not swing the legs or kick to generate momentum.
Common mistake: pushing down through the hands to lever the hips up. Let the abdominal contraction roll the pelvis instead.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Reverse Flyes
instructions: Set an incline bench to roughly a 30 to 45 degree angle and grab a pair of light dumbbells.
Lie face-down (prone) on the bench with your chest and stomach pressed against the pad and your head just past the top edge so it is not jammed into the bench.
Plant the balls of your feet on the floor behind you for stability and let the dumbbells hang straight down with a neutral grip, palms facing each other.
Set a slight, fixed bend in your elbows and gently retract your shoulder blades; brace your core and avoid arching your lower back. This is the starting position.
Exhale and raise the dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc, leading with your elbows and squeezing your shoulder blades together to drive the rear delts.
Lift until your arms are roughly parallel to the floor and in line with your shoulders; pause and hold the squeeze for a one-second count.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells slowly along the same arc back to the starting position, keeping tension on the rear delts.
Maintain the same slight elbow bend the entire set; do not let the arms straighten and turn it into a stiff-arm raise.
Common mistake: shrugging the traps or using momentum. Keep the neck relaxed, traps down, and use a light weight you can control.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Reverse Flyes With External Rotation
instructions: Set an incline bench to about a 30 degree angle and select a pair of light dumbbells.
Lie face-down (prone) on the bench with your chest and stomach pressed to the pad and your head just past the top edge.

Plant the balls of your feet on the floor with your heels lifted, and hold the dumbbells hanging below you with a pronated (palms-down) grip; arms hang nearly perpendicular to the bench with a slight bend in the elbows. This is the starting position.
Brace your core, keep your shoulder blades slightly retracted, and exhale as you raise the dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc led by the elbows.
As you lift, rotate your wrists about 90 degrees so your grip turns from palms-down (pronated) to palms facing each other (neutral), externally rotating the shoulders.
Continue raising until your arms reach about head level, squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top for a one-second count.
Inhale and reverse the motion slowly, rotating the wrists back to palms-down as you lower the dumbbells along the same arc to the start.
Keep the slight elbow bend fixed and let the movement happen at the shoulder; do not bend or straighten the elbows to cheat the weight up.
Common mistake: using too much weight, which kills the external rotation and recruits the traps. Stay light and controlled.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Reverse Grip Bent-Over Rows
instructions: Load a barbell and stand tall holding it with a supinated (palms-up) grip, hands about shoulder-width apart.
Set your feet hip- to shoulder-width apart with a slight bend in the knees and your weight back toward your heels.
Hinge forward at the hips, pushing your hips back and keeping your back flat and chest up, until your torso is roughly 45 degrees to almost parallel with the floor.
Let the bar hang straight down from your shoulders with arms perpendicular to the floor; keep your head in a neutral line with your spine. This is the starting position.
Brace your core and exhale as you row the bar up toward your lower abdomen, driving your elbows down and back close to your body.
Pull until the bar nears your lower belly and your shoulder blades squeeze together; hold the contraction for a one-second count.
Inhale and lower the bar slowly under control back to the fully extended starting position, keeping the torso angle fixed.
Keep the back flat and torso stationary throughout; do not jerk upright or use leg drive to swing the weight.
Common mistake: rounding the lower back or letting the bar drift forward. Keep the bar tracking close to the thighs and the spine neutral.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, then stand up by hinging at the hips and set the bar down with a flat back.

name: Reverse Grip Triceps Pushdown
instructions: Attach a straight or EZ bar to the high pulley of a cable machine and select your weight.
Face the machine with your feet about shoulder-width apart and grip the bar with a supinated (palms-up) grip at about shoulder width.

Pull the bar down by your sides until your arms are fully extended and your elbows are pinned tight against your torso; stand tall with a slight forward lean and core braced. This is the starting position.
Keep your upper arms and elbows locked stationary at your sides throughout the entire movement.
Inhale and let the bar rise under control, allowing only your forearms to move until the bar reaches about chest level and your triceps are stretched.
Exhale and push the bar back down by extending the elbows, contracting the triceps hard until your arms are fully straight.
Squeeze the triceps for a one-second count at the bottom, keeping the wrists straight and firm.
Do not let the elbows flare out or drift forward, and avoid leaning your bodyweight onto the bar to push it down.
Common mistake: using too much weight so the elbows lift and it becomes a pressing motion. Lighten the load to keep the elbows pinned.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Reverse Hyperextension
instructions: Load the reverse hyperextension machine with an appropriate weight and position the foot pads or roller for the swinging carriage.
Lie face-down on the top pad with your hips at the back edge so your legs hang off and can swing freely below.
Place your feet between or against the pads or rollers and grasp the front handles firmly to anchor your upper body.
Let your legs hang down and slightly forward under the platform so the hips are flexed; this is the starting position.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes as you extend your hips, swinging your legs back and up in a controlled arc.
Raise the legs until your body forms roughly a straight line, stopping short of overextending or arching the lower back.
Pause briefly at the top with the glutes and hamstrings contracted, exhaling through the effort.
Inhale and lower the legs slowly under control back to the hanging start position, letting the hips flex forward again.
Common mistake: hyperextending the lumbar spine and using momentum to fling the legs. Keep the motion smooth and stop at the straight-line position.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, keeping a firm grip on the handles throughout.

name: Reverse Lunge
instructions: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, chest up, shoulders back, and core braced; let your arms hang at your sides or place hands on hips for balance.
Keep your gaze forward and your weight balanced over the middle of your front foot before you begin.
Take a controlled step backward with one foot, landing on the ball of that rear foot while keeping most of your weight on the front leg.
Lower your body straight down by bending both knees until each reaches roughly a 90 degree angle; the rear knee should hover just above the floor.
Keep your front shin close to vertical, front knee tracking over the toes, and your torso upright with a tall chest.
Exhale and drive forcefully through the front heel to push yourself back up to the standing start position, bringing the rear foot back to meet the front.
Inhale as you descend and keep the movement controlled; avoid letting the front knee cave inward.
Common mistake: leaning the torso too far forward or letting the front knee drift past the toes. Keep the chest up and weight in the front heel.
Alternate legs each repetition, or complete all reps on one side first, repeating for the prescribed number.

name: Reverse Machine Flyes
instructions: Adjust the rear-delt (pec deck) machine handles fully to the rear so they start in front of your body, and select an appropriate weight.
Set the seat height so the handles align with shoulder level when you are seated.
Sit facing the pad with your chest against the back support, feet flat on the floor, and grasp the handles with a neutral grip, palms facing inward. This is the starting position.
Brace your core, keep your chest pressed to the pad, and maintain a slight fixed bend in your elbows.
Exhale and pull the handles out to your sides and back in a smooth semicircular arc, driving the movement from the shoulder joint and contracting the rear delts.
Continue until your arms are out to your sides and your shoulder blades squeeze together; pause at the rear for a one-second count.
Inhale and return the handles slowly under control to the starting position, keeping tension on the rear delts.
Keep the elbows at the same slight bend throughout and avoid yanking or using momentum to throw the handles back.
Common mistake: shrugging the traps or arching off the pad. Keep the chest pinned and the neck relaxed so the rear delts do the work.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Reverse Plank
instructions: Sit on the floor with your legs extended straight in front of you and your feet together.
Place your hands flat on the floor behind your hips, fingers pointing forward toward your feet, arms straight and shoulders stacked over the wrists.
Engage your glutes and core, then press through your palms and heels to lift your hips upward.
Raise the hips until your body forms a straight line from your head through your hips to your heels, with toes pointed or feet flat.
Squeeze your glutes hard, keep your chest open, and avoid letting the hips sag toward the floor.
Keep your neck in a neutral line with your spine, gazing upward or straight ahead, and breathe steadily throughout the hold.
Common mistake: dropping the hips or shrugging the shoulders up to the ears. Keep the hips lifted and pull the shoulders down and back.
Hold the position for the prescribed time, then lower the hips back to the floor under control.

name: Reverse Plate Curls
instructions: Select a weight plate and stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly soft, and core braced.
Grip the plate with both hands using a pronated grip with palms facing down or inward, grabbing it at roughly the 11 o'clock and 1 o'clock positions with fingers on one face and thumbs on the other.
Let your arms hang fully extended so the plate rests near your groin or upper thighs. This is the starting position.
Pin your elbows in close to your sides and keep your upper arms stationary throughout.
Exhale and curl the plate upward by contracting the biceps and forearms, keeping the wrists firm and the elbows tucked.
Continue until the plate is roughly aligned with your upper chest and your biceps and forearms are fully contracted; pause and squeeze for a one-second count.
Inhale and lower the plate slowly under control back to the starting position, resisting the descent.
Keep your torso upright and stationary; do not swing or lean back to heave the plate up.
Common mistake: letting the elbows flare out or drift forward. Keep them pinned to your ribs so the biceps and forearms stay loaded.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Reverse Triceps Bench Press
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a bench with your feet planted firmly on the floor, eyes roughly under the bar.
Grip the barbell with a close, supinated (palms-up) grip at about shoulder width; have a spotter assist or unrack carefully because this grip is less stable.
Lift the bar off the rack and hold it locked out straight over your chest with arms perpendicular to the floor. This is the starting position.
Brace your core, keep your shoulder blades retracted, and tuck your elbows in close to your torso throughout.
Inhale and lower the bar slowly toward your middle to lower chest, keeping the elbows tracking close to your sides to maximize triceps involvement.
Lower until the bar lightly touches the middle of your chest, then pause for a brief one-second count.
Exhale and press the bar back up by extending the elbows, driving primarily with the triceps until your arms are locked out again.
Use a controlled tempo, taking roughly twice as long to lower as to press up, and keep the wrists stacked over the elbows.
Common mistake: letting the elbows flare wide, which turns it into a chest press and strains the wrists. Keep elbows tucked and the grip secure.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, then carefully guide the bar back onto the rack when finished.

name: Rhomboids-SMR
instructions: Sit on the floor and place a foam roller on the ground behind you, then lie back so the roller sits under your upper back between the shoulder blades.
Cross your arms in front of your chest to protract (spread) your shoulder blades and expose the rhomboid and trap muscles to the roller.
Plant your feet flat on the floor and lift your hips off the ground so your bodyweight presses your upper back into the roller. This is the starting position.
Slowly roll back and forth over your middle and upper back by pushing through your feet, moving the roller a few inches at a time.
Shift your weight slightly to one side at a time to target the muscles along each side of the spine rather than rolling directly on the bones.
When you find a tender or tight spot, pause and hold the pressure there for 10 to 30 seconds, breathing steadily until the tension eases.
Keep your core gently engaged and avoid rolling onto your lower back or neck; stay over the upper-to-mid back region.
Continue for the desired duration, then lower your hips and remove the roller carefully.

name: Rickshaw Carry
instructions: Position the loaded rickshaw or farmer's frame at your starting point and stand in the center between the handles.
Set your feet about hip-width apart, centered so the load will be balanced on both sides.
Bend at the hips and knees to grip the handles firmly, keeping your back flat, chest up, and head in a neutral line.
Take a deep breath, brace your core hard, and drive through your heels to stand the frame up to lockout, keeping your shoulders back and spine neutral.
Once standing tall and stable, begin walking immediately with quick, short, controlled steps to keep the load from swinging.
Keep your chest up, head forward, traps and grip tight, and continue breathing in a steady rhythm as you move.
Maintain an upright, braced posture and avoid leaning excessively to either side; let the implement settle before each step.
Common mistake: taking long strides that let the load sway. Use fast, choppy steps and keep the frame controlled.
When you reach the end point, bend at the hips and knees with a flat back to set the frame down under control.

name: Rickshaw Deadlift
instructions: Load the rickshaw or deadlift frame with the desired weight and step into the center so you are positioned between the handles.
Set your feet about hip-width apart, centered within the frame so the load is balanced on both sides.
Bend at the hips to reach down and grip the handles, letting your shoulder blades protract slightly as you take hold.
With your feet and grip set, take a big breath, brace your core, lower your hips, and bend your knees into the start position.
Look forward, keep your chest up and your back flat and arched, and set your shoulders just in front of or over the handles.
Drive through your heels to push the floor away and lift the frame upward, keeping the load close to your body.
As the weight rises, pull your shoulder blades together and drive your hips forward to finish at a tall, locked-out standing position.
Inhale, then lower the weight under control by hinging at the hips and bending the knees, guiding the frame straight down to the ground with a flat back.
Common mistake: rounding the lower back or letting the hips shoot up first. Keep the chest up and drive hips and shoulders together.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, resetting your brace and position before each rep.

name: Ring Dips
instructions: Set a pair of gymnastic rings at roughly hip-to-shoulder height, spaced slightly wider than shoulder width and hanging from straps short enough that you can support yourself without your feet touching the ground.
Grip one ring in each hand with a neutral (palms-facing-in) grip, and turn the rings out so your thumbs point forward; this 'rings turned out' position keeps the shoulders stable.
Jump or press up to support yourself with both arms locked straight, elbows fully extended, rings pressed in tight against your hips or lower ribs.
Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and round your upper back slightly; keep your legs together or crossed at the ankles and lean your torso a few degrees forward to bias the chest and triceps.
Take a breath and brace, then lower under control by flexing the elbows, keeping them tracking back and slightly tucked rather than flaring straight out to the sides.
Continue descending until your shoulders drop below your elbows or your upper arms break past 90 degrees, fighting to keep the rings from drifting away from your body and avoiding any swinging.
Pause briefly at the bottom with the rings still pinned close, then drive back up by extending the elbows and pressing the rings down and in toward your hips.
As you near lockout, exhale and again turn the rings outward to finish stable and balanced, then reset before the next rep.
Common mistakes: letting the rings swing wide, dropping the shoulders too far forward, or bouncing out of the bottom. Keep every rep slow and owned. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

name: Rocket Jump
instructions: Stand tall in an open space with your feet about shoulder-width apart, toes pointing forward, and your weight balanced evenly across mid-foot.
Let your arms hang relaxed close to your body and set a neutral spine with your chest up and core lightly braced.
Initiate by dropping into a half squat: bend at the hips and knees, push your hips back slightly, and let your arms swing down and back behind you to load the jump.
Keep your heels down and knees tracking over your toes during this dip; do not collapse into a deep squat, a quarter-to-half depth is enough to load the legs.
Explode upward as forcefully as possible, extending the ankles, knees, and hips all at once (triple extension) while swinging your arms up overhead to drive height.
At the top, fully extend your entire body, reaching both arms straight overhead and stretching as tall as you can, like a rocket leaving the ground.
Spot your landing, then absorb the impact softly by landing on the balls of your feet first, rolling to flat, and immediately re-bending the hips and knees to cushion the force.
Common mistakes: landing with stiff, straight legs or letting the knees cave inward. Reset to a balanced stance before the next rep and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

name: Rocking Standing Calf Raise
instructions: Set a barbell in a squat rack at about upper-chest height and load it appropriately; performing this inside a rack is safest in case you need to re-rack quickly.
Step under the bar and place it across the meaty part of your upper back and rear shoulders, just below the base of your neck, gripping the bar with both hands a bit wider than shoulder width.
Unrack by driving up through your legs and straightening your torso, then take one or two steps back to clear the rack.
Set your feet in a shoulder-width stance with your toes pointed slightly outward; keep your head up and eyes forward, as looking down will shift you off balance.
Maintain a tall, straight back, brace your core, and keep a very slight, fixed bend in your knees throughout; the knees should never lock or bend further during the movement.
Exhale and raise your heels as high as possible by extending your ankles and squeezing your calves hard at the top, keeping the knees perfectly still.
Hold the fully contracted position for one second, feeling a strong calf contraction, then inhale and lower your heels slowly until you feel a deep stretch in the calves.
Now rock the other direction: lift your toes off the floor by contracting the shin (tibialis) muscles on the front of your lower leg as you exhale.
Hold this raised-toe position for a second, then lower the toes back down under control as you inhale. That heel-up then toe-up sequence is one full 'rocking' rep.
Common mistakes: bouncing through reps, bending the knees to cheat height, or rushing the stretch. Keep the tempo controlled and repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Rocky Pull-Ups/Pulldowns
instructions: Stand under a sturdy pull-up bar and grasp it with both palms facing forward (pronated grip) using a wide grip, hands noticeably wider than shoulder width.
Hang with both arms fully extended, then set your starting position by leaning your torso back roughly 30 degrees, arching your lower back slightly and sticking your chest out toward the bar.
Brace your core and pull your shoulder blades down and back to engage the lats before you start moving.
For the front portion, exhale and pull your torso up by driving the upper arms and shoulders down and back until the bar touches your upper chest; squeeze the back hard at the top.
Keep the forearms relaxed (they should only grip, not curl), and let only the arms move while the torso travels through space without excessive swinging.
After a one-second squeeze, inhale and lower slowly back to a full dead hang with arms extended and lats fully stretched.
For the back portion, repeat the pull but this time keep your torso more upright and lean your head slightly forward so the bar travels to touch the back of your neck.
Use that slight forward head lean to clear the bar safely behind your neck; do not yank or jerk, keep the path smooth and controlled.
Lower under control back to a full hang. One front-of-neck pull plus one behind-neck pull together count as the alternating 'Rocky' sequence.
Common mistakes: kipping or swinging for momentum and using too much load on the behind-neck portion. Keep both halves strict and repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Romanian Deadlift
instructions: Set a loaded barbell on the floor in front of you (or take it out of a rack at hip height); standing on a low platform can allow a deeper range of motion if desired.
Grip the bar with a pronated (palms-down) grip slightly wider than shoulder width; use wrist straps if grip is limiting on heavier sets.
Stand tall holding the bar at arm's length against the front of your thighs, feet about hip-width apart, toes forward, weight balanced over mid-foot.
Set your starting position: chest up, shoulders pulled back, lats engaged to keep the bar close, and a slight, fixed bend in the knees with the shins kept vertical.
Take a deep breath into your belly and brace your core hard; this intra-abdominal pressure protects your spine throughout the lift.
Begin the descent by pushing your hips straight back (hip hinge), letting your torso lower toward the floor while the knees stay only slightly bent, not squatting down.
Keep your back flat and arms straight, dragging the bar down close along your thighs and shins; lower only as far as your hamstring flexibility allows while keeping a neutral spine.
You should feel a strong stretch and tension in the hamstrings at the bottom; the bar typically reaches mid-shin to just below the knee.
Reverse the movement by driving your hips forward and squeezing the glutes to pull yourself back to a fully upright standing position, exhaling as you finish.

Common mistakes: rounding the lower back, letting the bar drift away from the legs, or turning it into a squat by bending the knees too much. Keep the bar close and the back flat, then repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Romanian Deadlift from Deficit
instructions: Stand on a raised platform, low box, or stacked plates a few inches high to increase the range of motion at the bottom of the lift.
Take a loaded barbell at arm's length in front of you with a pronated (palms-down) grip just outside shoulder width; use straps if grip fails before the hamstrings do.
Set your stance hip-width on the platform, toes forward, with the bar resting against the front of your thighs and weight balanced over mid-foot.
Establish a tall starting posture: chest up, shoulders back, lats tight to keep the bar close, and your spine in firm, neutral extension.
Take a deep breath, brace your core hard, and put a slight, fixed bend in your knees while keeping the shins fairly vertical.
Begin by flexing the knees slightly, then hinge at the hips, pushing your butt back as far as possible to lower the torso toward the floor.
Lower the bar dragging close along the legs as far as your flexibility allows; because you are elevated, you can descend deeper, feeling heavy tension build in the hamstrings.
Keep the back in absolute extension the entire time; never let it round, especially in the deepened bottom range where the stretch is greatest.
Reverse the motion by driving the hips forward and squeezing the glutes to return to a fully upright standing position, exhaling as you lock out.
Common mistakes: chasing extra depth by rounding the spine or letting the bar swing forward. Only go as deep as you can hold a flat back, then repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Rope Climb
instructions: Stand at the base of a securely anchored climbing rope and reach up to grab it with both hands stacked above your head, dominant hand on top.
Pull down firmly on the rope and take a small jump or pull to get your body off the ground and create initial tension.
Secure your feet using a foot lock: drape the rope along the outside of one leg and across the top of one foot, then pinch it down with the other foot to clamp it in place.
With the rope locked between your feet, you can stand on it to support your weight; reach as high as possible with both arms and grip tightly.
Pull yourself upward with your arms while simultaneously releasing the foot lock, driving your knees up toward your chest to gain height.
Re-secure your feet on the rope by re-pinching it between them at the new, higher position, then stand up on that foot lock to push yourself even higher.
Reach up again to take a new high hand hold, and repeat the pull-up, knee-tuck, re-lock, and stand sequence to climb steadily toward the top.
Keep your core braced and minimize swinging; rely on your legs to bear weight between pulls so your arms and grip last longer.
To descend, loosen the pinch of your feet on the rope and slide down in a controlled hand-over-hand motion, gripping firmly to manage your speed and protect your hands.
Common mistakes: climbing with arms only and skipping the foot lock, or sliding down too fast and burning the hands. Use the legs and control the descent.

name: Rope Crunch
instructions: Attach a rope handle to a high pulley on a cable stack and select an appropriate weight.
Kneel on the floor or a pad about one to two feet in front of and below the pulley, with your knees set hip-width for a stable base.
Grasp the rope with both hands and bring them down so they rest on either side of your head, near your ears or against the sides of your face; hold the rope there throughout.
Set your torso upright with hips fixed and a slight tension already in the cable pulling you up; this is the starting position.
Brace your abs and keep your hips stationary; this movement comes from flexing the spine, not from sitting back at the hips or pulling with the arms.
Exhale and crunch by flexing at the spine, rounding your upper back and bringing your rib cage down toward your pelvis as you pull the cable down with your trunk.
Aim to draw your elbows toward your thighs while keeping the hands fixed by your head, squeezing the abs hard at the bottom of the motion.
Pause at the fully contracted bottom position for a moment, feeling the abs work, then inhale and slowly uncurl back to the upright starting position under control.
To target the obliques, add a slight twist toward one knee as you crunch, or perform the set angled to one side.

Common mistakes: pulling the rope with the arms, swinging from the hips, or letting the weight yank you up too fast. Keep the motion a controlled spinal crunch and repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Rope Jumping
instructions: Choose a jump rope sized correctly: stand on the middle of the rope and the handles should reach roughly to your armpits or just below the shoulders.
Hold one handle in each hand with a relaxed grip, elbows close to your sides and forearms pointing slightly outward, and let the rope rest on the floor behind your heels.
Stand tall with feet together or hip-width, knees softly bent, core lightly braced, and your gaze forward.
Begin the turn by rotating the rope from your wrists, not your whole arms, swinging it up over your head and bringing it down toward the floor in front of you.
As the rope approaches your feet, perform a small, light hop just an inch or two off the ground, landing softly on the balls of your feet to clear the rope.
Keep the jumps low and quick; you only need to clear the rope, not jump high, which conserves energy and reduces joint impact.
Establish a steady, repeatable turning rhythm you can sustain, letting the wrists do the work while keeping the upper arms still.
Stay tall with a neutral spine and absorb each landing through the ankles and knees; avoid landing flat-footed or with locked legs.
Once comfortable, introduce variety with different speeds, alternating feet, or double-unders to challenge coordination and raise intensity.
Common mistakes: jumping too high, turning with the whole arm, or tensing the shoulders. Keep it light, low, and wrist-driven.

name: Rope Straight-Arm Pulldown
instructions: Attach a rope to a high pulley on a cable stack and select your working weight.
Stand a couple of feet back from the pulley with your feet staggered (one foot slightly ahead) for a stable, balanced base.
Grasp the rope with both hands using a neutral grip, palms facing each other, with your arms extended up and forward toward the pulley.
Hinge forward slightly from the hips with a flat back, brace your core, and keep a soft, fixed bend in the elbows that you will maintain the entire set; this is the starting position.
Keeping your arms straight (elbows fixed), initiate by driving the shoulders into extension, pulling the rope down in an arc toward your thighs.
Lead the movement with your lats rather than your arms or triceps; think about pushing the rope down and back using the muscles of your back.
As you reach the bottom near your thighs, spread the rope slightly apart and squeeze your lats hard, pausing for a moment in the fully contracted position.
Return slowly along the same arc to the starting position overhead, resisting the weight and stopping just before the stack fully rests so tension stays on the lats.

Common mistakes: bending the elbows to turn it into a triceps pushdown, rounding the back, or using momentum. Keep the arms locked-out straight and move from the shoulders. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

name: Round The World Shoulder Stretch
instructions: Stand up straight with your legs together and posture tall, holding a light body bar, broomstick, or dowel.
Position the bar behind your hips, gripping it with both hands wider than shoulder width, palms facing down (knuckles back) and thumbs pointing outward.
Set your core lightly so your lower back does not over-arch, and keep your chest open with shoulders relaxed down away from your ears.
Slowly raise the bar upward and behind you in a smooth arc, keeping your arms as straight as comfortable, lifting it up toward and over your head.
Move gradually and only go as far as your shoulder mobility allows; you should feel a gentle stretch across the front of the shoulders, chest, and biceps, never sharp pain.
Do not force the range of motion; if it becomes difficult to lift further, simply hold at that point and breathe.
Hold the stretch briefly at your comfortable end range, then slowly lower the bar back down behind your hips under control.
Common mistakes: arching the lower back to fake more range, using a grip too narrow, or jerking the bar up. Keep it slow, controlled, and within a pain-free range.

name: Rowing, Stationary
instructions: Sit down on the rowing machine's seat and place your feet on the foot pedals with your heels resting comfortably against the base of the pedals.
Secure the foot straps snugly across the balls of your feet so your feet stay anchored throughout the stroke.
Take hold of the handle with both hands using an overhand grip, and select your program or resistance/damper setting if applicable.

Sit up tall, brace your core, and assume the catch position: slide forward so your knees are bent and drawn up toward your chest, shins roughly vertical, torso leaning slightly forward from the hips with a flat back and arms extended.
Begin the drive by pushing hard against the foot pedals to extend your legs first; this is the main power source, so initiate with the legs, not the arms or back.
As your legs near full extension, lean your torso back slightly past vertical, then finish by pulling the handle into your upper abdominal area while squeezing your shoulder blades back.
Sequence the drive as legs, then back, then arms; protect your spine by powering primarily through the legs and hips rather than yanking with the lower back.
Begin the recovery by reversing the order: first extend the arms forward, then hinge the torso forward from the hips, then bend the knees to slide back toward the catch.
Glide smoothly back into the starting catch position and repeat, keeping a steady rhythm where the drive is powerful and the recovery is controlled and relaxed.
Common mistakes: opening the back too early, pulling with the arms first, or rounding the spine. Keep the legs-back-arms order on the drive.

name: Runner's Stretch
instructions: Start from a standing position, then step one leg straight back behind you, keeping both feet pointing forward.
Slowly lower your torso down toward the floor by bending the front knee and lowering into a deep lunge, controlling the descent.
Keep the front heel planted flat on the floor; if the heel lifts up, slide your back leg further back until the front heel can stay grounded.
Place both hands on the floor on either side of your front foot to support and stabilize your body.
Keep your front shin roughly vertical and your back leg long, feeling a stretch begin in the hip flexor of the rear leg.
To deepen the stretch, push your hips and butt up toward the ceiling, straightening the front leg somewhat to target the hamstring and glute of the front leg.
Then gradually lower your hips back down toward the floor to return tension to the hip flexor of the back leg, rocking gently between the two positions.
Breathe slowly and ease into each end range rather than bouncing, holding each comfortable stretch point for several seconds.
Common mistakes: letting the front heel pop up or bouncing aggressively. Keep the heel down and the movement smooth, then switch sides and repeat.

name: Running, Treadmill
instructions: Step onto the treadmill deck, standing on the side rails first, and use the menu to select a manual setting or a preset program.
Enter your age and weight if prompted so the machine can estimate calories burned, and set your desired incline/elevation to adjust intensity.
Clip the emergency stop safety cord to your clothing so the belt halts immediately if you stumble or move too far back.
Start the belt at a slow walking pace and step onto the moving belt, getting a feel for the speed before increasing it.
Gradually raise the speed to your target running pace, settling into a comfortable, sustainable stride near the middle of the belt.
Maintain proper running posture: stand tall with chest up, shoulders relaxed, a slight forward lean from the ankles, and arms swinging naturally at about 90 degrees.
Land softly with a midfoot strike under your hips and keep your stride relaxed; avoid overstriding far out in front of your body.
Only hold the handrails when necessary, such as when checking your heart rate or dismounting; running while gripping the rails ruins your form and reduces the benefit.
To finish, gradually reduce the speed to a walk for a cool-down before stepping off, then carefully dismount onto the side rails once the belt has slowed or stopped.
Common mistakes: drifting to the back of the belt, slouching, or clutching the handrails the whole time. Stay tall and centered.

name: Russian Twist
instructions: Sit on the floor and anchor your feet, either tucked under a fixed object or held by a partner, with your knees bent at roughly a right angle.
Lean your upper body back to create an imaginary V-shape between your torso and thighs, balancing on your sit bones.
Extend your arms straight out in front of you, perpendicular to your torso, with your hands clasped together; this is the starting position.
Brace your core hard and keep your spine long and chest up; do not let your lower back round as you lean back.
Exhale and rotate your torso to the right, twisting from the trunk until your clasped arms are roughly parallel with the floor on that side.
Keep the movement coming from your obliques and trunk rotation, not just swinging the arms; your hips and legs stay relatively still.
Hold the contraction for a second, then return through the center and rotate to the left, applying the same controlled technique to that side.
Maintain the V-position and your back angle throughout; resist the urge to drop your torso upright between twists.
Common mistakes: rounding the lower back, moving only the arms while the torso stays put, or rushing the reps. Keep it slow and twist from the core. Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Sandbag Load
instructions: Set up the event by placing the sandbags (or loading implements) a set distance from the loading platform, typically around 50 feet away.
Approach the first sandbag and set your feet hip-to-shoulder width on either side of or just behind it for a stable base.
Hinge at the hips and bend the knees to get low, reaching your arms as far around and underneath the bag as possible to hug it tight against your body.
Brace your core and keep your back as flat as you can, then lift by extending powerfully through the hips and knees, hauling the awkward bag up high against your chest and forearms.
Because sandbags are unwieldy, expect the load to shift; keep it pinned to your torso and adjust your grip as needed. Shouldering is usually not allowed, so carry it hugged to the chest.
Once the bag is secured against your body, move as quickly as possible toward the platform, taking short powerful steps while keeping the bag high and your core tight.
At the platform, get your hips under the load and drive up explosively through the hips, knees, and ankles to lift the bag as high as possible.
Place the bag onto the platform and push it far enough on to ensure it is stable and will not fall back off.
Turn and return to the pile to retrieve the next sandbag, then repeat the lift, carry, and load sequence as fast as possible until the event is complete.
Common mistakes: rounding the back under the awkward load, letting the bag drift away from the chest, or failing to fully extend the hips at the platform. Keep the bag tight and drive with the legs.

name: Scapular Pull-Up
instructions: Set up a pull-up bar high enough that your feet clear the floor when hanging at full arm extension, or be ready to bend your knees behind you.
Reach up and grip the bar with a pronated (overhand) grip, hands roughly shoulder-width apart, with your thumbs wrapped around the bar.

Hang from the bar with your arms completely straight and elbows locked. Let your shoulders rise up toward your ears so your shoulder blades are fully elevated. This dead hang is your starting position.
Brace your core lightly and keep your legs and hips relaxed and still, so the motion comes only from your shoulder blades and not from your arms.
Without bending your elbows at all, depress and retract your shoulder blades, pulling them down and slightly together in a reverse-shrugging motion. This drives your body up just a few inches.
Exhale as you depress, imagining you are tucking your shoulder blades into your back pockets. Your chest should lift slightly and your collarbones widen.
Pause for one second at the top with your shoulders pulled fully down and away from your ears, feeling the contraction in your traps and around the shoulder blades.
Inhale and slowly let your shoulders rise back up to the fully elevated dead hang, controlling the descent rather than dropping.
Keep your elbows locked throughout. The most common mistake is bending the arms and turning this into a partial pull-up, which defeats the purpose of isolating the scapulae.
Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, keeping each rep slow and deliberate.

name: Scapular Push-Up
instructions: Begin in a high plank position with your hands flat on the floor directly under your shoulders, fingers pointing forward, and your arms fully straight with elbows locked.
Extend your legs straight back with your feet about hip-width apart, balancing on the balls of your feet.
Set your body in one straight line from head to heels: brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and avoid letting your hips sag or pike upward.
Keep your head in neutral alignment, gaze slightly ahead of your hands, and lock your elbows for the entire exercise. Your arms act as rigid posts.
Inhale and let your chest sink toward the floor by allowing your shoulder blades to squeeze together (retract). Your torso lowers only an inch or two as the scapulae pinch.
From that retracted position, exhale and push the floor away forcefully, spreading your shoulder blades apart (protraction) and rounding your upper back toward the ceiling.
At the top, your upper back should be slightly domed and you should feel the muscles along the side of your ribs (serratus anterior) engage.
Keep your elbows straight the whole time; the only movement is your shoulder blades gliding together and apart. Bending the elbows turns this into a regular push-up and removes the serratus focus.
Move slowly and with control, about one to two seconds in each direction, and repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Scapular Wall Slide
instructions: Stand facing a wall with your feet about six to twelve inches away from it, feet hip-width apart.

Place both forearms flat against the wall with your elbows bent to roughly 90 degrees, forming a 'W' shape: elbows down near rib height, hands up, with the pinkie edges and forearms pressed into the wall.
Set your posture: stand tall, brace your core, tuck your ribs down, and avoid arching your lower back or letting your chin jut forward.
Gently pull your shoulder blades down and together to start, keeping both forearms and the backs of your hands in contact with the wall.
Slowly slide your forearms upward along the wall, straightening your arms overhead into a 'Y' shape while keeping the forearms, wrists, and hands pressed against the wall the entire time.
Exhale as you slide up. Reach only as high as you can while maintaining wall contact and without shrugging your shoulders up to your ears or arching your back.
Pause briefly at the top of the 'Y', feeling the muscles between and below your shoulder blades working.
Inhale and slowly slide your arms back down to the 'W' start, actively squeezing your shoulder blades down and together as you return.
Keep the movement smooth and controlled; the common mistakes are letting the arms peel off the wall, shrugging, or compensating by arching the lower back. Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Scissor Kick
instructions: Lie flat on your back on an exercise mat with your legs extended straight out and together.
Place your arms fully extended along your sides with palms facing down, or tuck your hands just under your glutes to support your lower back. Keep your arms still throughout.
Press your lower back firmly into the floor and brace your abdominals so there is no gap or arch under your lumbar spine. Maintaining this flat-back contact is the key to protecting your spine.
With a slight bend in your knees, lift both legs until your heels are about six inches off the ground. This is your starting position.
Keeping your core tight, raise your left leg up to about a 45-degree angle while simultaneously lowering your right leg until the heel is two to three inches from the floor.
Switch in a smooth, controlled scissoring motion: lower the left leg as you raise the right leg, passing the legs by each other without letting either touch down.
Breathe steadily and rhythmically throughout; do not hold your breath.

Keep the motion controlled and avoid swinging the legs wildly or letting your lower back lift off the mat. If your back starts to arch, raise both legs slightly higher to keep tension on the abs and pressure off the spine.
Continue alternating legs for the prescribed number of repetitions or time.

name: Scissors Jump
instructions: Start standing tall, then step one foot forward and one foot back into a lunge stance, keeping your feet about hip-width apart laterally for balance.
Lower into a lunge so the front knee is bent to roughly 90 degrees and tracks over the midline of the front foot, while the rear knee drops to nearly touch the ground.
Keep your torso upright, chest up, and core braced. Position your arms ready to swing, typically the opposite arm forward to the front leg.
Explode upward by extending forcefully through both legs, driving the floor away and swinging your arms up to generate as much lift as possible.
While airborne at the peak of the jump, quickly switch the position of your legs in the air, scissoring the front leg back and the rear leg forward.
Spot your landing and prepare your legs to absorb the impact.
Land softly back into the lunge stance with the opposite leg now in front, bending both knees to cushion the landing and immediately reload for the next jump.
Keep the front knee tracking over the foot and never let it cave inward; control the descent so your rear knee lightly approaches the floor rather than slamming it.
Move quickly and powerfully but with controlled landings, repeating for the prescribed repetitions and alternating legs each jump.

name: Seated Band Hamstring Curl
instructions: Anchor a resistance band low to the ground around a sturdy fixed object such as a rack upright or a heavy bench leg.
Place a flat bench a couple of feet away from the anchor point, positioned so the band line runs straight to the bench.
Sit on the bench facing away from the anchor and loop the band behind your ankles so it hooks against the backs of your heels.
Start with your legs extended straight out in front of you so the band is under tension. Sit tall and grip the edge of the bench for stability. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your thighs resting on the bench as the fixed point of the movement.
Exhale and flex your knees, curling your feet down and back toward the underside of the bench against the band's resistance.
You may need to lean your torso back slightly so your feet clear the floor as you curl; keep the movement coming from the knees, not from swinging the hips.
Squeeze your hamstrings hard at the fully bent position and pause for a second.
Inhale and slowly extend your knees back to the straight-leg starting position, resisting the band the whole way rather than letting it snap back.
Keep the motion controlled and avoid jerking; repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Seated Barbell Military Press
instructions: Set up a military press bench (an upright bench with a back pad) inside a rack, or have the loaded barbell racked at about shoulder height behind the bench.
Sit on the bench with your back firmly against the pad, feet flat on the floor and planted wide for a stable base, with a slight natural arch in your lower back.

Grip the bar with a pronated (overhand) grip slightly wider than shoulder width, so that when the bar is at shoulder level your forearms are vertical and form a 90-degree angle between forearm and upper arm.

Either have a spotter hand you the bar (easier on the rotator cuff) or carefully un-rack it yourself. Lift it overhead with arms locked, then hold it just in front of your head at about chin or shoulder level. This is your starting position.
Brace your core, keep your chest up, and keep your wrists straight and stacked over your elbows.
Inhale and lower the bar slowly and under control down to about collarbone level, keeping your elbows slightly forward of the bar.
Without bouncing or arching excessively, exhale and press the bar straight up overhead until your arms are fully extended and the bar is balanced over the back of your head.
Avoid leaning back into a decline-bench-press position or flaring the elbows straight out to the sides, both of which stress the shoulder joint.
Pause briefly at lockout, then lower under control for the next rep. Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, and carefully re-rack with a spotter's help when finished.

name: Seated Barbell Twist
instructions: Sit at the end of a flat bench with your torso upright and your feet planted flat on the floor about shoulder-width apart for a stable base.
Rest a light, unloaded or lightly loaded barbell across the tops of your thighs.
Grip the bar with a pronated (palms-down) grip, hands wider than shoulder width apart.

Carefully lift the barbell up and overhead until your arms are fully extended, then lower it behind your head so it rests across the base of your neck and the back of your shoulders. This is your starting position.
Sit tall with your chest up, core braced, and keep your head, hips, and feet stationary so the rotation comes only from your trunk.
Exhale and slowly twist your torso to one side, rotating from the waist so you feel your obliques contract on that side. Only rotate as far as feels comfortable.
Inhale and return smoothly through center, then exhale and twist to the opposite side, keeping the bar level and the motion slow and controlled.
Do not yank or twist explosively; forcing the rotation beyond your comfortable range can strain the lower back. Keep your hips and feet anchored throughout.
Continue alternating sides with a slow, controlled tempo for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Seated Bent-Over One-Arm Dumbbell Triceps Extension
instructions: Sit at the end of a flat bench holding a single dumbbell in one hand with a neutral grip (palm facing your torso).
Place your feet flat on the floor, slightly wider than hip-width, for balance.
Bend forward at the waist while keeping your back flat and straight until your torso is nearly parallel to the floor. Keep your head up and your gaze forward.

Raise your working upper arm until it is tucked tight against your side and parallel to the floor, with your forearm hanging straight down toward the floor and the dumbbell beneath your elbow. There should be about a 90-degree angle between forearm and upper arm. This is your starting position.
Rest your non-working hand on your knee or the bench for support and keep your upper arm pinned in place throughout.
Keeping your upper arm completely stationary, exhale and extend your forearm backward using your triceps until your arm is fully straight and the dumbbell is roughly parallel to the floor behind you.
Squeeze the triceps hard at full extension for a one-second contraction.
Inhale and slowly lower the dumbbell back to the 90-degree starting position under control, moving only at the elbow.
Do not let the upper arm drop or swing; only the forearm should move. Keep your back flat to protect the spine.
Complete all reps on one arm, then switch the dumbbell to the other hand and repeat.

name: Seated Bent-Over Rear Delt Raise
instructions: Place a pair of dumbbells on the floor just in front of a flat bench.
Sit on the end of the bench with your knees together and your feet flat on the floor, with the dumbbells positioned behind or beside your calves.

Bend forward at the waist, keeping your back flat and straight, and reach down to pick up the dumbbells so your palms face each other (neutral grip). Keep your chest near your thighs. This is your starting position.
Maintain the bent-over position with your torso resting close to your thighs and your core braced; keep a slight, fixed bend in your elbows throughout.
Exhale and raise both dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc until your arms are roughly parallel to the floor, leading with your elbows and keeping your pinkies slightly higher than your thumbs.
Focus on squeezing your rear deltoids and the muscles between your shoulder blades at the top; avoid shrugging your traps up toward your ears.
Pause for a one-second contraction at the top with your arms level.
Inhale and slowly lower the dumbbells back down along the same arc to the starting position under control.
Do not swing your torso or pull the arms backward like a row; keep the motion strictly out to the sides. Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Seated Bent-Over Two-Arm Dumbbell Triceps Extension
instructions: Sit at the end of a flat bench holding a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip (palms facing your torso).
Place your feet flat on the floor, slightly wider than hip-width, for a stable base.
Bend forward at the waist while keeping your back flat and straight until your torso is nearly parallel to the floor. Keep your head up and gaze forward.

Raise both upper arms until they are tucked against your sides and parallel to the floor, with your forearms hanging straight down and the dumbbells beneath your elbows. There should be about a 90-degree angle between forearm and upper arm. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and lock your upper arms in place against your ribs; they stay fixed for the whole movement.
Keeping your upper arms stationary, exhale and extend both forearms backward using your triceps until your arms are fully straight and the dumbbells are roughly parallel to the floor behind you.
Squeeze the triceps hard at full extension for a one-second contraction.
Inhale and slowly lower the dumbbells back to the 90-degree starting position under control, moving only at the elbows.
Only the forearms should move; do not let the upper arms drop or swing, and keep your back flat to protect the spine. Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Seated Biceps
instructions: Sit on the floor with your knees bent and feet flat, with a partner standing or kneeling directly behind you.
Extend both arms straight back behind you with your elbows fully straight and your palms facing each other (neutral position).
Have your partner firmly grasp your wrists. Sit tall with your chest up and core lightly braced. This is your starting position.
Attempt to flex your elbows, contracting your biceps as if trying to curl your hands forward, while your partner holds your wrists firmly so no actual movement occurs (an isometric contraction).
Hold this steady contraction for 10 to 20 seconds, breathing normally and keeping the rest of your body relaxed.
After the hold, relax your arms completely and let your partner gently and slowly pull your wrists upward and back to stretch the biceps.
Communicate clearly with your partner, telling them when the stretch feels sufficient so they stop pulling before any pain or overstretching occurs.
Ease out of the stretch slowly and repeat as desired, always keeping the partner's pull gentle and controlled.

name: Seated Cable Rows
instructions: Attach a V-bar (double-D handle) to a low pulley row machine; the neutral grip keeps your palms facing each other and is easiest on the shoulders.
Sit on the bench facing the pulley and place your feet flat on the front platform or crossbar, with your knees slightly bent and not locked.
Lean forward, keeping the natural alignment of your spine, and grasp the V-bar handles with both hands.

Pull back to sit upright so your torso is roughly perpendicular to the floor, arms extended in front of you. Keep your chest up, shoulders back, and a slight arch in your lower back. You should feel a stretch in your lats. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your torso stationary; do not rock back and forth to move the weight.
Exhale and pull the handle toward your lower abdomen, keeping your elbows tucked close to your sides and driving them straight back behind you.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together hard at the end of the pull when the handle reaches your abdomen, holding the contraction for a second.
Inhale and slowly extend your arms to return the handle to the start, allowing your shoulder blades to spread and feeling the stretch in your lats, but do not let your lower back round forward.
Keep the movement smooth and avoid using momentum from the lower back; let your back muscles do the work. Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Seated Cable Shoulder Press
instructions: Set the cable stations at a low position with single handles attached, or use a dual-cable machine, and select an appropriate weight on each stack.
Sit on a bench positioned centered between the two low pulleys, with your back supported and your feet flat on the floor.
Grasp a handle in each hand and bring them up to about shoulder height. Your upper arms should be roughly 90 degrees to your torso, out to the sides, with your elbows bent to about 90 degrees.
Sit tall with your head and chest up and your core braced. This is your starting position.
Exhale and press both handles up and slightly inward, extending through the elbows until the handles meet together above your head and your arms are nearly straight.
Keep your wrists firm and stacked over your elbows, and do not lock the elbows out aggressively.
Pause briefly at the top with the handles together overhead.
Inhale and slowly lower the handles back down to the starting position at shoulder level, maintaining constant tension on the cables and resisting the pull on the way down.
Avoid arching your lower back excessively or shrugging your traps. For a variation, you can perform it with your back off the pad and alternate hands. Repeat for the prescribed repetitions.

name: Seated Calf Raise
instructions: Sit on the seated calf raise machine and place the balls of your feet on the lower edge of the foot platform with your heels hanging off the back.
Choose your toe orientation: pointed straight forward works the calves evenly, toes turned in emphasizes the outer calf, and toes turned out emphasizes the inner calf.
Position your lower thighs, just above the knees, snugly under the lever pad, adjusting the pad height so it sits firmly across your thighs without pinching.
Place your hands on top of the lever pad to hold it in place and keep it from slipping forward.
Push up onto the balls of your feet to lift the lever slightly, then release the safety bar to the side. This is your starting position.
Inhale and slowly lower your heels toward the floor by bending at the ankles until you feel a deep stretch in your calves at the bottom.
Exhale and raise your heels by extending your ankles, pushing through the balls of your feet as high as possible while squeezing the calves.
Hold the fully contracted top position for a one-second squeeze.

Keep the movement slow and controlled through a full range of motion; avoid bouncing at the bottom or doing short, partial reps. Repeat for the prescribed repetitions, then re-engage the safety bar to finish.

name: Seated Calf Stretch
instructions: Sit up straight on an exercise mat with good upright posture and your core lightly engaged.
Bend one knee and place that foot flat on the floor to stabilize your torso and support your back.
Extend the other leg straight out in front of you with the knee as straight as comfortable.
Flex the ankle of the straight leg, pulling your toes back toward your shin to begin the stretch in the calf.
Loop a band or towel around the ball of the extended foot, or simply reach forward and grasp your toes with your hand if you can reach.
Gently pull the toes toward you, deepening the stretch through the calf and the back of the lower leg, while keeping the leg straight and your back tall.
Hold the stretch for 10 to 20 seconds, breathing slowly and avoiding any bouncing or jerking.
Release gently, switch the position of your legs, and repeat the stretch on the other side.

name: Seated Close-Grip Concentration Barbell Curl
instructions: Load an EZ-curl bar or straight barbell with a light to moderate weight and stand it on the floor between your feet in front of a flat bench.
Sit on the end of the bench with your feet flat on the floor, slightly wider than shoulder width, and your knees bent at roughly 90 degrees so your thighs are nearly parallel to the floor.
Reach down and take a supinated (palms-up) grip on the bar with your hands closer than shoulder width apart, about 6 to 8 inches between them.

Lift the bar and brace the back of your upper arms flat against your inner thighs, positioning your elbows about three and a half inches behind your knees so the bar hangs at arm's length just above the floor.
Lean your torso slightly forward, brace your core, and keep your upper arms locked motionless against your thighs throughout the set. This is your starting position.
Exhale and curl the bar upward by flexing only at the elbows, contracting the biceps and driving the bar toward your shoulders over a controlled one to two second count.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top, where your forearms are vertical, and hold the peak contraction for a full second.
Inhale and lower the bar slowly back to the starting position over two to three seconds, resisting gravity until your arms are fully extended and the biceps are stretched.
Keep your upper arms pinned to your thighs and avoid using your shoulders, leaning back, or swinging the bar to gain momentum.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Seated Dumbbell Curl
instructions: Select a pair of dumbbells and sit on the end of a flat bench with your back tall, chest up, and feet planted firmly on the floor about shoulder width apart.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at arm's length down by your sides, with your elbows tucked close to your torso.
Rotate your wrists so your palms face inward toward your thighs in a neutral grip. This is your starting position.
Brace your core, keep your upper arms stationary against your sides, and avoid rocking your torso for the entire set.
Exhale and curl one or both dumbbells upward, beginning to rotate your wrist so the palm turns to face up once the dumbbell passes your thigh.
Continue curling until your palm faces forward and the biceps is fully contracted with the dumbbell at shoulder level.
Squeeze the biceps and hold the contracted position for a one second peak contraction.
Inhale and slowly lower the dumbbell back down over two to three seconds, rotating your wrist back to the neutral starting grip as you reach full arm extension.
Keep only your forearms moving and resist the urge to swing the weight or let your elbows drift forward.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Seated Dumbbell Inner Biceps Curl
instructions: Grab a pair of dumbbells and sit on the end of a flat bench, sitting tall with your chest up and feet flat on the floor about shoulder width apart.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at arm's length, with your elbows tucked in close to your torso.
Rotate your wrists so your palms face inward toward each other in a neutral grip. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your upper arms fixed against your sides throughout the movement.
Exhale and curl the dumbbells upward and slightly outward, gradually rotating your wrists so the palms turn to face up and out, keeping your forearms tracking in line with your outer deltoids.
Continue until the biceps are fully contracted and the dumbbells reach shoulder height with palms supinated.
Squeeze the biceps, emphasizing the inner head, and hold the peak contraction for one second.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells slowly back to the start over two to three seconds, rotating your wrists back to the neutral grip as your arms fully extend.
Move only at the elbows and avoid swinging your torso or letting your elbows flare forward for momentum.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Seated Dumbbell Palms-Down Wrist Curl
instructions: Place two light dumbbells on the floor in front of a flat bench.
Sit on the edge of the bench with your feet flat on the floor about shoulder width apart.
Pick up a dumbbell in each hand and lay your forearms along the tops of your thighs with your palms facing down, so your wrists and hands hang just past your kneecaps over the edge of your thighs.
Lean slightly forward so your forearms are firmly supported and stationary against your thighs. This is your starting position.
Lower your knuckles toward the floor by letting your wrists extend downward, allowing the dumbbells to roll toward your fingertips for a full stretch in the forearms.
Exhale and curl your wrists upward as high as possible by extending them, lifting the back of your hands toward your shins.
Squeeze the forearm extensors at the top and hold for a brief one second.
Inhale and slowly lower your wrists back down to the fully stretched starting position over a controlled count.
Keep your forearms pressed flat to your thighs so the motion comes only from the wrists, never the elbows.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, then lower the dumbbells to the floor when finished.

name: Seated Dumbbell Palms-Up Wrist Curl
instructions: Place two light dumbbells on the floor in front of a flat bench.
Sit on the edge of the bench with your feet flat on the floor about shoulder width apart.
Pick up a dumbbell in each hand and lay your forearms along the tops of your thighs with your palms facing up, so your wrists and hands hang just past your kneecaps over the edge of your thighs.
Lean slightly forward so your forearms are firmly supported and stationary against your thighs. This is your starting position.
Let your wrists drop and the dumbbells roll down toward your fingertips, lowering as far as comfortable to fully stretch the wrist flexors.
Exhale and curl your wrists upward by flexing them, raising the dumbbells toward your forearms in a smooth, controlled arc.
Squeeze the forearm flexors at the top of the curl and hold for a brief one second.
Inhale and slowly lower your wrists back to the fully stretched starting position over a controlled count.
Keep your forearms pinned flat to your thighs so the motion comes only from the wrists, never the elbows.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, then lower the dumbbells to the floor when finished.

name: Seated Dumbbell Press
instructions: Set a utility or military press bench to an upright position with the back support nearly vertical and grab a pair of dumbbells.
Sit down with your back flat against the pad, your head up, and your feet planted firmly on the floor for a stable base, resting the dumbbells upright on your thighs.
Use a knee kick to clean the dumbbells up one at a time to shoulder height, bringing them to either side of your head.
Rotate your wrists so your palms face forward and position the dumbbells at about ear level with your elbows pointing down and slightly forward. This is your starting position.
Brace your core, keep your lower back lightly arched against the pad, and pin your shoulder blades back and down.
Exhale and press the dumbbells straight up and slightly inward until your arms are nearly locked out and the dumbbells almost touch at the top.
Keep your wrists stacked over your elbows and do not let the dumbbells drift forward or your back arch excessively off the pad.
Pause for a second at the top, then inhale and lower the dumbbells under control back to ear level over two to three seconds.
