Lower your heels slowly toward the floor as you inhale, letting them sink below the level of your toes until you feel a deep stretch in your calves.
Exhale and push through the balls of your feet, raising your heels as high as possible by extending your ankles and squeezing your calves.
Hold the fully contracted top position for one second.
Keep your knees fixed and your torso upright throughout; do not bounce out of the bottom or bend the knees to cheat the rep.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, using a slow controlled tempo and full range of motion.

name: Standing Concentration Curl
instructions: Take a single dumbbell in your working hand and stand with your feet about shoulder width apart.
Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back until your torso is angled forward, and let your working arm hang straight down toward the floor.
Rotate the arm so your palm faces forward (supinated) and your elbow points out and away from your body; the upper arm should stay roughly perpendicular to the floor. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your upper arm completely stationary throughout the movement.
Exhale and curl the dumbbell up by flexing only at the elbow, focusing on contracting the biceps.
At the top of the rep, squeeze the biceps hard and pause for a moment.
Inhale and lower the dumbbell back down slowly under control to the fully extended starting position.
Do not swing the weight or let your upper arm move; isolate the biceps by keeping everything but the forearm still.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch the dumbbell to the other hand and repeat.

name: Standing Dumbbell Calf Raise
instructions: Place a sturdy, stable board or step about 2 to 3 inches tall on the floor for the balls of your feet.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with a neutral grip, palms facing your thighs, and stand tall.
Step the balls of both feet onto the board so your heels hang off the back and can drop below the level of your toes. Keep your torso upright and core braced. This is your starting position.
Set your toes pointing straight ahead (or slightly inward to bias the outer calf, or slightly outward to bias the inner calf).
Exhale and raise your heels as high as possible by pushing through the balls of your feet and contracting your calves, keeping a slight fixed bend in the knees.
Hold the top contraction for one second, standing as tall on your toes as you can.
Inhale and lower your heels slowly back down past the level of the board until you feel a full stretch in your calves.
Keep your body upright and avoid bouncing or bending the knees to cheat; let the calves do all the work.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Standing Dumbbell Press
instructions: Stand with your feet about shoulder width apart and hold a dumbbell in each hand.
Raise the dumbbells to about head or ear height with your palms facing forward, elbows bent to roughly 90 degrees and pointing down and out to the sides. This is your starting position.
Brace your core hard, squeeze your glutes, and keep your ribs down so your torso stays rigid and upright.

Maintaining strict form with no leg drive and no leaning back, exhale and press both dumbbells straight up overhead until your arms are fully extended and the weights are roughly over the crown of your head.
Keep your wrists stacked over your elbows and the dumbbells tracking straight up, stopping just short of clanging them together.
Pause briefly at the top with arms extended.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells slowly back down to the head-height starting position under control.
Do not arch your lower back or use your legs to bounce the weight up; if you cannot press strictly, reduce the load.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Standing Dumbbell Reverse Curl
instructions: Stand up straight with your feet about shoulder width apart and a dumbbell in each hand.
Use a pronated grip with your palms facing down toward the floor, and let your arms hang fully extended at your sides. This is your starting position.
Pin your elbows close to your torso, lift your chest, and brace your core to keep your body still.
Keeping your upper arms locked in place, exhale and curl the dumbbells upward by contracting the biceps and forearms until the weights reach shoulder level.
Hold the top contracted position for one second and squeeze.
Inhale and slowly lower the dumbbells back down to the fully extended starting position under control.
Keep your wrists firm and the palms-down position throughout; do not let the wrists curl up or swing the weights with your body.
Only your forearms should move; avoid using momentum or rocking your torso.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Standing Dumbbell Straight-Arm Front Delt Raise Above Head
instructions: Stand tall with your feet about shoulder width apart and hold a light dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs, palms facing your thighs.
Keep your arms straight with only a slight, fixed bend at the elbows that stays locked throughout. Brace your core and keep your chest up. This is your starting position.
Exhale and raise both dumbbells forward and upward in a smooth semicircular arc, leading with the front of your shoulders.
Continue lifting in one controlled path all the way up until your arms are fully overhead at arm's length above your head.
Keep your torso upright and still; do not swing, lean back, or use leg drive to throw the weights up.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells slowly back down along the exact same path to the starting position in front of your thighs.
Use a light weight and controlled tempo, since this long lever puts significant demand on the shoulders.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Standing Dumbbell Triceps Extension
instructions: Stand with your feet about shoulder width apart and grasp a single dumbbell with both hands.
Cup one end of the dumbbell in both palms with your thumbs wrapped around the handle, then press it overhead until your arms are fully extended and the top plate points up toward the ceiling.

Keep your upper arms close to your head with the elbows pointing forward and roughly perpendicular to the floor. Brace your core and keep your ribs down so you don't arch your lower back. This is your starting position.
Inhale and lower the dumbbell in a controlled semicircular path down behind your head by bending only at the elbows, until your forearms nearly touch your biceps.
Keep your upper arms stationary and your elbows from flaring out wide; only the forearms should move.
Exhale and extend your elbows to drive the dumbbell back up to the fully extended overhead starting position, squeezing the triceps at the top.
Keep your wrists firm and the dumbbell controlled, since it is directly above your head; do not let it drop quickly.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Standing Dumbbell Upright Row
instructions: Stand tall with your feet about shoulder width apart and hold a dumbbell in each hand with a pronated grip (palms facing your body), hands slightly less than shoulder width apart.
Let the dumbbells rest against the front of your thighs with your arms extended and a slight bend at the elbows. Keep your back straight, chest up, and core braced. This is your starting position.
Exhale and pull the dumbbells straight up along the front of your body, leading with your elbows and keeping the weights close to your torso.
Continue lifting until the dumbbells reach roughly upper-chest or chin height, ensuring your elbows stay higher than your forearms throughout.
Pause for a second at the top and squeeze the traps and side shoulders.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells slowly back down to the starting position at your thighs under control.
Keep your torso stationary and avoid swinging or using momentum; if you feel pinching in the shoulders, do not pull as high.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Standing Elevated Quad Stretch
instructions: Stand facing away from a bench or step with your back about two to three feet in front of it.
Lift one leg behind you and rest the top of that foot, either your instep or the ball of your foot, on the bench, whichever feels more comfortable.
Keep your standing (supporting) knee slightly bent, and make sure that knee does not travel out past your toes.
Stand tall, tuck your pelvis slightly under, and keep your hips square to the front to deepen the stretch through the front of the thigh and hip of the elevated leg.
Hold the position and breathe slowly until you feel a stretch in the quadriceps of the elevated leg, keeping your torso upright rather than leaning forward.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds, then switch sides and repeat with the other leg elevated.

name: Standing Forward Fold
instructions: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, toes pointing straight ahead and weight balanced evenly across both feet.
Lengthen your spine and lift through the crown of your head, drawing your shoulders down and back to start from a tall, neutral posture.
Place your hands on your hips and inhale to prepare, keeping a micro-bend in your knees so you do not lock or hyperextend them.
Exhale and hinge forward from your hip joints rather than rounding the spine first, sending your hips back slightly as your torso lowers toward your thighs.
Let your head, neck, and arms hang completely relaxed toward the floor, releasing all tension in your shoulders and jaw.
Fold only until you feel a comfortable stretch along the back of your thighs; bend your knees more if your hamstrings are tight or your lower back rounds aggressively.
Keep your weight slightly forward over the balls of your feet rather than rocking back into your heels, and breathe slowly and deeply throughout.
Hold for 20 to 60 seconds, allowing gravity to deepen the stretch with each exhale.
To exit, bend your knees, brace your core, and roll up slowly one vertebra at a time, bringing your head up last to avoid dizziness.

name: Standing Front Barbell Raise Over Head
instructions: Load a barbell and stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft and core braced.
Grip the bar with both palms facing down (pronated) using a grip slightly narrower than shoulder width, and let the bar rest against the front of your thighs at arm's length.
Set your posture with chest up, shoulders pulled back and down, spine neutral, and a slight bend kept in your elbows that you will maintain the entire set.
Brace your abs and glutes to lock your torso in place so the movement comes only from your shoulders, not from leaning back.
Exhale and raise the barbell in a smooth arc straight out in front of you and continue up until it is directly overhead.
Keep your arms nearly straight with that fixed slight elbow bend, and avoid shrugging your traps up toward your ears as the bar rises.
Pause briefly at the top with the bar over the crown of your head, feeling the front and side delts working.
Inhale and lower the barbell under control along the same path back down to the front of your thighs.
Move at a controlled tempo and do not use momentum or a backward lean to swing the weight up; if you must arch, the weight is too heavy.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Standing Gastrocnemius Calf Stretch
instructions: Stand facing a step, low box, or curb, positioning yourself a comfortable arm's reach away from it.
Place your right heel on the edge of the step with your right knee fully extended and locked straight, since a straight knee targets the larger gastrocnemius muscle.
Keep your left leg back on the floor with the knee slightly bent, supporting most of your bodyweight, and rest your left hand on your left thigh for stability.
Maintain a straight, tall back and square hips throughout; do not round forward through your shoulders.
Hinge forward from your hips and reach your right hand toward your right toes.
Gently pull the toes of your right foot up toward your shin until you feel a clear stretch through the back of your right calf.
Hold the stretch for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing slowly and avoiding any bouncing.
Release gradually, then switch legs and repeat on the left side.

name: Standing Hamstring and Calf Stretch
instructions: Loop a belt, resistance band, yoga strap, or rope around the ball of one foot, holding one end in each hand.
Stand tall and step that foot slightly forward, planting the heel on the floor in front of you.
Keep your front leg straight while bending your back (supporting) leg slightly, and keep your torso upright with a neutral spine.
Lift the toes of your front foot off the ground by flexing the ankle, so only the heel stays in contact with the floor.
Hinge forward gently from the hips while keeping your front knee straight, leaning your chest toward the front leg.
Pull upward on the strap to draw the top of your front foot toward your shin, increasing the stretch through the calf and back of the leg.
Adjust how far you lean and how hard you pull until you feel a firm but tolerable stretch along the hamstring and calf, never sharp pain.
Hold for 10 to 20 seconds while breathing steadily, then release and repeat with the other foot.

name: Standing Hamstring Stretch
instructions: Stand facing a low surface such as a step, bench, or sturdy chair, positioned within easy reach.
Place one heel on top of the surface with that leg fully straight and the toes pointing up toward the ceiling.
Keep your standing leg straight or with a very slight knee bend, and square your hips so both hip bones face forward.
Set a tall posture with your chest lifted, shoulders relaxed, and spine long before you begin to fold.
Hinge forward from your hips, leading with your chest rather than rounding your upper back, and reach your hands toward the toes of the elevated foot.
Lower only until you feel a firm stretch along the back of the elevated thigh; you do not need to touch your toes.
Keep the elevated leg straight throughout, as bending it removes the stretch from the hamstring.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing slowly and deepening gently with each exhale.
Rise back up under control, then switch legs and repeat.

name: Standing Hip Circles
instructions: Stand next to a wall, pole, or rack and rest one hand lightly on it for balance, keeping your supporting leg straight and grounded.
Shift your weight fully onto the supporting leg, keeping a soft knee and bracing your core to stay upright.
Raise the opposite knee in front of you to roughly hip height so the hip and knee are each bent to about 90 degrees; this is your starting position.
Keeping the knee bent, slowly open the lifted leg out to the side by rotating from the hip, drawing the knee outward as far as your hip mobility allows.
Continue the circle by sweeping the knee around and back toward the front, tracing as large a circle as possible with the knee.
Move slowly and deliberately, keeping your torso tall and still so the motion comes purely from the hip joint, not from twisting your back.
Complete the prescribed number of circles in one direction, then reverse and circle the same number of times in the opposite direction.
Lower the leg, then switch to the other side and repeat.

name: Standing Hip Flexors
instructions: Stand up straight with your spine vertical and your core gently braced, positioning your left foot slightly in front of your right.
Keep your feet roughly hip-width apart with both toes pointing forward and your hips squared to the front.
Bend both knees and lift the heel of your back (right) foot off the floor so you are on the ball of that foot.
Tuck your pelvis slightly under into a posterior tilt by squeezing the glute on the back leg, which protects the lower back and increases the stretch.
Press the right hip gently forward and downward until you feel a stretch across the front of the right hip and upper thigh.
Keep your torso upright and avoid arching your lower back excessively; the stretch should be felt in the hip flexor, not the spine.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds while breathing steadily, then relax.
Switch your stance so the right foot is forward and repeat the stretch on the left hip flexor.

name: Standing Inner-Biceps Curl
instructions: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, feet about shoulder-width apart and knees slightly soft.
Let the dumbbells hang at arm's length with your elbows tucked close against your torso.
Rotate your hands so your palms face inward toward your body in a neutral (hammer) grip; this is your starting position.
Keep your upper arms pinned to your sides and stationary so only the forearms move during the curl.
Exhale and curl the weights upward, and as you raise them gradually rotate your wrists so that at the top your palms face up (fully supinated).
Continue curling until the biceps are fully contracted and the dumbbells are near shoulder level, keeping your forearms aligned with your outer deltoids rather than drifting inward.
Squeeze the biceps hard and hold the top position for about one second.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells slowly back to the start, reversing the wrist rotation so your palms return to the neutral, facing-in position.
Avoid swinging your torso or using momentum; keep the movement strict and controlled.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Standing Knee Raise Hold
instructions: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, weight evenly distributed, and arms relaxed or lightly placed on your hips.
Lengthen your spine, lift your chest, and draw your shoulders down and back into a tall, stable posture.
Brace your core by gently drawing your navel toward your spine to create a solid base before lifting.
Shift your weight onto one leg, keeping that knee soft and your supporting foot firmly planted.
Lift the opposite knee up in front of you to hip height so your thigh is roughly parallel to the floor.
Fix your gaze on a stationary point ahead of you to help maintain balance, and keep your standing hip from collapsing outward.
Hold the lifted knee steady, resisting any wobble by keeping the core tight and the standing glute engaged, for the prescribed duration.
Lower the leg under control, reset your stance, then switch legs and repeat.

name: Standing Lateral Stretch
instructions: Stand with your feet slightly wider than hip-width apart, toes pointing forward and knees slightly bent.
Distribute your weight evenly between both feet and brace your core gently to protect your lower back.
Place your right hand on your right hip to support and stabilize your spine.
Raise your left arm straight up overhead in a vertical line, or place your left hand behind your head with the elbow pointing up.
Inhale to lengthen your spine, then exhale and incline your torso smoothly to the right, bending sideways through the waist.
Reach the left arm up and over to feel the stretch run along the left side of your torso, from hip to ribs to underarm.
Keep your weight balanced evenly on both legs and avoid pushing your hips out to the left; the bend should be a clean side flexion, not a lean.
Hold for 15 to 30 seconds while breathing into the stretched side, then return to upright.
Switch your hand positions and repeat the stretch bending to the left side.

name: Standing Leg Curl
instructions: Adjust the standing leg curl machine so the thigh pad sits against the front of your working thigh and the lever pad rests against the back of your lower leg a few inches below the calf, just above the Achilles.
Set the machine so that when you stand in position your torso bends forward at the waist roughly 30 to 45 degrees, which improves hamstring recruitment.
Step in and place the front of your working thigh against the support pad, then position the back of your lower leg under the roller pad.
Grip the side handles for support, keep your toes pointed straight, and let the working leg hang fully extended; this is your starting position.
Keep your torso bent forward and your hips pressed into the pad so your upper leg stays fixed throughout the movement.
Exhale and curl your working leg upward by bending the knee, bringing the heel toward your glutes as far as possible without lifting your thigh off the pad.
Squeeze the hamstring hard at the top and hold the fully contracted position for about one second.
Inhale and lower the leg slowly and under control back to full extension, resisting the weight on the way down.
Avoid jerking the weight or swinging your hips; keep the motion strict and smooth.
Complete the prescribed repetitions, then repeat with the other leg.

name: Standing Long Jump
instructions: Choose a soft landing surface such as sand or a rubber mat, and mark a clear starting line on the floor.
Stand behind the line with your feet about shoulder-width apart and toes just behind the mark.
Drop into a partial squat by hinging at the hips and bending the knees, keeping your chest up and weight over the middle of your feet.
Swing both arms back behind you as you load into the squat to build a countermovement, keeping your core braced.
Explosively swing your arms forward and up while driving powerfully through your legs, extending the hips, knees, and ankles to jump forward as far as possible.
Reach your legs out in front of you in the air, then prepare to land with your feet ahead of your hips.
Land softly on both feet at the same time, bending your knees and hips to absorb the impact and avoid falling backward.
Measure the distance from the starting line to the rear of your landing heels and record the result to track progress.
Reset fully and rest briefly between maximal-effort jumps.

name: Standing Low-Pulley Deltoid Raise
instructions: Attach a single handle to the low pulley of a cable machine and select a light weight, since this is an isolation movement for the side and rear delt.
Stand to the right side of the machine so the cable runs across the front of your body, and grab the handle with your left hand using a pronated grip with the palm facing down.
Let your left arm rest across the front of your body, and grip the machine frame with your right hand for support and balance.
Set your stance with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, back erect, and core braced; this is your starting position.
Exhale and raise your left arm out and across your body in an arc, lifting until the hand reaches about shoulder height.
Keep your arm nearly straight with only a slight elbow bend, and avoid shrugging your trap or twisting your torso to assist.
Pause and squeeze the delt at the top for about one second.
Inhale and lower the handle slowly and under control along the same path back to the starting position, resisting the cable.
Complete the prescribed repetitions, then switch sides so you stand on the left of the machine and work the right arm.

name: Standing Low-Pulley One-Arm Triceps Extension
instructions: Attach a single handle to the low pulley of a cable machine and grab it with your left hand.
Turn to face away from the machine so the cable runs up behind you, keeping the handle at the side of your body with your arm extended down.
Use both hands to raise the handle up overhead until your left upper arm is fully vertical and the palm faces forward.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, one foot slightly staggered for stability, core braced and back straight.
Place your right hand on your left elbow to keep the upper arm fixed and prevent it from drifting; this is your starting position.

Keeping your left upper arm close to your head and perpendicular to the floor, inhale and lower the handle in a semicircular arc behind your head by bending only at the elbow, until your forearm touches your bicep.
Keep the upper arm completely stationary throughout so only the forearm moves; the elbow should not flare out or drop.
Exhale and extend the elbow to drive the handle back up to the starting position overhead, contracting the triceps fully.
Avoid leaning forward or using your body to assist; let the triceps do the work.
Complete the prescribed repetitions, then switch arms and repeat.

name: Standing Military Press
instructions: Set a barbell in a squat rack at about chest height and load your weight.
Grip the bar with both palms facing forward (pronated), hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.
Step under the bar, bend your knees slightly, and unrack it onto the front of your shoulders so it rests across your collarbones and front delts.
Take one or two steps back and set your feet shoulder-width apart with toes pointing slightly out, knees soft and core tightly braced.
Squeeze your glutes and brace your abs to lock your torso so you do not lean back during the press; keep your wrists stacked over your elbows.

Exhale and press the bar straight up overhead, moving your head slightly back out of the bar's path, then push your head through so the bar finishes balanced over the back of your neck with arms locked out; this is your top position.
Pause briefly at lockout with the bar over the crown of your head and shoulders, ribs down and glutes tight.
Inhale and lower the bar slowly and under control back down to your collarbones, again tucking your chin to clear the bar's path.
Keep the bar moving in a tight vertical line and avoid excessive backward lean or pressing the bar forward.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then re-rack the bar in the squat rack.

name: Standing Olympic Plate Hand Squeeze
instructions: Select a weight plate light enough that you can hold it by the smooth outer ridge with your fingertips, and pick up one in each hand.
Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, arms hanging straight at your sides, holding each plate by the rim with a neutral grip and palms facing your body.
Brace your core and keep your shoulders back and down so your posture stays upright throughout; this is your starting position.
Keep your wrists straight and your upper arms still so the movement happens only in your fingers and hands.
Inhale and slowly open your fingers, allowing the plate to lower in your grip until your fingers are nearly extended but still securely holding the weight.
Exhale and close your hands, curling your fingers to raise the plate back up to the starting position and crushing your grip on the rim.
Squeeze hard at the top to fully contract the forearm muscles, and control the lowering phase rather than letting the plate slip.
Keep both hands moving with control and never let the plate fall; lower it deliberately to protect your toes and fingers.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions in your program.

name: Standing One-Arm Cable Curl
instructions: Set the pulley on a cable tower to the lowest position and attach a single stirrup handle. Select a moderate weight you can control with one arm.

Grab the handle with the working arm using a supinated grip (palm facing up and forward), then step back from the machine until your arm is straight out in front and fully supporting the load with tension on the cable.
Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, chest up, shoulders back, and core braced. Place your free hand on your hip or waist to stabilize your torso.
Pin the working upper arm tightly against your side so the elbow stays fixed and points straight down at the floor. This is your starting position.
Exhale and curl the handle upward by flexing only at the elbow, keeping the upper arm completely stationary and the wrist neutral.
Continue curling until your forearm presses against your bicep and the muscle is fully contracted; squeeze hard at the top for one second.
Inhale and lower the handle slowly under control along the same path, taking about two to three seconds until the arm is fully extended and you feel a stretch in the bicep.
Keep your torso upright throughout; do not lean back or swing the body to lift the weight, as momentum removes tension from the bicep.
Complete all reps on one arm, then switch the handle to the other hand and repeat for the same number of reps.

name: Standing One-Arm Dumbbell Curl Over Incline Bench
instructions: Set an incline bench to roughly 45 degrees and stand behind it as if spotting a lifter seated on it.
Hold a dumbbell in the working hand with a supinated grip (palm facing up) and drape that arm over the top edge of the incline pad so the back of your upper arm rests against the padding.
Press your chest into the top of the incline backrest and set your feet in a wide, stable stance with weight evenly distributed.
Place your non-working hand on the corner or side of the bench frame for balance and support.
Let the dumbbell hang with the arm fully extended against the pad; the upper arm should be locked in place by the bench. This is the starting position.
Exhale and curl the dumbbell upward by bending only at the elbow, keeping the upper arm pressed motionless against the pad.
Continue until the bicep is fully contracted and the dumbbell reaches shoulder level, then hold and squeeze the peak for one second.
Inhale and lower the dumbbell slowly under control over two to three seconds back to the fully extended starting position, feeling a stretch at the bottom.
Avoid letting the upper arm lift off the pad or using a swinging motion; the pad enforces strict isolation of the bicep.
Finish all reps on one arm, then switch hands and repeat for the same number of reps.

name: Standing One-Arm Dumbbell Triceps Extension
instructions: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, core braced, and a slight natural arch in the lower back.
Hold a dumbbell in the working hand and press it straight overhead until the arm is fully extended and locked out.
Rotate the hand so the palm faces forward and the small finger points toward the ceiling, with the dumbbell positioned directly above your head. This is the starting position.
Keep the working upper arm close to your head and perpendicular to the floor; you may place the free hand against the working tricep or on your hip to keep the elbow tracking in.
Inhale and lower the dumbbell in a smooth semicircular arc behind your head by bending only at the elbow, keeping the upper arm stationary.
Continue lowering until your forearm nearly touches your bicep and you feel a stretch in the tricep; keep the elbow pointed up and tucked in, not flaring out.
Exhale and drive the dumbbell back up to the fully extended starting position using the tricep, locking out the elbow at the top.
Move only the forearm throughout; do not let the upper arm drift forward or the elbow flare, and avoid arching the lower back to push the weight.
Complete all reps on one arm, then switch hands and repeat for the same number of reps.

name: Standing Overhead Barbell Triceps Extension
instructions: Load a straight barbell or an EZ-bar and grip it with a pronated grip (palms facing forward), hands set slightly closer than shoulder-width apart.
Stand tall with feet about shoulder-width apart, knees soft, core braced, and a slight natural arch in the lower back.
Press the bar overhead until your arms are fully extended and locked out, with the elbows kept in and pointing forward. This is the starting position.
Keep your upper arms close to your head and perpendicular to the floor so the elbows stay fixed throughout the movement.
Inhale and lower the bar in a controlled semicircular arc behind your head by bending only at the elbows, keeping the upper arms motionless.
Continue until your forearms nearly touch your biceps and you feel a deep stretch in the triceps; do not let the elbows flare outward.
Exhale and extend the elbows to drive the bar back overhead to the locked-out starting position, squeezing the triceps at the top.
Move only the forearms; keep the upper arms still and avoid arching the lower back or using leg drive to heave the weight up.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, keeping the bar path tight and controlled.

name: Standing Palm-In One-Arm Dumbbell Press
instructions: Stand next to an incline bench with feet shoulder-width apart, and hold the bench frame with your non-working hand for balance.
Hold a dumbbell in the working hand using a neutral grip (palm facing in toward your body).

Raise the dumbbell to shoulder height so the upper arm is roughly parallel to the floor and the forearm is perpendicular, elbow bent about 90 degrees, palm still facing in. This is the bottom press position.
Brace your core, keep your chest up, and avoid leaning the torso; the free hand on the bench keeps you stable.
Exhale and press the dumbbell straight up overhead until the arm is fully extended, maintaining the neutral palm-in grip the entire time.
Pause briefly at the top with the arm locked out and the dumbbell directly above the shoulder.
Inhale and lower the dumbbell slowly under control back down until the elbow returns to the 90-degree bottom position.
Feel the contraction for a second at the bottom, then press again; keep the wrist neutral and stacked over the elbow throughout.
Do not flare the elbow excessively or arch the lower back to drive the weight up; keep the movement strict and balanced.
Complete all reps on one arm, then switch hands and repeat for the same number of reps.

name: Standing Palms-In Dumbbell Press
instructions: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, core braced, and a slight natural arch in the lower back.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip (palms facing each other toward your body).

Raise both dumbbells to shoulder height so your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor and forearms perpendicular, elbows bent about 90 degrees and palms still facing in. This is the starting position.
Keep your chest up, shoulders down and back, and wrists stacked over the elbows.
Exhale and press both dumbbells straight overhead until your arms are fully extended, maintaining the neutral palm-in grip throughout.
Pause at the top with arms locked out and the dumbbells directly above your shoulders without clanging them together.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells slowly under control back down until the elbows return to the 90-degree starting position.
Keep the core tight and avoid leaning back or arching the lower back to heave the weight; let the shoulders and triceps do the work.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, keeping both arms moving symmetrically.

name: Standing Palms-Up Barbell Behind The Back Wrist Curl
instructions: Set a barbell on a squat rack at about mid-thigh height, or have a partner hand it to you, so you can grasp it behind your body.
Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, facing away from the rack, and grip the bar behind your glutes with hands shoulder-width apart.
Use a pronated grip so your palms face back and away from your glutes, and let the bar hang at arm's length against the back of your thighs. This is the starting position.
Keep your torso upright, chest up, eyes forward, and arms straight and stationary throughout the movement.
Exhale and curl the bar upward by flexing only at the wrists, rolling the bar up in a small semicircular motion toward the ceiling.
Squeeze the forearms hard and hold the peak contraction for one second at the top.
Inhale and slowly lower the bar back down by extending the wrists until the bar returns to the fully hanging starting position, feeling a stretch in the forearms.
Move only the wrists; keep the arms, elbows, and shoulders completely still and do not let the body sway.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, then return the bar to the rack by bending the knees, or hand it to a partner.

name: Standing Pelvic Tilt
instructions: Stand with your feet hip-distance apart and your weight balanced evenly over both feet.
Bend your knees slightly so they stay soft and springy rather than locked.
Place your hands on your hips and keep your chest tall and shoulders relaxed down.
Gently rock your pelvis forward and backward a few times to find a comfortable range of motion and loosen the lower back.
Tuck your tailbone forward and under by gently contracting your glutes and lower abdominals, flattening the natural curve of the lower spine.
Hold the tucked position, feeling a gentle stretch and lengthening through the lower back.
Breathe slowly and steadily, holding for 15 to 30 seconds without forcing the movement.
Release back to a neutral pelvis and repeat as needed, keeping all movement smooth and controlled.

name: Standing Quad Stretch
instructions: Stand tall near a wall or sturdy object you can touch with one hand for balance if needed.
Shift your weight onto one leg, keeping that knee soft and the supporting foot firmly planted.
Bend the opposite knee and reach back with the same-side hand to grasp that ankle or the top of the foot.
Pull the heel toward your glute while keeping both knees close together and aligned side by side.
Tuck your pelvis slightly under and keep your torso upright; avoid arching the lower back or letting the bent knee drift forward.
Hold the position, feeling a stretch along the front of the thigh and hip flexor, for 20 to 30 seconds while breathing steadily.
Release the foot slowly under control, then switch to the other leg and repeat for the same duration.

name: Standing Rope Crunch
instructions: Attach a rope handle to a high pulley on a cable tower and select a moderate, controllable weight.
Grasp both ends of the rope and turn to face away from the machine with your back to the cable tower.
Pull the rope down so your hands are positioned beside your head with the rope ends resting against your upper chest or collarbones.
Kneel down or stand with feet shoulder-width apart, hips set back slightly, and brace your core. This is the starting position.
Exhale and crunch downward by flexing your spine, curling your elbows toward your thighs and rounding the upper back.
Drive the contraction from the abdominals, not the arms or hips; keep the hands fixed at your head so the weight is moved by trunk flexion.
Continue crunching down as far as your range allows, squeezing the abs hard at the bottom for one second.
Inhale and slowly return to the upright starting position under control, keeping tension on the abs and avoiding letting the weight yank you back up.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, keeping the hips relatively stationary throughout.

name: Standing Soleus And Achilles Stretch
instructions: Stand facing a wall about an arm's length away, with feet hip-distance apart and one foot slightly in front of the other.
Place both hands on the wall at shoulder height for support and balance.
Keep both heels flat on the floor throughout the stretch.
Bend both knees, sinking your weight down and forward over the back leg while keeping the rear heel pressed into the ground.
Feel the stretch low in the back calf near the Achilles tendon rather than high in the calf belly; the bent rear knee targets the soleus.
Hold the position for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing slowly and keeping the heel down.
Switch the front and back foot positions and repeat the stretch on the other leg for the same duration.

name: Standing Toe Touches
instructions: Stand tall with feet together or hip-distance apart, and clear some space in front of and behind you.
Keep your legs straight but with a very slight softness in the knees to avoid locking them.
Slowly bend forward at the hips, hinging at the waist and letting your upper body fold down toward your legs.
Let your arms, hands, and head hang down naturally toward the floor, relaxing your neck and shoulders.
Allow gravity to gently increase the stretch through the hamstrings and lower back; do not bounce or force the reach.
Hold the relaxed hanging position for 10 to 20 seconds while breathing slowly and steadily.
To finish, bend the knees slightly and roll up through the spine one vertebra at a time to return to standing without straining the back.

name: Standing Towel Triceps Extension
instructions: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, and core braced, with a partner standing behind you to provide resistance.
Hold one end of a towel with both hands and press your arms fully overhead, elbows in and upper arms perpendicular to the floor, palms facing each other. This is the starting position.
Have your partner grip the other end of the towel from below and behind you so they can apply downward resistance as you press.
Communicate with your partner so they apply steady, controllable tension rather than jerking the towel.
Inhale and lower your hands in a semicircular arc behind your head by bending only at the elbows, keeping the upper arms close to your head and stationary as your partner gives resistance.
Continue until your forearms nearly touch your biceps and you feel a stretch in the triceps, keeping the elbows pointing up and tucked in.
Exhale and extend the elbows to press the towel back up to the overhead starting position against your partner's resistance, squeezing the triceps at the top.
Move only the forearms and keep the upper arms fixed; avoid arching the lower back to overcome the resistance.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, then switch roles with your partner if desired.

name: Standing Two-Arm Overhead Throw
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a medicine ball in both hands in front of your chest, knees soft and core braced.
Position yourself facing a sturdy wall a few feet away, or face a partner who can return the ball.
To load the throw, reach the ball deep up and behind your head while bending the knees slightly and leaning your torso back, loading the hips and core.
Keep your arms relatively straight and your eyes on your target as you cock the ball back overhead.
Explosively reverse the motion by flexing forward at the hips and snapping the torso and arms forward, using your whole body to generate power.
Release the ball forcefully forward and slightly downward toward the wall or partner, finishing with the arms extended in front.
Catch the ball as it rebounds off the wall or is returned by your partner, absorbing it back into the loaded overhead position.
Reset your stance and breathing between throws, and repeat explosively for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Star Jump
instructions: Begin in a relaxed athletic stance with feet shoulder-width apart, arms held close to the body, and core lightly braced.
Initiate the movement by squatting down about halfway, hinging at the hips and bending the knees while keeping your chest up.
Explode upward as powerfully as possible, jumping straight up and extending the ankles, knees, and hips fully.
At the peak of the jump, spread your arms and legs out wide away from the body into a star shape, fully extending your whole body in midair.
Bring your arms and legs back in toward the body as you descend in preparation for landing.
Land softly on the balls of your feet with knees bent, absorbing the impact through your legs and hips to protect the joints.
Reset into the starting stance and repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, prioritizing explosive height and soft landings.

name: Step Mill
instructions: Step carefully onto the stepmill, using the handrails for support as you get on so you don't trip on the moving stairs.
Select your desired option from the console menu, choosing either a manual setting or a preset program, and enter your age and weight if prompted to estimate calories burned.
Begin at a slow, manageable speed to find your rhythm before increasing the pace or resistance level.
Stand tall with an upright posture, chest up, shoulders back, and core engaged; avoid hunching or leaning heavily on the handrails.
Step with full foot placement on each stair and let your legs drive the movement, keeping a steady controlled cadence.
Maintain a light grip on the handles for balance and safety, but support your own bodyweight through your legs rather than hanging on the rails.
Breathe steadily and keep your gaze forward; adjust speed or program intensity to keep your effort in your target range.
When finished, gradually slow the pace to cool down, then carefully step off the machine while holding the rails.

name: Step-Up
instructions: Set a sturdy box, bench, or platform in front of you at a height that puts your knee at roughly 90 degrees when your foot is on top; lower platforms are safer for beginners, higher ones increase quad and glute demand.
Stand tall facing the box with your feet hip-width apart, chest up, shoulders back, and core braced. Let your arms hang at your sides or place hands on hips.
Place your entire working foot flat on top of the box, planting it firmly with the heel down; do not let the heel hang off the edge.
Shift your weight forward over the planted foot and keep your torso slightly forward so your knee tracks over your mid-foot, not caving inward.
Drive forcefully through the heel of the top foot to push your body straight up, exhaling as you rise, until that leg is fully extended and you are standing tall on the box.
Avoid pushing off the floor with the trailing foot; let the top leg do the work so the quad and glute are loaded, not the calf of the bottom leg.
Bring the trailing foot up to lightly tap the box or hover beside the working foot, keeping your torso upright and balanced.
Lower under control by stepping the trailing foot back down to the floor, inhaling as you descend, while the working foot stays planted and the working leg controls the descent.
Complete all reps on one leg or alternate legs as prescribed, keeping each rep slow and controlled rather than bouncing off the bottom.

name: Step-up with Knee Raise
instructions: Position a box or bench in front of you at a height that puts your knee near 90 degrees when your foot is on it. Stand facing it with feet together, chest up, and core braced.
Let your arms hang at your sides or bend them slightly so you can swing them naturally for balance and momentum.
Place your left foot flat and firmly on top of the box, heel down and fully on the surface so it does not slip.
Shift your weight over the left foot and drive through that heel, extending the left hip and knee to stand up tall on the box. Exhale as you rise.
As you reach the top, do not push off the floor with the right foot; let the left leg do the work to load the glute and quad.
At the top, drive your right knee up and forward as high as you can, flexing the right hip and knee to roughly hip height or above, balancing on the planted left leg for one count.
Keep your torso upright and core tight during the knee drive so you do not lean back or lose balance.
Lower the right leg back down and step it to the floor under control, then bring the left foot down to return to the start. Inhale as you descend.
Repeat the full sequence leading with the opposite leg, alternating sides or completing all reps per side as prescribed.

name: Stiff Leg Barbell Good Morning
instructions: Set the barbell in a squat rack at about upper-chest height and load it. Working inside the rack adds safety in case you need to dump the bar.

Step under the bar and position it across the meat of your upper back and rear shoulders (the traps, slightly below the neck), not on your neck. Grip the bar with both hands just outside shoulder width to lock it tight against your back.
Unrack by bracing your core and pushing up with your legs to lift the bar off the hooks, then take one or two steps back to clear the rack.

Set your feet shoulder-width apart with toes pointing forward or slightly out. Keep your knees nearly straight with only the slightest soft bend (this is the stiff-leg version), chest up, and gaze forward.
Brace your abs hard, pull your shoulder blades together to keep the bar locked, and set a flat, neutral spine. This is your starting position.
Keeping your legs essentially stationary and your back flat, push your hips straight back and hinge forward at the hips, inhaling as you descend, lowering your torso toward parallel with the floor.
Lower only as far as you can while keeping a flat back and feeling a strong stretch in the hamstrings; do not round your lower back to gain extra depth.
Reverse the motion by squeezing your glutes and driving your hips forward to raise your torso back upright, exhaling as you rise to the starting position.
Keep the bar path controlled throughout and avoid bouncing at the bottom; the movement should be a smooth hip hinge, not a back-rounding bend.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, then carefully step forward and re-rack the bar.

name: Stiff-Legged Barbell Deadlift
instructions: Load a barbell and set it on the floor or pull it from a rack at hip height. Grasp the bar with an overhand (pronated) grip, hands just outside hip width; use straps or wrist wraps if grip limits you on heavy sets.
Stand with the bar against your thighs, feet shoulder-width or slightly narrower, toes forward, torso upright and tall.
Keep your knees only slightly bent and locked in that position for the whole set; the knees stay nearly straight throughout (this is the stiff-leg version).
Brace your core, pull your shoulders back and down, and set a flat, neutral spine with your chest up. This is your starting position.
Keeping your knees fixed and back flat, push your hips back and hinge forward, lowering the bar close to the front of your legs as if reaching toward the top of your feet. Inhale as you descend.
Lower until you feel a strong stretch in the hamstrings, typically with the bar around mid-shin; do not let your lower back round to chase more range of motion.
Keep the bar tracking close to your legs the entire descent so the load stays over your mid-foot and off your lower back.
Reverse by driving your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand back up tall, extending the hips until you return to the starting position. Exhale as you rise.
Keep the movement controlled with no jerking or bouncing at the bottom, and maintain the slight knee bend without turning it into a squat.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Stiff-Legged Dumbbell Deadlift
instructions: Grasp a dumbbell in each hand and hold them at arm's length in front of your thighs, palms facing your body (neutral grip).
Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width or slightly narrower, toes pointing forward, and your torso upright.
Set a very slight bend in your knees and keep it locked there for the entire set; the knees stay nearly straight throughout (this is the stiff-leg version).
Brace your core, draw your shoulder blades back and down, lift your chest, and set a flat, neutral spine. This is your starting position.
Keeping your knees fixed and back flat, push your hips back and hinge forward, lowering the dumbbells down the front of your legs toward the tops of your feet. Inhale as you descend.
Lower until you feel a deep stretch in the hamstrings; stop before your lower back begins to round, which protects the spine.
Keep the dumbbells close to your legs throughout so the load stays balanced over your mid-foot.
Reverse the motion by driving your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand back up tall to the starting position. Exhale as you rise.
Move smoothly and under control with no swinging or bouncing, and resist the urge to bend the knees more as you fatigue.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Stomach Vacuum
instructions: Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, and place your hands on your hips. You can also perform this kneeling on all fours or lying on your back once you are comfortable.
Keep your spine neutral, chest lifted, and shoulders relaxed. This is your starting position.
Inhale slowly and deeply through your nose, filling your lungs as fully as possible.
Exhale completely through your mouth, pushing out all the air while simultaneously drawing your stomach in and up as far as you can, as if trying to touch your navel to your spine.
At the bottom of the exhale, hold the contraction by pulling the lower abdomen inward and bracing the deep transverse abdominis muscle; you should feel a strong inward hollowing.
Hold this isometric contraction for about 20 seconds while breathing shallowly and normally through your nose, keeping the stomach pulled in the whole time.
Do not hold your breath to the point of dizziness; the goal is to keep the abdominal wall drawn in while still allowing small breaths.
Release by relaxing the abdomen and returning your stomach to the neutral starting position.
Rest briefly, then repeat for the prescribed sets, working up from 20 seconds toward 40 to 60 seconds per hold as you progress.

name: Straight Bar Bench Mid Rows
instructions: Place a loaded barbell on the floor at the end of a flat bench, with the bar running across the end of the bench so you can stand over it.
Stand up on the bench, straddling the bar with one foot on either side, feet roughly shoulder-width apart and firmly planted for balance.
Hinge at the hips, pushing your butt back and keeping your chest up, until your torso is angled forward over the bar. Maintain a flat, neutral spine throughout.
Reach down and grip the bar with a pronated (overhand) grip at about shoulder width, arms hanging straight down toward the floor. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your knees softly bent so your lower back stays flat and supported as you row.
Row the bar up to your lower chest or upper abdomen by first retracting your shoulder blades, then flexing the elbows and driving them back and up. Exhale as you pull.
Keep the movement smooth and controlled with no jerking or heaving the torso; the back and arms move the weight, not momentum.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top and pause briefly to maximize the contraction in the mid-back.
Lower the bar slowly back to full arm extension, letting it travel all the way down to a complete stretch. Inhale as you descend.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, keeping your torso angle and flat back consistent on every rep.

name: Straight Raises on Incline Bench
instructions: Set an incline bench to roughly a 30 to 45 degree angle and place a barbell on the floor behind the head end of the bench.
Lie face down (prone) on the bench so your chest is supported against the pad and your head extends just past the top edge.

Reach down and grip the barbell with a pronated (overhand) grip at about shoulder width, then lift it off the floor with straight arms so it hangs directly beneath your shoulders. This is your starting position.
Keep your arms fully extended with only a slight fixed bend in the elbows; the elbows do not bend during the movement.
Brace your core, keep your chest pressed into the pad, and avoid arching or twisting your spine.
Raise the barbell forward and up in a wide arc out in front of your head, keeping your arms straight, until your hands reach about head height or slightly above. Exhale as you lift.
Lead the movement from the shoulders and keep the bar path smooth and controlled; do not swing or use momentum from the legs.
Pause briefly at the top to feel the contraction in the front and side delts, then lower the bar back down under control to the starting position. Inhale as you lower.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, keeping the tempo controlled in both directions.

name: Straight-Arm Dumbbell Pullover
instructions: Stand a single dumbbell upright on the end of a flat bench so it is stable and ready to grasp.
Lie perpendicular across the bench so that only your upper back and shoulders rest on the pad, your torso forming a cross with the bench.
Plant your feet firmly on the floor with your knees bent at about 90 degrees, and let your hips drop slightly below the level of the bench. Your head will be off the bench.

Grasp the dumbbell with both hands by cupping your palms flat against the underside of the top plate, fingers interlocked or pressed together for a secure hold. Always confirm the dumbbell collars and plates are tight so it cannot come apart over your face.
Press the dumbbell up so it is held straight over your chest at arm's length with only a slight, fixed bend in the elbows. This is your starting position.

Keeping your arms straight and that elbow angle fixed, lower the dumbbell slowly in a wide arc back behind and below your head, inhaling as you descend, until you feel a deep stretch across the chest and lats.
Lower only as far as your shoulder mobility comfortably allows; keep your hips down and core braced so your lower back does not overarch.
Reverse the motion by pulling the dumbbell back over your chest along the same arc, exhaling as you raise it, leading with the chest and lats rather than bending the elbows.
Pause for a second at the top over your chest, then repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, keeping the movement slow and controlled throughout.

name: Straight-Arm Pulldown
instructions: Attach a straight bar to the high pulley of a cable or pulldown machine and set an appropriate weight.
Grasp the bar with a pronated (palms-down) grip slightly wider than shoulder width, then step back about two feet from the stack.
Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, knees softly bent, and hinge your torso forward at the hips by about 20 to 30 degrees with a flat, neutral spine.
Extend your arms up toward the pulley with only a slight fixed bend in the elbows; if your arms are not fully reaching the top, step back a little more until they are.
Brace your core, keep your chest up, and engage your lats so they are tight. This is your starting position.
Keeping your arms straight with that fixed elbow angle, pull the bar down in an arc by contracting the lats, driving your hands down toward the front of your thighs. Exhale as you pull.
Lead the movement from your lats and shoulders, not the triceps; the elbows stay locked at the same angle the entire rep.
Squeeze your lats hard at the bottom when the bar reaches your thighs, keeping your torso angle steady and not swinging.
Allow the bar to rise back up under control along the same arc to the fully stretched starting position. Inhale as you return.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, keeping the motion smooth and the lats engaged throughout.

name: Stride Jump Crossover
instructions: Set a sturdy plyometric box of moderate height and stand to one side of it.
Place your inside foot (the one nearest the box) flat on top of the box close to the edge, with your outside foot on the floor. Your stance is staggered across the box.
Set a slight bend in your knees and hips, keep your chest up, core braced, and let your arms be ready to swing.
Begin by swinging both arms upward and explosively pushing through the top leg to jump as high as possible off the box.
As you rise, drive the opposite knee upward toward your chest to gain height and switch your leg positions in the air.
Travel laterally over the box so you land on the opposite side from where you started, absorbing the landing with soft, bent knees.
Land in the mirror-image stance: the foot that started on the box is now on the ground, and the opposite foot is now planted on top of the box.
Stabilize for a moment, keeping your knees tracking over your toes and your core tight to control the landing.
Immediately repeat the explosive jump, crossing back over to the original side, and continue alternating for the prescribed reps.

name: Sumo Deadlift
instructions: Load the barbell on the floor and step up to it so the bar sits over the middle of your feet, almost touching your shins.
Set a very wide stance with your feet near the collars and your toes pointed out at roughly 30 to 45 degrees so your shins will line up with your feet.
Bend at the hips and knees to drop down and grip the bar with your hands directly below your shoulders and inside your legs, about shoulder-width apart. Use a double-overhand, mixed, or hook grip.
Drop your hips, lift your chest, look forward, and pull the slack out of the bar; let your arms hang straight and relax your shoulders to effectively lengthen the arms.
Brace your core hard, set a flat neutral spine, and push your knees out so they track over your toes. This is your starting position.
Take a breath and brace, then drive your feet down and out through the floor, spreading the floor apart, keeping your weight on the back half of your feet as you extend the hips and knees together.
Keep the bar tracking straight up and close to your body; the hips and shoulders should rise at the same rate without the hips shooting up first.
As the bar passes the knees, drive your hips forward into the bar, squeeze your glutes, and pull your shoulder blades together to lock out standing tall.
Do not hyperextend or lean excessively back at the top; finish upright with hips fully extended and knees locked.
Return the bar to the floor under control by pushing the hips back first, then bending the knees, keeping the bar close to your body the whole way down.
Reset your brace and position before each rep rather than bouncing the bar off the floor.

name: Sumo Deadlift with Bands
instructions: Loop short resistance bands over the ends of the loaded barbell, then step into them so the bands run under the back half of each foot, directly where you drive into the floor.
Position the bar over the middle of your feet, almost touching your shins, with the bands tensioned evenly on both sides.
Set a very wide stance with your feet near the collars and toes pointed out about 30 to 45 degrees so your shins align with your feet.
Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar with your hands inside your legs and directly below your shoulders, using a double-overhand, mixed, or hook grip.
Drop your hips, lift your chest, look forward, brace your core hard, and set a flat neutral spine. Push your knees out over your toes. This is your starting position.
Take a breath and brace, then drive your feet down and out through the floor, spreading the floor, keeping weight on the back half of your feet as you extend the hips and knees together.
Expect the band tension to increase as you rise, so accelerate through the top to overcome the added resistance near lockout.
As the bar passes the knees, drive your hips forward into the bar, squeeze your glutes, and retract your shoulder blades to lock out standing tall.
Keep the bar tracking straight and close to your body; do not let the hips rise faster than the shoulders.
Lower the bar under control against the band tension by pushing the hips back first, then bending the knees, keeping the bar close to your body.
Reset your brace and stance before each rep rather than bouncing off the floor.

name: Sumo Deadlift with Chains
instructions: Attach heavy chains to the sleeves of the loaded barbell, or drape the middle of each chain over the bar, keeping the chain ends clear of the plates so they do not snag when you lower the bar.
Position the bar over the middle of your feet, almost touching your shins.
Set a very wide stance with your feet near the collars and toes pointed out about 30 to 45 degrees so your shins line up with your feet.

Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar with your hands inside your legs and directly below your shoulders, using a double-overhand, mixed, or hook grip. Relax the shoulders to effectively lengthen the arms.
Drop your hips, lift your chest, look forward, brace your core, and set a flat neutral spine. Push your knees out over your toes. This is your starting position.
Take a breath and brace, then drive your feet down and out through the floor, spreading the floor, with your weight on the back half of your feet, extending the hips and knees together.
As more chain links lift off the floor the load increases, so keep driving and accelerate through the top of the lift to overcome the rising weight.
As the bar passes the knees, drive your hips forward into the bar, squeeze your glutes, and pull your shoulder blades together to lock out standing tall.
Keep the bar path straight and close to your body, and do not let the hips shoot up ahead of the shoulders.
Lower the bar under control by pushing the hips back first, then bending the knees, keeping the bar close to your body until the chains and plates settle on the floor.
Reset your brace and stance before each rep rather than bouncing the bar.

name: Superman
instructions: Lie face down (prone) on the floor or an exercise mat with your body fully extended and your legs straight together.
Extend your arms straight out in front of you overhead, palms down, with your neck in a neutral position and forehead near the floor. This is your starting position.
Brace your core lightly and keep your neck neutral so you do not crane your head up or strain it.
Simultaneously raise your arms, chest, and legs off the floor by contracting your lower back and squeezing your glutes, exhaling as you lift.
At the top you should look like Superman flying, with only your hips and lower abdomen still in contact with the floor.
Hold the contracted position for about two seconds, squeezing the lower back and glutes hard without jerking higher.
Lift only as high as is comfortable; the goal is a firm contraction, not maximum height that strains the spine.
Slowly lower your arms, chest, and legs back down to the floor under control, inhaling as you descend.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, keeping each rep smooth and controlled rather than bouncing off the floor.

name: Superman Hold
instructions: Lie face down (prone) on the floor or an exercise mat with your legs straight and together and your arms extended overhead, palms down.
Keep your neck in a neutral position with your gaze toward the floor so you do not strain your neck. This is your starting position.
Brace your core lightly to support your spine before you lift.
Simultaneously raise your arms, chest, and legs off the floor by contracting your lower back and squeezing your glutes, so only your hips and lower abdomen remain on the ground.
Exhale as you lift and hold the top position, keeping a steady squeeze in your glutes and lower back throughout.
Lift only to a comfortable height and avoid overarching the neck or lower back; quality of contraction matters more than height.
Maintain the hold for the prescribed time while breathing steadily and shallowly rather than holding your breath.
Lower your arms, chest, and legs back to the floor under control to finish the set.

name: Supine Chest Throw
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a mat or padded floor with your knees bent to roughly 90 degrees and feet planted hip-width apart for a stable base.
Press your lower back gently into the floor and brace your core so your torso stays anchored; your hips and back should not lift during the throw.
Hold a light-to-moderate medicine ball with both hands, palms cupped on the underside of the ball and thumbs pointing inward, fingers spread for control.
Start with the ball resting on your chest, elbows flared out to the sides and pointing toward the floor, as if at the bottom of a bench press.
Inhale and set your shoulder blades, then explosively extend both arms straight up, driving the ball vertically through your fingertips at the top.
Release the ball at full extension so it travels as high and as straight up as possible, exhaling sharply as you throw.
Track the ball with your eyes the entire time and keep your head on the floor so you can react.
Catch the ball with both hands as it descends, letting your elbows bend to absorb the impact and decelerate it back to your chest.
Reset to the chest position, re-brace, and repeat for the prescribed reps, prioritizing maximal speed and a clean vertical path over throwing for height alone.
Common mistakes: letting the ball drift forward instead of straight up, and using a ball heavy enough that you can no longer throw explosively.

name: Supine One-Arm Overhead Throw
instructions: Lie on your back on a mat with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, roughly hip- to shoulder-width apart, positioned so you can sit up toward a partner or sturdy wall a few feet in front of you.
Hold a light medicine ball in one hand only, cradling it in your palm with fingers spread; the opposite arm rests at your side or is used for balance.

Extend the ball-side arm fully overhead behind you, reaching back so the ball nearly touches the floor above your head and you feel a stretch through your abs and the front of your shoulder. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and exhale as you initiate the movement, snapping your shoulder and arm forward while simultaneously crunching your trunk up off the floor.
Sweep the arm in a single fluid arc and release the ball forward at the top of the sit-up, aiming for maximum distance toward your partner or the wall.
Keep the throwing elbow relatively extended and lead with the shoulder; the power should come from your abs and shoulder working together, not from the elbow alone.
Allow your sit-up momentum to carry you up but stay controlled so you do not strain your neck or lower back.
Catch or retrieve the ball, lie back down, re-extend the arm overhead, and repeat for the prescribed reps before switching to the other arm.
Common mistakes: throwing only with the arm while keeping the torso flat, and using a ball too heavy to release explosively.

name: Supine Two-Arm Overhead Throw
instructions: Lie on your back on a mat with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip- to shoulder-width apart, facing a partner or a solid wall a few feet ahead.
Hold a medicine ball with both hands, fingers spread around the sides and thumbs near each other for control.
Extend both arms fully overhead and behind you, lowering the ball toward the floor above your head until you feel a stretch through your abdominals and lats. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and take a breath, keeping your lower back from over-arching by gently engaging your abs.
Exhale forcefully and explode the movement by snapping both arms forward while crunching your torso up off the floor in one coordinated motion.
Release the ball forward and slightly upward at the peak of the sit-up, driving for maximum distance toward your partner or wall.
Keep the arms relatively straight and let the power originate from your abs and shoulders rather than from bending the elbows.
Stay controlled through the sit-up to protect your neck and lumbar spine, keeping your chin slightly tucked.
Retrieve the ball, lie back, reach overhead again to reset, and repeat for the prescribed reps.
Common mistakes: arching the lower back excessively at the start, and relying on arm strength instead of a powerful trunk flexion.

name: Suspended Fallout
instructions: Anchor your suspension trainer securely to a rack or fixed overhead point and adjust the straps so the handles hang at about waist height or slightly below.
Stand facing away from the anchor, grasp a handle in each hand with a neutral grip (palms facing each other) and arms extended straight in front of you.

Walk your feet back and lean forward into the straps, taking an incline plank position with a straight line from head to heels and your weight supported through the handles. This is your starting position.
Brace your core hard, squeeze your glutes, and tuck your ribs down so your spine stays neutral with no sag in the lower back.
Keeping your arms locked straight, inhale and slowly let your body fall forward by allowing your shoulders to flex, raising your arms up and over your head as you descend toward the floor.
Lower only as far as you can while maintaining a perfectly rigid, straight torso; the shoulders are the only joints that move.
Pause at the deepest point where your arms are extended overhead and you feel a strong stretch and contraction through your abs.
Exhale and reverse the motion, pulling your arms back down in front of you and driving your body back to the upright starting plank using your core, not your lower back.
Adjust difficulty by walking your feet closer to the anchor (harder) or farther away and more upright (easier).
Common mistakes: letting the hips sag or pike, and bending the elbows to cheat the range of motion.

name: Suspended Push-Up
instructions: Anchor your suspension trainer securely to the top of a rack or a fixed overhead point and adjust the straps so the handles hang roughly mid-shin to knee height.
Grasp a handle in each hand with a neutral or slightly angled grip, then walk your feet back and lean forward into a plank push-up position with arms fully extended.
Set your body in a straight rigid line from head to heels, hands stacked under your shoulders, feet together or hip-width for balance. This is your starting position.
Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and pull your shoulder blades down and slightly back to stabilize the inherently unstable handles.
Inhale and descend slowly by flexing your elbows, keeping them tucked at roughly a 45-degree angle to your torso rather than flaring wide.
Lower until your elbows break past 90 degrees and your chest reaches the level of the handles, fighting to keep the straps from wobbling.
Pause briefly at the bottom while maintaining a straight, tight torso with no hip sag.
Exhale and press back up through your palms to full arm extension, controlling the straps the entire way.
Make it harder by walking your feet farther back to lower your body angle, or easier by standing more upright.
Common mistakes: letting the hips drop, flaring the elbows out wide, and allowing the handles to swing from poor shoulder stability.

name: Suspended Reverse Crunch
instructions: Anchor your suspension trainer to a rack and adjust the straps so the foot cradles hang about a foot off the floor.
Sit on the floor facing away from the anchor, place one foot then the other into the cradles, and turn over into a push-up plank position with hands under your shoulders.
Set a straight line from head to heels with your feet suspended in the straps, core braced and hips level so they neither sag nor pike. This is your starting position.
Pull your shoulder blades down and grip the floor with your hands to create a stable upper-body base.
Exhale and begin the movement by flexing your knees and hips, drawing your knees up toward your chest.
As your knees travel forward, posteriorly tilt your pelvis and let your lower spine round so the work stays in your abs rather than your hip flexors.
Continue until your knees are tucked close to your torso and your abs are fully contracted at the top.
Pause briefly, then inhale and slowly extend your legs back out under control to the straight starting plank.
Keep the movement controlled throughout to manage the swing of the suspended straps.
Common mistakes: letting the hips sag in the start position, swinging the legs for momentum, and crunching only at the hips without tilting the pelvis.

name: Suspended Row
instructions: Anchor your suspension trainer securely overhead and adjust the straps so the handles hang at about chest height when you stand upright.
Grasp a handle in each hand with a neutral grip (palms facing each other), arms fully extended in front of you.
Walk your feet forward and lean back, taking the weight onto the straps so your body forms a straight, rigid line from head to heels. This is your starting position.
Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and keep your chest up and head neutral with no sag in the hips.
Initiate the pull by retracting your shoulder blades, then flex your elbows to row your chest up toward the handles.
Drive your elbows back and down alongside your torso, keeping your wrists straight and pulling until the handles reach the sides of your chest.
Exhale through the pull and squeeze your mid-back muscles at the top of the contraction.
Pause briefly, then inhale and lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension under control, keeping the body rigid.
Adjust difficulty by walking your feet farther forward to make your body more horizontal (harder) or more upright (easier).
Common mistakes: leading with the hands instead of the shoulder blades, letting the hips sag, and shortening the range by not fully extending the arms at the bottom.

name: Suspended Split Squat
instructions: Anchor your suspension trainer and adjust the straps so a single foot cradle hangs 18 to 30 inches off the floor.
Stand facing away from the anchor and place the top of your rear foot into the cradle behind you, laces down, leaving your front foot planted a stride length ahead.
Set your front foot flat with weight on the heel and midfoot, stand tall with your chest up and gaze forward, and let your front knee carry a slight bend. This is your starting position.
Brace your core, keep your torso upright, and let your arms hang or rest on your hips for balance.
Inhale and descend by flexing your front knee and hip, lowering straight down until your front thigh approaches parallel to the floor and your rear knee drops beneath your hip.
Keep your weight on the heel of your front foot and let your front knee track in line with your toes, not caving inward.
Keep the suspended rear leg relaxed; it provides balance and stretch rather than driving the movement.
Pause at the bottom, then exhale and reverse the motion, pushing through your front heel to extend the hip and knee back to standing.
Complete all prescribed reps on one leg, then switch the rear foot to the other side.
Common mistakes: leaning the torso too far forward, letting the front knee drift past or inside the toes, and pushing through the toes instead of the heel.

name: Svend Press
instructions: Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, and core braced so your torso stays stable throughout.
Take two lightweight weight plates (smooth-sided) and sandwich them together between your palms, fingers pointing forward and thumbs up.
Press the plates firmly against each other and hold them flat against the center of your chest; the constant inward squeeze creates the isometric chest contraction that drives this exercise.
Keep your shoulders down and back, chest up, and elbows pointing out to the sides. This is your starting position.
Maintaining maximum inward pressure on the plates, exhale and press your hands straight out in front of you until your arms are fully extended at chest height.
Squeeze your chest hard at full extension and consciously keep the plates from slipping by pressing your palms together throughout.
Pause for a moment at the top while keeping the chest contracted.
Inhale and slowly draw the plates back to your chest along the same horizontal path, never releasing the inward squeeze.
Move at a controlled tempo; this is a high-tension, light-weight exercise where the squeeze matters more than the load.
Common mistakes: relaxing the inward pressure so the plates loosen, pressing upward instead of straight forward, and using plates too heavy to keep pinned together.

name: T-Bar Row with Handle
instructions: Wedge one end of a barbell into a landmine attachment or a sturdy corner so it cannot slide, and load the free end with an appropriate weight.
Straddle the bar facing the loaded end, and hook a Double-D (V-grip) row handle around the bar just behind the collar so the weight is centered.
Squat down with a flat back, grip the handle with both hands in a neutral grip, then drive through your hips and legs to lift the weight and stand up.
Set a wide, athletic stance with knees slightly bent, hinge at the hips to push your butt back, and keep your chest up and back flat at a torso angle of roughly 45 degrees.
Let your arms hang fully extended with the handle below your chest, shoulders slightly forward in a controlled stretch. This is your starting position.
Brace your core, then pull the handle toward your upper abdomen by first retracting your shoulder blades and then flexing your elbows.
