Drive your elbows up and back, keeping them close to your body, and exhale as you squeeze your mid-back at the top.
Pause briefly when the handle reaches your torso and your shoulder blades are fully retracted.
Inhale and lower the weight slowly back to full arm extension, keeping your back flat and torso angle fixed.
Common mistakes: jerking the weight with your lower back or hips to cheat, rounding the spine, and standing too upright so the pull becomes a shrug instead of a row.

name: Tate Press
instructions: Sit on the end of a flat bench with a dumbbell resting on each thigh, palms facing each other.
Lie back while using your thighs to kick the dumbbells up, one at a time, until you hold them above your chest.
Position the dumbbells slightly wider than shoulder width with a pronated grip (palms facing forward, toward your feet) and your elbows flared out to the sides. This is your starting position.
Plant your feet flat on the floor, keep your glutes and upper back on the bench, and brace your core to stabilize your torso.
Keeping your upper arms fixed in position, inhale and slowly lower the dumbbells inward and down in a semicircular arc until they nearly touch the top of your chest.
Maintain full control of the dumbbells throughout the descent and do not let the upper arms move or the weights rest on your chest.
Exhale and press the dumbbells back up along the same semicircular path using your triceps, keeping the weights drawn toward each other as they rise.
Lock out your arms in the top contracted position and squeeze your triceps for a one-second hold.
Lower under control, taking roughly twice as long on the descent as the ascent.
Common mistakes: letting the upper arms drift instead of keeping them stationary, using too much weight that breaks form, and resting the dumbbells on the chest between reps.

name: The Straddle
instructions: Sit upright on the floor with a tall, lengthened spine and your weight balanced on your sit bones.
Extend both legs straight out in front of you and spread them apart into a wide V, keeping your knees facing the ceiling and toes pointing up.
Press the backs of your thighs and calves gently into the floor and keep your legs straight without harshly locking the knees.
Place your hands on the floor in front of you and inhale to lengthen your spine even taller.
Exhale and hinge forward from your hips, walking your hands out and leaning your chest toward the floor as far as is comfortable while keeping your back relatively flat.
Aim to feel a steady stretch through your hamstrings and inner thighs, never a sharp or painful pull.
Hold the stretch for 10 to 20 seconds, breathing slowly and relaxing a little deeper on each exhale.
Slowly walk your hands back and sit up to release.
Common mistakes: rounding the lower back to reach farther, and bouncing into the stretch instead of holding it steadily.

name: Thigh Abductor
instructions: Select an appropriate weight on the abductor machine, then sit down with your back flat against the pad.
Position your outer thighs and knees against the pads with your legs together at the start, feet resting on the footplates.
Grip the handles on each side of the seat to anchor your upper body, and sit tall with your back against the backrest. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your entire upper body, from the waist up, stationary throughout the movement.
Exhale and slowly press your legs outward against the pads, driving your knees apart as far as the machine comfortably allows.
Lead the movement with your outer thighs and glutes, keeping your feet and knees aligned and your torso still.
Pause and squeeze your glutes and outer hips for a second at the fully open position.
Inhale and slowly return your legs back toward each other under control, resisting the pad on the way in rather than letting it snap shut.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, keeping the tempo smooth.
Common mistakes: leaning the torso forward or jerking the legs open for momentum, and letting the pads slam back without control on the return.

name: Thigh Adductor
instructions: Select an appropriate weight on the adductor machine, then sit down with your back flat against the pad.
Position your legs so the inner thighs and knees rest against the inside of the leg pads, with your legs spread apart at the start and feet on the footplates.
Grip the handles on each side of the seat to stabilize your upper body, and sit tall against the backrest. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your entire upper body, from the waist up, stationary throughout the movement.
Exhale and slowly squeeze your legs together against the pads, drawing your knees toward each other using your inner-thigh muscles.
Keep the movement smooth and controlled; avoid any fast jerking motion that could strain the groin.
Pause and feel the contraction in your inner thighs for a second when your knees come together.
Inhale and slowly let your legs return to the spread starting position under control, resisting the pads on the way out rather than letting them fling open.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, keeping the tempo steady.
Common mistakes: using too much weight that forces jerky reps, and letting the legs snap open at the end of each rep instead of controlling the stretch.

name: Thoracic Rotation
instructions: Get onto all fours (quadruped) with your hands directly under your shoulders and your knees directly under your hips.
Set a neutral spine with a flat back, core lightly braced, and head in line with your torso.
Place one hand behind your head with the elbow pointing out to the side; the other hand stays planted on the floor for support.
Keeping your hips level and your lower back stable, exhale and rotate your raised elbow downward, bringing it toward the opposite supporting wrist to wind up the rotation.
Reverse the motion and rotate that same elbow up toward the ceiling, opening your chest and turning through your mid-back (thoracic spine).
Follow your moving elbow with your eyes and let your head turn naturally with the rotation, rotating as far as feels comfortable.
Keep the movement coming from your upper back, not from arching your lower back or twisting your hips.
Return to the start and repeat for the prescribed reps, then switch the hand position and rotate to the other side.
Common mistakes: rotating from the lumbar spine or hips instead of the thoracic region, and letting the supporting arm collapse.

name: Thread the Needle
instructions: Begin on all fours (quadruped) with your hands under your shoulders and knees under your hips, spine neutral and core gently engaged.
Inhale and reach one arm out to the side, then thread it underneath your body, sliding it across the floor with the palm facing up.
Continue sliding the arm through until your shoulder and the side of your head lower gently to the floor.
Keep your hips up and stacked over your knees so the stretch concentrates in your upper back and the back of your shoulder.
Let the supporting hand stay planted or reach it overhead along the floor to deepen the rotation through your thoracic spine.
Relax into the position, breathing slowly and allowing your mid-back and shoulder to release.
Hold the stretch for 20 to 30 seconds, keeping the movement gentle and pain-free.
Press back up through the supporting hand, unwind your threaded arm to return to all fours, then repeat on the other side.
Common mistakes: collapsing the hips toward the floor, and forcing the rotation rather than easing into a comfortable stretch.

name: Tire Flip
instructions: Stand facing a large tire lying flat on the ground with your feet roughly hip-to-shoulder width apart and your toes a few inches back from the tire's edge so your shins can angle into it.

Squat down into a position closer to a deadlift than a full squat, hinging at the hips and bending the knees, and slide your hands under the bottom tread of the tire with an underhand grip, fingers curled into the tread.
Drive your chest forward and down into the tire so your torso is pressed against it, keeping your back flat and your spine neutral, with your gaze forward.
Brace your core and take a sharp breath before initiating the lift.
Explosively extend through the hips, knees, and ankles in one powerful drive, pushing into the tire and up rather than just pulling, exhaling forcefully as you accelerate.
As the tire rotates up toward a 45-degree angle and the momentum carries it, quickly step in close and drive one knee up into the lower face of the tire to support it momentarily.
Rapidly switch your hands from the underhand bottom grip to a pushing position on the upper portion of the tire, palms flat.
Push the tire forward and over as hard as possible, extending your arms and hips to complete the flip so it lands flat again.
Reset your stance, walk to the new edge of the tire, and repeat for the prescribed reps, moving quickly but never letting your lower back round.

Keep the tempo explosive on the lift but stay controlled in your setup; the most common mistake is squatting too deep or trying to curl the tire with your arms instead of driving with the legs and hips.

name: Toe Touchers
instructions: Lie flat on your back on the floor or an exercise mat with your spine and lower back pressed firmly into the surface.

Bring your legs together so they touch, then slowly raise them toward the ceiling until they are nearly perpendicular to the floor, keeping a slight bend at the knees so your feet stay roughly parallel to the floor overhead.
Extend your arms straight up off the floor at about a 45-degree angle, reaching toward your feet with palms facing each other; this is your starting position.
Inhale to set your brace, keeping your lower back glued to the floor throughout.
Exhale as you contract your abs and curl your shoulder blades and upper torso off the floor, reaching your hands up to try to touch your toes.
Pause for a moment at the top, squeezing your abdominals hard while your arms stay long and pointed toward your toes.
Inhale as you slowly and under control lower your torso and arms back down to the starting position, resisting the descent rather than dropping.
Move at a deliberate tempo and lead with your abs, not your arms; avoid yanking with your shoulders or letting your legs swing, and keep the crunch coming from the ribcage flexing toward the pelvis.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Toe Walk
instructions: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, arms relaxed at your sides or held out for balance, and your core lightly braced.
Press through the balls of both feet to rise up onto your toes, lifting both heels as high as you can.
Keep your knees nearly straight and your ankles firm so you are balancing on the balls of your feet.
Begin walking forward in small, controlled steps while staying high on your toes, never letting your heels touch the ground between steps.
Maintain a tall posture with your chest up, shoulders back, and gaze forward to help you balance.
Breathe steadily and naturally throughout; do not hold your breath.
Move at a slow, deliberate tempo, focusing on a strong contraction in your calves with each step.
Walk for the prescribed distance or time, then lower your heels under control to finish.
Avoid rushing or letting your heels dip between steps; the goal is to keep constant tension on the calves by staying as high as possible the entire time.

name: Toes-to-Bar
instructions: Stand under a pull-up bar and grip it with an overhand (pronated) grip slightly wider than shoulder width, then let your body hang fully with your arms straight.
Engage your shoulders by pulling them down slightly away from your ears and brace your core so you are in an active hang, not a dead hang.
Establish a stable starting position with your legs together and only a slight bend in the knees, letting any swing settle before you begin.
Inhale to brace, then exhale as you drive your toes up toward the bar by flexing your hips and crunching your abs, keeping your legs fairly straight.
Continue lifting until your toes touch or come close to the bar between your hands, using your lats to pull the bar slightly back as your feet rise.
Briefly pause at the top with your abs and hip flexors fully contracted.
Inhale as you lower your legs back down under control to the starting hang, resisting gravity rather than dropping.
Keep the movement controlled and avoid kipping or swinging; if you cannot reach the bar with straight legs, bend the knees slightly but still drive from the abs, not momentum.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, keeping your grip firm and shoulders active throughout.

name: Torso Rotation
instructions: Stand upright with your feet shoulder-width apart and a slight bend in your knees, holding an exercise ball with both hands.
Extend your arms in front of you so the ball is straight out at about chest height, keeping a small bend in the elbows; this is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your hips and lower body facing forward and relatively still throughout the movement.
Exhale as you rotate your torso smoothly to one side, keeping your eyes on the ball and your arms extended, twisting from the trunk rather than swinging your arms.
Pause briefly at the end of the rotation, feeling the contraction in your obliques.
Inhale as you rotate back through the center and continue smoothly to the opposite side.
Keep a controlled, deliberate tempo and let the rotation come from your waist and obliques, not from your shoulders or your hips swiveling.
Maintain a tall posture with your chest up and avoid leaning back or letting your lower back arch.
Repeat, alternating sides, for 10 to 20 repetitions per side.

name: Trail Running/Walking
instructions: Wear sturdy, well-fitting trail shoes with good grip and lace them snugly to protect your ankles on uneven terrain.
Begin at an easy walking or jogging pace on flat ground for a few minutes to warm up your calves, hamstrings, glutes, and quads before tackling hills.
Stand tall with a slight forward lean from the ankles, eyes scanning the trail a few steps ahead for roots, rocks, and changes in footing.
When climbing uphill, drive through your calves and glutes, shorten your stride, and pump your arms to help propel yourself; lean slightly into the hill.
Breathe rhythmically and deeply, matching your breath to your stride, and slow your pace as needed to keep your breathing controlled on steep sections.
On the descent, take smaller steps, keep your knees bent to absorb impact through the joints and ankles, and slow down to maintain control and avoid falling.
Keep your core engaged the whole time to stabilize your torso over uneven ground.
Maintain a steady, sustainable effort rather than sprinting; a 150 lb person can burn over 200 calories in 30 minutes walking uphill and well over 500 calories running the trail.
Cool down with a few minutes of easy walking at the end, and stretch your calves and hamstrings once finished.

name: Trap Bar Deadlift
instructions: Load a trap bar (hex bar) to an appropriate weight resting on the ground and step into the center of the frame so you are surrounded by the bar.
Set your feet about hip-width apart with your weight balanced over your midfoot, centered between the handles.
Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to lower down and grasp both handles with a neutral grip, arms straight and directly at your sides.
Set your back flat with a neutral spine, lift your chest, pull your shoulders back, and look forward; your hips should sit between your knees and shoulders.
Take a big breath into your belly and brace your core hard before you pull.
Initiate the lift by driving through your heels, pushing the floor away, and extending your hips and knees together so the bar rises in a straight vertical line.
Stand fully upright at the top with your hips and knees locked out and shoulders back, without leaning back or hyperextending; exhale as you pass the hardest point.
Lower the weight under control by hinging the hips back and bending the knees, keeping the bar close and your back flat, until the plates touch the floor.
Reset your brace and position between reps; never allow your lower back to round, and keep the bar handles pressed evenly into your hands so the load stays centered.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Tree Pose
instructions: Stand tall with your feet together, weight evenly distributed, arms relaxed at your sides, and your gaze fixed on a single steady point in front of you.
Shift your weight onto one leg and root that foot firmly into the floor, spreading your toes and engaging the muscles of that leg, glute, and ankle for stability.
Bend the opposite knee and place the sole of that foot against your inner thigh or inner calf, pressing the foot and leg together; never place the foot directly on the side of the knee.
Open the bent knee out to the side while keeping your hips square and level facing forward.
Bring your palms together at your chest in a prayer position, or extend your arms overhead, and find a steady gaze to help you balance.
Breathe slowly and evenly through your nose, lengthening your spine and lifting through the crown of your head with each inhale.
Keep your standing leg active and your core engaged to resist wobbling, pressing the lifted foot and standing leg into each other for stability.
Hold the pose for the prescribed number of breaths or time, staying relaxed in the face and shoulders.
Slowly release the lifted foot back to the floor with control, then repeat on the opposite side.

name: Tricep Dumbbell Kickback
instructions: Hold a dumbbell in each hand with your palms facing your torso (neutral grip), standing with feet about hip-width apart and a slight bend in your knees.
Hinge forward at the waist until your torso is almost parallel to the floor, keeping your back flat and your head up with your gaze slightly forward.

Pull your upper arms in tight against your sides and raise your elbows until your upper arms are parallel to the floor, with your forearms hanging straight down so each arm forms a 90-degree angle; this is your starting position.
Keeping your upper arms completely stationary and pinned to your sides, exhale as you contract your triceps to extend your forearms back until your arms are fully straight.
Squeeze your triceps hard at the top with your arms fully extended and roughly parallel to the floor, holding for a brief pause.
Inhale as you slowly lower the dumbbells back to the 90-degree starting position under control.
Use a controlled tempo throughout and focus on moving only the forearm; the most common mistake is letting the upper arm drop or swing, which removes tension from the triceps.
Keep your wrists firm and avoid using momentum to throw the weights back.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Tricep Side Stretch
instructions: Stand or sit tall with good posture, shoulders relaxed and down, and your core lightly engaged.
Bring your right arm straight across the front of your body toward your left shoulder.
Use your left hand to gently hold just above the right elbow and draw the right arm closer across your chest until you feel a comfortable stretch in the back of the upper arm and shoulder.
Keep the stretch gentle and never force it; you should feel a mild pull, not pain.
Breathe slowly and deeply, relaxing further into the stretch with each exhale.
Hold for 10 to 20 seconds while keeping your shoulders down and avoiding shrugging toward your ears.
Release the right arm slowly and return to a neutral position.
Repeat the stretch on the left arm, holding for the same duration.

name: Triceps Overhead Extension with Rope
instructions: Attach a rope to a low pulley and select an appropriate weight on the stack.
Grasp both ends of the rope with a neutral grip, palms facing each other, and turn to face away from the cable machine.
Step forward and bring your hands up so the rope is behind your head, with your elbows bent and pointing straight up toward the ceiling.
Stagger your stance with one foot slightly forward and lean gently away from the machine to create stability; this is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your upper arms fixed in place beside your head, elbows pointing up throughout.
Exhale as you extend through the elbows, driving your hands up and forward above your head until your arms are nearly fully straight.
Squeeze your triceps hard at the top of the movement, holding briefly for peak contraction.
Inhale as you slowly lower the rope back behind your head under control, allowing your elbows to bend fully without letting your upper arms drift.
Keep a controlled eccentric and avoid flaring the elbows out wide or letting them drop forward; the upper arms should stay locked in position with only the forearms moving.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Triceps Pushdown
instructions: Attach a straight or slightly angled bar to a high pulley and select an appropriate weight.
Grasp the bar with an overhand grip (palms facing down) at about shoulder width and step back so the cable has tension.
Stand upright with your torso straight and a very slight forward lean, feet about hip-width apart for a stable base.
Tuck your upper arms in close to your sides and keep them perpendicular to the floor, with your forearms pointing up toward the pulley as they hold the bar; this is your starting position.
Exhale as you contract your triceps to push the bar down until it nearly touches the front of your thighs and your arms are fully extended straight down.
Keep your upper arms stationary against your torso the entire time so only your forearms move.
Hold the fully contracted position for a second, squeezing your triceps hard.
Inhale as you slowly let the bar rise back to the starting position under control, allowing your elbows to bend to about 90 degrees without letting them drift forward.
Maintain a controlled tempo and avoid leaning over the bar or using your bodyweight and shoulders to push it down; keep the work in the triceps.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Triceps Pushdown - Rope Attachment
instructions: Attach a rope attachment to a high pulley and select an appropriate weight.
Grasp the rope with a neutral grip, palms facing each other, and step back so the cable is under tension.
Stand upright with your torso straight and a very slight forward lean, feet about hip-width apart for stability.
Tuck your upper arms close to your sides and keep them perpendicular to the floor, with your forearms pointing up toward the pulley; this is your starting position.
Exhale as you contract your triceps to drive the rope down, and as your arms approach full extension spread the two ends of the rope apart, bringing each hand toward the outside of your thighs.
Finish with your arms fully extended and perpendicular to the floor, knuckles rotated slightly outward for a strong peak contraction.
Keep your upper arms stationary against your torso so that only your forearms move throughout.
Hold the contracted position for a second, squeezing the triceps hard.
Inhale as you slowly let the rope rise back to the starting position under control, bringing your hands back together as your elbows bend.
Use a controlled tempo and avoid leaning into the rope or letting your elbows flare forward; the spreading of the rope at the bottom is what maximizes the triceps contraction.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Triceps Pushdown - V-Bar Attachment
instructions: Attach a V-bar to a high pulley and select an appropriate weight.
Grasp the V-bar with an overhand grip (palms facing down and inward) so your thumbs sit higher than your little fingers, and step back so the cable is under tension.
Stand upright with your torso straight and a very slight forward lean, feet about hip-width apart for a stable base.
Tuck your upper arms close to your sides and keep them perpendicular to the floor, with your forearms pointing up toward the pulley as they hold the bar; this is your starting position.
Exhale as you contract your triceps to push the bar down until it nearly touches the front of your thighs and your arms are fully extended straight down.
Keep your upper arms stationary against your torso the entire time so only your forearms move.
Hold the fully contracted position for a second, squeezing the triceps hard.
Inhale as you slowly let the V-bar rise back to the starting position under control, allowing your elbows to bend without letting them drift forward.
Maintain a controlled tempo and avoid using your shoulders or bodyweight to push the bar down; keep your elbows pinned and the tension in the triceps.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Triceps Stretch
instructions: Stand or sit tall with good posture, your chest lifted, and your core lightly engaged.
Raise one arm overhead, then bend the elbow so that hand reaches down behind your head toward the middle of your upper back.
Reach across with your opposite hand and grasp the bent elbow.
Gently pull the elbow back and toward the center of your head until you feel a comfortable stretch along the back of the upper arm and down the side of your lat.
Keep the stretch gentle and never force it past a mild, comfortable pull.
Breathe slowly and deeply, relaxing a little deeper into the stretch with each exhale, and keep your shoulders down rather than shrugged.
Hold for 10 to 20 seconds, keeping your torso upright and avoiding any side-bending or arching of the lower back.
Release the arm slowly and return to neutral, then repeat the stretch on the other side.

name: Tuck Crunch
instructions: Lie flat on your back on the floor or an exercise mat with your spine and lower back pressed firmly into the surface.

Cross your legs by wrapping one ankle over the other, then raise your legs until your thighs are perpendicular to the floor with a slight bend at the knees, so your shins and toes stay roughly parallel to the floor.
Lift your arms from the floor and cross them over your chest; this is your starting position.
Inhale to set your brace, keeping your lower back pressed firmly into the floor throughout.
Exhale as you contract your abs and slowly curl your shoulder blades and upper torso off the floor, crunching your ribcage toward your pelvis.
Pause briefly at the top, squeezing your abdominals hard.
Inhale as you slowly lower your torso back down to the starting position under control, resisting the descent rather than flopping back.
Keep your legs still in the tucked position and avoid pulling with your neck or swinging your legs to generate momentum.
Use a controlled tempo and focus on the abs doing the work; the most common mistake is rushing the reps and using hip flexors instead of the abdominals.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Tuck Front Lever
instructions: Set up under a sturdy pull-up bar that is high enough that your feet will not touch the ground when you hang. Chalk your hands if needed for grip security.
Jump or reach up and grip the bar with a pronated (overhand) grip at roughly shoulder width, arms fully extended, hanging in a dead hang.
Depress and retract your shoulder blades, pulling them down and back away from your ears so your shoulders are packed and active rather than passively hanging.
Brace your core hard, posteriorly tilt your pelvis, and tuck your knees tightly into your chest so your shins are close to your thighs.
Exhale as you pull down on the bar with straight arms and lean your shoulders back, raising your hips until your torso is horizontal and parallel to the floor, back facing the ground.
Keep your arms locked straight throughout; the movement comes from your lats and shoulders driving the bar toward your hips, not from bending the elbows.
Hold the horizontal tuck position with a flat, braced torso, breathing in short controlled breaths while keeping the core locked.
Maintain the hold for the prescribed time, keeping hips level with shoulders and resisting the urge to let the hips sag toward the floor.
To finish, control the descent of your hips and lower back to a passive hang under tension rather than dropping.
Form cue: think about pulling the bar down to your waist with straight arms to keep the lats engaged, and never let your shoulders shrug up toward your ears.

name: Two-Arm Dumbbell Preacher Curl
instructions: Adjust the preacher bench so the top of the pad sits just below your armpits when seated; if using an incline bench, set it to a steep angle and drape your arms over the top.
Sit down and grab a dumbbell in each hand with a supinated (palms-up) grip, then lay the backs of your upper arms flat against the pad so your armpits rest near the top edge.
Extend your arms so the dumbbells hang at roughly shoulder height with a slight bend retained at the elbow; sit tall with your chest against the top of the pad. This is your starting position.
Inhale as you slowly lower both dumbbells under control until your upper arms are nearly fully extended and you feel a deep stretch in the biceps, keeping the upper arms pinned to the pad.
Take about 2-3 seconds on the lowering (eccentric) phase and avoid bouncing or fully snapping the elbows straight at the bottom, which stresses the joint.
Exhale as you curl both dumbbells upward by contracting the biceps, bringing the weights up to shoulder height until the biceps are fully contracted.
Squeeze the biceps hard for a one-second pause at the top of the contraction.
Keep your upper arms and elbows firmly planted on the pad the entire set; do not let them slide up or lift off.
Form cue: let the elbows do the work and keep the wrists neutral and stacked rather than curling them, so the load stays on the biceps and off the forearms.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, controlling both directions evenly.

name: Two-Arm Kettlebell Clean
instructions: Stand with your feet roughly shoulder-width apart and place two kettlebells on the floor between your feet, handles aligned with each other.
Push your hips back into a hinge, keep your back flat and chest up, look straight ahead, and grip a kettlebell in each hand with a firm overhand grip. This is your starting position.
Inhale and brace your core, keeping the shoulders pulled back and the spine neutral.
Drive explosively through your legs and hips, extending your knees and snapping your hips forward to generate upward momentum on the kettlebells.
As the kettlebells rise, pull them in close to your body and rotate your wrists around the bells so they settle into the rack position on the front of your shoulders, palms facing in.
Tame the arc by keeping the elbows tucked to your ribs as the bells flip up, so they land softly on the forearms rather than crashing onto the wrists.
Exhale as the kettlebells reach the racked position and stand fully upright with a stable, braced trunk.
Inhale as you guide the kettlebells back down, letting them swing between the legs as you hinge at the hips to the starting position.
Tempo: the lift up is explosive and powered by the legs and hips, while the lowering is controlled through the hip hinge.

Form cue: the clean is a hip-driven movement, not an arm curl; keep the arms relaxed and let the hip snap do the work, and avoid letting the kettlebells bang your wrists by catching them with soft elbows.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Two-Arm Kettlebell Jerk
instructions: Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart with two kettlebells on the floor between your feet, and clean them to the rack position by hinging at the hips and driving through the legs to swing them up to your shoulders.

In the rack position, the kettlebells rest on the front of your shoulders with palms facing forward, elbows tucked in, and the bells supported by your forearms; stand tall and braced. This is your starting position.
Inhale, brace your core, and keep your torso upright with weight balanced over your midfoot.
Dip by bending the knees a few inches in a quick quarter-squat, keeping the torso vertical and the kettlebells riding down with your shoulders.
Reverse rapidly and explosively, driving through the legs to extend the hips and knees and propel both kettlebells upward off your shoulders.
Exhale sharply as you punch your arms up; immediately after the leg drive, dip a second time and drop your body under the kettlebells to receive them.
Catch the kettlebells overhead with arms locked out straight, wrists stacked over the shoulders and elbows fully extended, in a partial squat.
Stand up fully from the dip to finish with the kettlebells locked out overhead, body stacked and stable.
Lower the kettlebells back to the rack position under control, absorbing the descent by bending the knees slightly.

Form cue: the overhead lockout is driven by your legs, not your shoulders; the second dip lets you get under the weight quickly, and your arms should be straight and rigid at the top rather than pressing.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, maintaining a tight rack between reps.

name: Two-Arm Kettlebell Military Press
instructions: Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart and clean two kettlebells to the rack position by hinging at the hips and driving through the legs to swing them up to your shoulders.

Settle into the rack with the kettlebells resting on the fronts of your shoulders, palms facing forward, elbows tucked to your ribs and the bells supported by the forearms. This is your starting position.
Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and engage your lats to create a stable base; stand tall with a neutral spine.
Inhale and, keeping your legs and hips completely still with no dip or leg drive, press both kettlebells straight up and slightly out.

Exhale as you press; as the kettlebells pass your head, move your head back slightly and lean into the weights so the bells finish racked behind the line of your head with arms fully locked out overhead.
Pause briefly at the top with the kettlebells stacked over your shoulders, arms straight, and wrists neutral.
Inhale as you lower the kettlebells under control back down to the rack position, taking about 2-3 seconds on the descent.
Keep your lats, glutes, and stomach contracted throughout for stability and to protect the lower back from arching.

Form cue: this is a strict press with no leg or hip momentum; keep the ribs down and core braced so you do not lean back excessively, and let the wrists stay straight so the load sits over the forearm bones.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Two-Arm Kettlebell Row
instructions: Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart and place two kettlebells on the floor just in front of your feet, handles aligned.
Bend your knees slightly, then push your hips back to hinge forward at the waist, lowering your torso until it is close to parallel with the floor, keeping the back flat and chest up.
Grab both kettlebells with a firm overhand grip, arms hanging straight down toward the floor. This is your starting position.
Inhale and brace your core, keeping your spine neutral and your head in line with your spine, gaze a few feet in front of you.
Exhale as you pull both kettlebells up toward your stomach, leading with the elbows and retracting your shoulder blades together at the top.
Drive the elbows up and back close to your body, squeezing the mid-back muscles when the kettlebells reach your torso.
Pause briefly at the top in the fully contracted position, feeling the shoulder blades pinch together.
Inhale as you lower the kettlebells under control back to the starting position with arms fully extended, taking about 2 seconds on the descent.
Keep your back straight and torso fixed throughout; do not jerk the torso upward or use momentum to heave the weights.
Form cue: think about pulling with your back rather than your arms by initiating the row with the shoulder blades and elbows, and avoid rounding the lower back at any point.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Typewriter Pull-Up
instructions: Set up under a pull-up bar high enough that your feet clear the floor in a dead hang; chalk up if needed for grip.
Grip the bar with a wide pronated (overhand) grip, hands noticeably wider than shoulder width, arms fully extended in a dead hang.
Depress and retract your shoulder blades to pack the shoulders, and brace your core so your body stays rigid with no swinging.
Inhale, then exhale as you pull your chin up and over the bar, driving your elbows down and pulling your chest toward the bar to reach the top position.
From the top, shift your torso laterally toward one hand by bending that arm fully while extending the opposite arm out straight, keeping your chin high above the bar.
Slide horizontally across to the other side, reversing the arm bends so the previously straight arm bends and the bent arm straightens, all while keeping your chin above bar height.
Keep the movement slow and controlled as you travel side to side; do not let your body drop below the bar during the shift.
After completing the side-to-side traverse, lower yourself under control back to a full dead hang, taking about 2-3 seconds on the descent.
Breathe in short controlled breaths during the lateral shifts, keeping the core and lats engaged the entire time.

Form cue: stay tall and keep your chin above the bar throughout the typewriter slide; the working side does most of the pulling while the straight arm assists, and avoid kipping or swinging to cheat across.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, alternating the lead side.

name: Underhand Cable Pulldowns
instructions: Sit down at a lat pulldown machine with a wide bar attached to the top pulley and adjust the knee pad so it sits snugly on top of your thighs to anchor your body against the resistance.
Reach up and grab the bar with a supinated (underhand, palms facing your torso) grip, with your hands set closer than shoulder width apart.
With your arms fully extended overhead, lean your torso back about 30 degrees, create a slight arch in your lower back, and stick your chest out. This is your starting position.
Inhale and brace your core, keeping the chest tall and the shoulders pulled down away from your ears.
Exhale as you pull the bar down toward your upper chest by driving your shoulders and upper arms down and back, leading with the elbows.
Continue until the bar touches or nearly touches your upper chest and your shoulder blades are squeezed together at the bottom.
Pause for a second in the fully contracted position and consciously squeeze your back muscles, keeping the elbows close to your body.
Keep your torso stationary and only the arms moving; do not lean back further or heave the weight down with momentum.
Inhale as you slowly return the bar to the starting position over about 2-3 seconds until your arms are fully extended and your lats are fully stretched.
Form cue: think of your hands as hooks and pull with your elbows and lats rather than your biceps, and avoid letting the forearms do extra work beyond holding the bar.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Upper Back Stretch
instructions: Stand or sit tall with good posture, feet about hip-width apart and core gently engaged.
Extend both arms straight out in front of you at roughly chest height.
Clasp your fingers together with your palms facing away from you and your thumbs pointing down toward the floor.
Exhale as you reach your clasped hands forward and round your upper back, pushing your shoulder blades apart and separating them as far as comfortable.
Tuck your chin slightly toward your chest and let your head follow the round of the upper spine to deepen the stretch across the mid and upper back.
Feel a comfortable stretch spreading across the muscles between and around your shoulder blades, never any sharp pain.
Breathe slowly and steadily, relaxing a little deeper into the stretch with each exhale.
Hold the position for 20-30 seconds without bouncing, keeping the movement static and gentle.
Form cue: the goal is to actively push the hands away and spread the shoulder blades rather than just leaning forward, and keep the shoulders relaxed down rather than shrugged up to the ears.
Slowly release, return to an upright posture, and repeat as needed.

name: Upper Back-Leg Grab
instructions: Sit on the floor with your legs extended straight out in front of you and your knees held together.
Sit tall with a neutral spine to begin, feet flexed or relaxed as comfortable.
Exhale as you bend forward at the hips, reaching your torso down toward your thighs.
Wrap both arms around the underside of your thighs and hug them, hooking your hands so you can gently pull yourself deeper.
Continue bringing your chest down toward your knees, keeping the legs extended and the knees together, until you feel a stretch along the back of your thighs.
Hold this position to target the hamstrings, breathing slowly and relaxing into the stretch with each exhale.
To shift the emphasis to your middle and lower back, keep hugging your thighs but pull your back away from your knees, rounding the spine to open the upper back.
Hold each variation for 20-30 seconds without bouncing, staying within a comfortable range with no sharp pain.
Form cue: lead the forward fold with your chest and hips rather than just rounding your neck, and use the arm hug to gently assist the stretch instead of yanking yourself down.
Slowly release and return to an upright seated position, then repeat as needed.

name: Upright Barbell Row
instructions: Stand with your feet about hip- to shoulder-width apart and grasp a barbell with an overhand (pronated) grip set slightly less than shoulder width apart.
Let the bar rest against the top of your thighs with your arms fully extended and a slight bend retained in your elbows; keep your back straight and chest up. This is your starting position.
Inhale and brace your core, keeping your torso upright and stationary with the shoulders pulled back.
Exhale as you use the sides of your shoulders to lift the bar, raising your elbows up and out to the sides while keeping the bar close to your body.
Continue pulling until the bar nearly touches your chin, ensuring your elbows lead the motion and always stay higher than your forearms and the bar.
Pause for a second at the top of the movement in the fully contracted position, feeling the contraction in the shoulders and traps.
Inhale as you lower the bar slowly and under control back down to the starting position over about 2 seconds.
Keep your torso fixed throughout; avoid swinging, leaning back, or using momentum to jerk the bar upward.
Form cue: drive with the elbows leading high and wide, and stop the pull if you feel any pinching in the shoulders, lowering the range slightly to keep the joints comfortable.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Upright Cable Row
instructions: Attach a straight bar to a low pulley cable station and stand facing the machine with your feet about hip- to shoulder-width apart.
Grasp the bar with a pronated grip (palms facing your thighs) set slightly less than shoulder width apart, and let the bar rest against the top of your thighs.
Stand upright with your arms extended, a slight bend at the elbows, back straight, and chest up; step back enough so there is tension on the cable. This is your starting position.
Inhale and brace your core, keeping your torso upright and stationary throughout the movement.
Exhale as you use the sides of your shoulders to lift the bar, raising your elbows up and out while keeping the bar close to your body.
Continue pulling until the bar nearly touches your chin, making sure your elbows lead and remain higher than your forearms.
Pause for a second at the top of the movement, squeezing the traps and shoulders in the contracted position.
Inhale as you slowly lower the bar back down to the starting position over about 2 seconds, maintaining cable tension.
Keep your torso fixed and avoid leaning back or swinging to move the weight.
Form cue: let the constant cable tension keep your shoulders working through the full range, lead with high elbows, and reduce the height of the pull if you feel any shoulder impingement.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Upright Row - With Bands
instructions: Stand on the middle of an exercise band with your feet about hip- to shoulder-width apart so that there is tension at arm's length.
Grasp the handles with a pronated grip (palms facing your thighs) set slightly less than shoulder width apart, letting the handles rest against the tops of your thighs.
Stand tall with your arms extended, a slight bend at the elbows, back straight, and chest up. This is your starting position.
Inhale and brace your core, keeping your torso upright and stationary throughout.
Exhale as you use the sides of your shoulders to lift the handles, raising your elbows up and out while keeping the handles close to your body.
Continue pulling until the handles nearly touch your chin, ensuring your elbows lead the motion and stay higher than your forearms.
Pause for a second at the top of the movement in the contracted position, feeling the squeeze in the traps and shoulders.
Inhale as you lower the handles slowly and under control back to the starting position; note that band resistance increases as you rise, so resist on the way down.
Keep your torso fixed and avoid swinging or using momentum.
Form cue: keep tension on the band the entire rep and lead with high elbows; if your shoulders pinch at the top, lower the finishing height to keep the joints comfortable.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.

name: Upward Stretch
instructions: Stand tall with your feet about hip-width apart, knees soft, and core gently engaged to keep your back straight.
Extend both arms straight up above your head and bring your palms together, fingers pointing toward the ceiling.
Inhale to lengthen through your spine, lifting tall through the crown of your head.
Exhale as you slowly push your hands up and slightly back, reaching toward the ceiling while keeping your back straight and ribs from flaring.
Feel the stretch lengthen through your shoulders, the sides of your chest, and your lats as you reach upward and back.
Keep your gaze forward and avoid arching your lower back excessively; the reach should come from the shoulders and upper back.
Hold the stretch for 20-30 seconds, breathing slowly and reaching a little higher on each exhale.
Form cue: keep the shoulders pulling away from the ears and the core braced so you stretch the shoulders and lats rather than collapsing into the lower back.
Slowly lower your arms back down and relax, then repeat as needed.

name: V-Bar Pulldown
instructions: Sit down at a lat pulldown machine with a V-bar (close-grip neutral attachment) connected to the top pulley, and adjust the knee pad so it sits snugly on top of your thighs to anchor your body.
Reach up and grab the V-bar with both hands so your palms face each other in a neutral grip.
With your arms extended overhead, stick your chest out and lean your torso back slightly, about 30 degrees, to better engage the lats. This is your starting position.
Inhale and brace your core, keeping your chest tall and shoulders pulled down away from your ears.
Exhale as you pull the V-bar down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down and squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Continue until the bar nearly touches your chest and the lats are fully contracted, keeping the elbows tracking down close to your sides.
Pause for a second in the contracted position and consciously squeeze your back muscles.
Keep your torso stationary throughout; do not rock back and forth or use body momentum to move the weight.
Inhale as you slowly return the bar to the starting position over about 2-3 seconds until your arms are fully extended and your lats are fully stretched.
Form cue: think about pulling with your elbows and lats rather than your hands and biceps, and let the shoulders rise into a full stretch at the top of each rep.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: V-Bar Pullup
instructions: Place the middle of a V-bar over the middle of a pull-up bar so the V-bar handles hang down, allowing you to grip them in a neutral position (skip this step if your station already has neutral grip handles).
Reach up and take hold of the V-bar handles, one in each hand, with palms facing each other, then hang with arms fully extended.
Depress and retract your shoulder blades to pack the shoulders, stick your chest out, and lean back slightly to better engage the lats. This is your starting position.
Inhale and brace your core so your body stays rigid without swinging.
Exhale as you pull your torso up by driving your elbows down and squeezing your shoulder blades, leaning your head back slightly so you clear the pull-up bar.
Continue pulling until your chest nearly touches the V-bar and your lats are fully contracted at the top.
Pause for a second in the contracted position, feeling the squeeze across the upper back and lats.
Inhale as you lower yourself slowly and under control back to the fully extended dead hang over about 2-3 seconds.
Keep the movement strict with no kipping or swinging; let the lats and back do the work rather than just the arms.
Form cue: think about pulling your elbows down toward your hips and driving your chest to the bar, and avoid shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears at the bottom.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: V-Up
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your legs straight and together, and your arms extended overhead so your biceps frame your ears. Press your lower back gently into the floor and brace your core so there is no arch in your lumbar spine.
Point your toes slightly and keep a small, steady tension through your abdominals; this is your starting position.
Exhale forcefully and simultaneously lift your straight legs and your torso off the floor, hinging at the hips so your body folds into a sharp V shape.
Reach your hands toward your toes at the top, balancing on your tailbone and glutes, with your chin tucked slightly toward your chest.
Pause for a beat at the top and consciously squeeze your abdominals, feeling the contraction from your upper abs down to your lower abs.
Inhale and lower your torso and legs back down under control over roughly two to three seconds, resisting gravity rather than dropping.
Let your shoulders and heels lightly touch the floor without fully relaxing, then begin the next repetition.
Form cue: keep your legs and arms as straight as possible; bending the knees turns this into an easier tuck-up and reduces the work on the abs.
Form cue: drive the movement with your abs, not momentum from your arms; if you find yourself flailing your hands to swing up, slow the tempo down.

name: Vertical Swing
instructions: Stand with your feet roughly shoulder-width apart, toes turned out very slightly, and a single dumbbell on the floor between your feet.

Hinge at the hips with a flat back, soft knees, and grip the top of the dumbbell handle with both hands, palms facing you. Keep your chest up, shoulders pulled back, and head in a neutral line with your spine.
Lift the dumbbell so it hangs at arm's length between your legs; brace your core and set your weight through your mid-foot and heels. This is your starting position.
Inhale and hinge at the hips, allowing the dumbbell to swing back between your legs as your knees bend slightly; keep your back flat and your arms relaxed and straight.
Powerfully reverse the motion by snapping your hips forward and extending your knees and ankles, driving through the floor to propel the dumbbell upward overhead in a vertical line.
Exhale sharply as you extend; let the momentum from your hips, not your arms, carry the dumbbell up so it finishes directly above your head with arms extended.
Control the descent as the dumbbell falls back down, absorbing the load by hinging at the hips and softening the knees.
Draw the dumbbell back toward your torso and into the next backswing in one smooth, continuous rhythm.
Form cue: the power comes from an explosive hip snap, like a kettlebell swing, not from lifting with the shoulders or lower back.
Form cue: keep your spine neutral and core braced throughout; never round your lower back at the bottom of the swing.

name: Walking Lunge
instructions: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, chest up, shoulders back, and core braced. Let your arms hang at your sides or place your hands on your hips. Clear a straight path in front of you with enough room to walk forward.
Inhale and take a controlled step forward with one leg, planting the foot flat and keeping your torso upright.

Lower your hips straight down by bending both knees until your front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor and your front knee tracks over your toes; your back knee should descend toward the floor without slamming into it.
Keep your weight balanced through the heel and mid-foot of your front leg, with the ball of your back foot on the ground for stability.
Exhale and drive forcefully through the front heel to stand up, bringing your back leg forward and through into the next lunge without pausing in a standing position.
Repeat the movement on the opposite leg, continuing to walk forward and alternating legs with each step.
Maintain a controlled tempo: about two seconds down, a brief pause at the bottom, and a strong push up.
Form cue: keep your front knee aligned over your ankle and avoid letting it cave inward or shoot far past your toes.
Form cue: keep your torso tall and resist leaning forward; lead with your hips dropping straight down rather than your chest pitching over the front leg.
Form cue: take a long enough step that both knees can reach roughly 90 degrees; too short a stride overloads the knees.

name: Walking, Treadmill
instructions: Step onto the treadmill deck by standing on the side rails first, then straddling the belt. Clip the safety stop cord to your clothing so the machine halts if you stumble.

Power on the console and select a program; most treadmills have a manual mode, or you can choose a preset and enter your age and weight to estimate calories burned. Set the incline to zero to start, raising it later to increase intensity.
Begin the belt at a slow speed and step onto it gradually, building up to a moderate-to-brisk walking pace rather than a leisurely stroll.
Stand tall with your head up, shoulders relaxed and back, chest open, and core lightly engaged; let your eyes look forward, not down at your feet.
Walk with a natural heel-to-toe foot strike, rolling from the heel through to push off the toes, and let your arms swing freely in opposition to your legs.
Breathe rhythmically and steadily through the walk; you should be able to hold a short conversation at a moderate effort.
Only hold the handrails when necessary, such as when stepping on or off or checking your heart rate; gripping them continuously reduces calorie burn and encourages poor posture.
Adjust speed and incline to keep the effort challenging but sustainable for the duration of your session.
To finish, gradually reduce the speed to a cool-down pace, then stop the belt and carefully step onto the side rails before dismounting.
Form cue: avoid leaning on the handrails or hunching forward; an upright posture engages your legs and core properly and protects your lower back.

name: Wall Angels
instructions: Stand with your back against a flat wall, feet about six inches out from the base, knees slightly bent. Press your tailbone, mid-back, and the back of your head into the wall, gently flattening your lower back so there is minimal gap.
Bring your arms up against the wall and bend your elbows to roughly 90 degrees, forming a goalpost or W shape, with the backs of your hands, wrists, forearms, and elbows all touching the wall.
Brace your core to keep your ribs down and prevent your lower back from arching off the wall. This is your starting position.
Inhale and slowly slide your arms upward along the wall, straightening your elbows as your hands travel toward the overhead position, keeping every contact point pressed to the wall.
Reach only as high as you can while maintaining contact; do not let your hands, forearms, or lower back peel away from the wall.
Exhale and slowly slide your arms back down to the starting goalpost position, squeezing your shoulder blades down and together as your elbows return toward your sides.
Move slowly and deliberately through a comfortable, pain-free range; this is a mobility drill, not a strength lift.
Form cue: if your wrists or forearms lift off the wall as you reach up, that marks the limit of your current mobility; stay within that range rather than forcing it.
Form cue: keep your lower back from arching by actively drawing your ribs toward your hips throughout the slide.

name: Wall Handstand Hold
instructions: Face a sturdy wall and place your hands on the floor about six to twelve inches from the base, shoulder-width apart, fingers spread wide and pointing forward. Set your shoulders directly over your wrists.
Kick or walk up into a handstand with either your chest or your back facing the wall, using the wall to catch and support your balance.
Stack your hips directly over your shoulders and your shoulders over your wrists so your body forms one straight vertical line from wrists to ankles.
Brace your core hard, squeeze your glutes, point your toes toward the ceiling, and actively push the floor away to keep your shoulders elevated and elbows locked.
Keep your head in a neutral position, gazing at the floor between your hands rather than craning to look forward.
Hold the position while breathing steadily and shallowly through the diaphragm; do not hold your breath.
Maintain even pressure across your whole hand, gripping the floor with your fingertips to make micro-adjustments and stay balanced.
To come down, bend at the hips and step or lower one leg at a time back to the floor under control.
Form cue: avoid letting your lower back overarch into a banana shape; keep ribs tucked and glutes engaged for a tall, straight line.
Form cue: actively press through your shoulders rather than sinking into them, which protects the shoulder joints and keeps you stable.

name: Wall Sit
instructions: Stand with your back flat against a wall and your feet planted about shoulder-width apart, roughly two feet out from the base of the wall, toes pointing forward.
Press your entire back, including your lower back and shoulders, firmly against the wall and engage your core.
Slowly slide down the wall by bending your knees until your thighs are parallel to the floor and your knees form a 90-degree angle.
Position your knees directly over your ankles, not past your toes, and drive your weight down through your heels. This is your hold position.
Keep your back pressed flat against the wall and your hands resting on your thighs or held out in front of you for balance.
Hold the position isometrically, breathing steadily and continuously rather than holding your breath, while your quads stay under constant tension.
Push the hold as long as your form holds, then slide back up the wall to stand and release the contraction.
Form cue: if your knees travel forward past your toes, walk your feet further from the wall so your shins stay roughly vertical.
Form cue: resist the urge to push down on your thighs with your hands to take load off the legs; keep the burn in the quads, not in your arms.

name: Wall Walk
instructions: Lie face down with your feet flat against the base of a wall and your hands on the floor under your shoulders, then press up into a high plank with your body straight and your heels against the wall.
Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and set your shoulders over your wrists; this is your starting position.
Begin walking your feet up the wall one at a time while simultaneously walking your hands backward toward the wall.
Continue moving your hands closer and your feet higher in small, controlled steps, climbing toward a handstand position with your chest facing the wall.
Walk up only as far as your strength and shoulder stability allow, ideally until your hips stack over your shoulders and your nose is close to the wall.
Keep your core tight and avoid letting your lower back sag or overarch as your body becomes more vertical.
Breathe steadily and avoid holding your breath; exhale as you push and grind through the harder portions of the walk.
Reverse the movement with control, walking your hands forward and your feet back down the wall one step at a time until you return to the plank.
Form cue: keep the movement slow and deliberate; rushing makes you lose tension and risks collapsing at the shoulders.
Form cue: maintain a braced, hollow-body trunk throughout so your spine stays neutral instead of arching as you invert.

name: Warrior I
instructions: Begin standing tall at the top of your mat with feet together. Step one foot back about three to four feet into a long stance, keeping both feet roughly hip-width apart side to side for stability.
Turn your back foot out to about a 45-degree angle and press the outer edge of that foot firmly into the floor; keep your front foot pointing straight ahead.
Bend your front knee until it stacks directly over your front ankle, ideally bringing the front thigh toward parallel with the floor, while keeping the back leg strong and extended.
Square your hips and chest to face forward over the front leg, gently drawing the front hip back and the back hip forward so the pelvis is level.
Inhale and reach both arms straight overhead, palms facing each other or touching, with shoulders relaxed down away from your ears.
Lengthen your spine upward, lift through your chest, and gaze forward or slightly up past your hands.
Hold the posture, breathing slowly and deeply, while grounding through both feet and squeezing the front glute to support the bent knee.
To switch sides, inhale to straighten the front leg, step the feet together, and repeat with the opposite leg back.
Form cue: keep your front knee tracking over the middle toes, never collapsing inward, and don't let it drift past your ankle.
Form cue: avoid overarching your lower back as you raise your arms; keep your tailbone gently tucked and ribs drawn down.

name: Warrior III
instructions: Begin standing tall, then shift your weight fully onto one leg, the standing leg, with a micro-bend in that knee to avoid locking it out.
Engage your core and the glute of your standing leg to create a stable base before you begin to tip forward.
Inhale to lengthen the spine, then exhale and hinge forward at the hips while simultaneously extending your other leg straight out behind you.
Continue hinging until your torso and your lifted back leg form one straight line parallel to the floor, creating a T shape balanced over the standing leg.
Reach your arms forward past your head, alongside your ears, or extend them back along your sides, keeping your shoulders relaxed and squared toward the floor.
Flex the foot of your lifted leg and keep both hips level, resisting the tendency for the raised hip to open upward toward the ceiling.
Fix your gaze on a steady point on the floor a few feet ahead to help you balance, and breathe slowly and evenly throughout the hold.
To exit, bend the standing knee slightly, draw the lifted leg back in, and rise to standing before switching sides.
Form cue: keep your hips square and level; rotating the lifted hip open is the most common fault and twists the lower back.
Form cue: actively reach the back heel away from the crown of your head to keep the body long and prevent the back from rounding or sagging.

name: Weighted Ball Hyperextension
instructions: Position yourself face down over an exercise ball so the ball supports your hips and lower abdomen, with your torso draped forward and parallel to the floor.
Spread your feet and press the balls of your feet into the floor, slightly wider than hip-width, to create a stable base; brace them against a wall if balancing is difficult.
Hold a weighted plate either tucked under your chin against your chest or behind your neck, securing it firmly with both hands. This is your starting position.
Exhale and slowly raise your torso upward by extending at the waist and lower back until your body forms a straight line from head to heels, or slightly above parallel.
Squeeze your lower back and glutes at the top and hold the contraction for a full second without hyperextending excessively.
Inhale and slowly lower your torso back down over the ball under control to the starting position, letting the ball support the stretch.
Maintain a controlled tempo throughout: about two seconds to lift, a one-second pause, and two to three seconds to lower.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.
Form cue: avoid jerking or swinging up with momentum; the lower back should do the work in a smooth, deliberate arc.
Form cue: do not over-arch at the top by throwing your head back; rise only to a neutral straight-line position to protect the spine.

name: Weighted Ball Side Bend
instructions: Lie sideways over an exercise ball so the left side of your torso, including your waist, hip, and lower ribs, presses into the ball, with your body in a straight line.
Set your feet on the floor with legs crossed or staggered and braced for stability, anchoring against a wall if needed to keep from rolling off the ball.
Hold a weighted plate in your right hand directly against the right side of your head, smooth side resting on your head, and place your left hand across your torso onto your left obliques.
Keep your right elbow pointing up and your body aligned over the ball. This is your starting position.
Exhale and raise the right side of your torso upward by laterally flexing at the waist, lifting against the resistance of the plate.
Squeeze your right-side obliques hard at the top and hold the contraction for a full second.
Inhale and slowly lower your torso back down over the ball to the starting position, feeling a stretch through the obliques.
Move under control throughout, avoiding any twisting; the motion is a pure side-to-side bend in one plane.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, then switch sides so the right side of your torso rests on the ball and the weight is in your left hand.
Form cue: keep the movement strictly lateral and do not rotate the torso forward or back, which shifts work off the obliques.
Form cue: control the lowering phase rather than flopping over the ball, keeping constant tension on the working obliques.

name: Weighted Bench Dip
instructions: Set up two flat benches perpendicular to your body, one behind you and one in front, spaced so your legs can rest extended across the front bench.
Sit on the edge of the rear bench and place your hands on its edge just outside your hips, shoulder-width apart, fingers gripping the edge and arms fully extended.
Slide your hips off the bench and rest your heels on the front bench so your legs are straight and parallel to the floor and your torso is perpendicular to the ground.

Have a partner carefully place a dumbbell or weighted plate across your upper thighs near your hips; a partner is strongly recommended to avoid injury when loading and unloading the weight. This is your starting position.
Inhale and slowly lower your body by bending at the elbows until your upper arms reach an angle slightly less than 90 degrees with your forearms.
Keep your elbows tucked in close to your body and pointing straight back, with your forearms staying roughly vertical throughout the descent.
Exhale and press through your triceps to push your torso back up, extending your elbows fully to return to the starting position.
Use a controlled tempo, lowering over about two seconds and pausing briefly at the bottom before driving up.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, then have your partner remove the weight before you dismount.
Form cue: keep your hips close to the bench as you lower; drifting forward shifts strain onto the shoulders.
Form cue: avoid flaring your elbows out to the sides, which stresses the shoulder joint and reduces triceps engagement.

name: Weighted Crunches
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your knees bent at about 90 degrees and your feet flat on the floor or resting on a bench for support.
Hold a medicine ball or weight plate either hugged against your chest or pressed straight up above your torso with arms extended. This is your starting position.
Press your lower back gently into the floor and brace your core to remove any arch in your lumbar spine.
Exhale and slowly curl your shoulders and upper back off the floor, raising your shoulder blades roughly four inches up while your lower back stays planted on the floor.
Lead the movement by flexing your abs and rolling your shoulders forward, not by pulling with your neck or yanking the weight upward.
At the top, squeeze your abdominals hard and hold for a brief pause to maximize the contraction.
Inhale and slowly lower your shoulders back down to the starting position under control over about two seconds.
Keep the weight stable and close to your body throughout if holding it overhead, so it does not pull you off balance.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.
Form cue: keep your chin a fist-width off your chest and avoid pulling your head forward; the work should be felt in the abs, not the neck.
Form cue: this is a short, controlled curl, not a full sit-up; your lower back stays in contact with the floor the entire time.

name: Weighted Jump Squat
instructions: Position a lightly loaded barbell across the upper back of your shoulders, resting on your traps, and grip it firmly with hands just outside shoulder width; alternatively use a weighted vest, sandbag, or other resistance.
Keep the load light enough that it does not noticeably slow your jump; this is an explosive power exercise, not a heavy strength lift.
Stand with your feet just outside shoulder width, toes turned out slightly, with your head and chest up and core braced. This is your starting position.
Inhale and use a quick countermovement, squatting partially down by bending at the hips and knees while keeping your torso upright and back flat.
Immediately reverse direction and explode upward, extending forcefully through your hips, knees, and ankles to drive off the ground into a jump.
Exhale sharply during the explosive jump and maintain good posture with a tight core throughout the airborne phase.
As you return to the ground, land softly on the balls of your feet then through to your heels, absorbing the impact by bending your hips and knees to cushion the landing.
Reset your stance and posture, then either flow directly into the next rep or pause briefly to re-brace before jumping again.
Form cue: keep the dip shallow and fast; a deep, slow squat kills the stretch-reflex and turns this into a strength move rather than a power move.
Form cue: always land soft with bent knees and never on locked legs, to protect your knees and lower back from the impact.

name: Weighted Pull Ups
instructions: Attach a weight plate to a dip belt and secure the belt around your waist so the plate hangs between your legs; alternatively hold a dumbbell between your feet or use a weighted vest.
Grip the pull-up bar with an overhand, pronated grip (palms facing away) at about shoulder width, then hang with both arms fully extended.

Lean your torso back about 30 degrees, create a slight curve in your lower back, and stick your chest out toward the bar. Engage your core and pull your shoulder blades down. This is your starting position.
Exhale and pull your torso up by driving your elbows down and back, leading with your chest until your head rises above the level of your hands.
Concentrate on squeezing your shoulder blades back and down and contracting your lats hard at the top of the movement.
Hold the top contracted position for a brief moment, with your chin clearing the bar and chest near it.
Inhale and slowly lower your torso back down under control until your arms are fully extended and your lats are completely stretched.
Maintain a controlled tempo, especially on the descent, taking about two to three seconds to lower rather than dropping.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.
Form cue: avoid kipping or swinging the legs to cheat the weight up; the added load makes strict, controlled reps essential to protect the shoulders and elbows.
Form cue: initiate each rep by depressing the shoulder blades before bending the arms, so the lats drive the pull rather than the biceps alone.

name: Weighted Sissy Squat
instructions: Stand upright next to a squat rack or any sturdy vertical post, with your feet roughly shoulder-width apart and rise up onto the balls of your feet so your heels are off the floor.

Grip a beam of the rack with one hand for balance, and hold a weight plate flat against your chest with the opposite hand and forearm, keeping it pressed snugly so it does not shift during the set. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your hips, torso, and head aligned in one straight line from knees to shoulders throughout the movement.
Inhale as you bend your knees and drive them forward, simultaneously leaning your torso backward so your body stays in a straight diagonal line, lowering under control toward the floor.

Continue descending slowly over about three seconds until your shins are roughly parallel with the floor and your knees and thighs form close to a 90-degree angle, feeling a deep stretch through the front of your thighs.
Pause for one second at the bottom, keeping the heels lifted and the hips extended so the tension stays on the quadriceps rather than the hip flexors.
Exhale and contract your quadriceps to pull your body back up to the upright starting position, leading with the knees as they straighten.

Avoid letting your hips bend forward or sticking your butt back, as that turns the movement into a regular squat and removes tension from the quads; the body should hinge only at the knees and ankles.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then carefully set down the plate.

name: Weighted Sit-Ups - With Bands
instructions: Anchor both resistance bands around the base or rear legs of a decline bench, then route the handles forward toward the inside of the bench so you can reach them while lying back.
Sit on the decline bench and hook your legs securely under the foot pads or roller, adjusting so your knees are bent at about 90 degrees and your feet are locked in.
Reach back and grasp a band handle in each hand using a pronated (palms-forward) grip, then bring the handles down near your collarbones and rotate to a neutral grip with palms facing your torso.

Keep your arms pinned stationary against your chest for the entire set so the bands load the abs, not the arms, then lie back until your torso is near the decline surface. This is your starting position.
Exhale and curl your torso upward by flexing your abdominals, rolling your spine off the bench one vertebra at a time until your upper body is roughly perpendicular to the floor.
Squeeze your abs hard and hold the fully contracted top position for one second, resisting the pull of the bands.
Inhale as you lower your torso back down slowly over two to three seconds, controlling the band tension rather than letting it yank you down.
Avoid pulling with your hip flexors or jerking with momentum; initiate every rep from the abdominals and keep the chin slightly tucked to protect the neck.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Weighted Squat
instructions: Position two flat benches parallel to each other, roughly shoulder-width apart, so you can stand with one foot on each bench and a gap between them for the weight to hang.
Loop a dip/weight belt around your waist and attach the desired load so it hangs between your legs, then step up so each foot is planted firmly on a bench with toes angled slightly outward.

Stand tall with the weight hanging freely between the benches, let your arms extend down at your sides (or lightly grip the bench edges for balance), and look straight ahead with a tall chest. This is your starting position.
Brace your core, keep your back straight and head up, then inhale as you bend at the knees and hips and lower your body down between the benches under control.
Descend until the angle between your thighs and calves is slightly less than 90 degrees, with your upper legs just below parallel, allowing the hanging weight to drop into the gap.
Keep your knees tracking in line with your toes and do not let them drift past your toes, which would place undue stress on the knee joint.
Exhale and drive back up by pushing through the balls of your feet and straightening your legs until you return to the fully upright starting position.
Maintain control of the swinging weight throughout and avoid bouncing out of the bottom; the eccentric should take about twice as long as the ascent.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then step down and remove the belt.

name: Wide Stance Barbell Squat
instructions: Set the barbell in a squat rack at about mid-chest height and load it evenly, performing this lift inside the rack with safety pins set for protection.
Step under the bar and place it across the back of your shoulders just below the base of your neck (low to mid-trap position), gripping the bar firmly with both hands a bit wider than shoulder width.
Unrack the bar by pushing up through your legs while straightening your torso, then take one or two steps back to clear the rack.
Set your feet in a stance noticeably wider than shoulder width with your toes pointed out about 30 degrees, keeping your head up, chest tall, and back flat. This is your starting position.
Take a deep breath into your belly, brace your core hard, and begin descending by pushing your hips back and bending your knees, keeping the knees tracking out over your toes.
Lower under control until the angle between your thighs and calves is slightly less than 90 degrees, with your upper legs just below parallel to the floor; inhale through this lowering phase.
Keep your knees pushed out in line with your toes and your weight on the heels and mid-foot, never letting the knees cave inward or drift past the toes.
Exhale and drive up forcefully by pushing through your heels and extending the hips and knees together until you return to the upright starting position.
Keep your chest up and back tight throughout, avoiding any rounding of the lower back, and use a controlled tempo with a slower descent than ascent.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then step forward and re-rack the bar securely.

name: Wide Stance Stiff Legs
instructions: Position a loaded barbell on the floor and stand with a wide stance, feet considerably wider than shoulder width with toes pointed slightly outward.

Hinge at the hips, pushing them as far back as possible, and bend down to grasp the bar with a pronated (palms-down) grip just inside your legs, keeping your legs nearly straight with only a slight knee bend.
Set your back flat, raise your head and chest, and pull the slack out of the bar so your arms hang straight down. This is your starting position.
Inhale and brace your core, then drive the movement by engaging the hips and pushing them forward, letting the bar rise close to your body as your arms hang straight.
