Continue extending the hips until you are standing fully upright with shoulders back, exhaling as you reach the top and squeezing your glutes and hamstrings.
Reverse the motion by pushing your hips back and lowering the bar under control, feeling a strong stretch through the hamstrings and adductors as the wide stance lengthens them.
Keep your back flat and the bar tracking close to your legs throughout; never round the lower back, and let the stretch come from the hip hinge rather than bending the spine.
On successive reps the bar need not touch the floor; stop just short and reverse to keep constant tension on the hamstrings.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Wide-Grip Barbell Bench Press
instructions: Lie back on a flat bench with your feet planted firmly on the floor, eyes roughly under the bar, and your shoulder blades pinched together and pressed down into the bench.
Grip the bar with a wide, pronated (palms-forward) grip about three inches wider than shoulder width on each hand, and maintain a slight natural arch in your lower back.
Unrack the bar and hold it locked out straight over your chest so it sits perpendicular to your torso and the floor. This is your starting position.
Inhale and lower the bar slowly and under control until it lightly touches your mid-chest, keeping your elbows at roughly a 45-to-60-degree angle from your torso.
Pause for one second at chest level without bouncing the bar off your ribcage, keeping the wrists stacked over the elbows.
Exhale and press the bar back up powerfully using your chest muscles until your arms are locked out over the chest, then squeeze the chest hard in the top position for a moment.
Use a controlled tempo where the lowering phase takes at least twice as long as the press; the wide grip increases pec stretch, so manage the descent carefully.
Keep your glutes on the bench, feet flat, and avoid flaring the elbows straight out to 90 degrees, which strains the shoulders.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then re-rack the bar securely.

name: Wide-Grip Decline Barbell Bench Press
instructions: Lie back on a decline bench and lock your feet securely under the foot pads or rollers at the high end so your body is stable on the incline.
Set your shoulder blades retracted and pressed into the bench, then grip the bar with a wide, pronated (palms-forward) grip about three inches wider than shoulder width on each hand.
Have a spotter help you unrack, or lift the bar off yourself, and hold it locked out straight over your lower chest, perpendicular to your torso and the floor. This is your starting position.
Inhale and lower the bar slowly and under control until it lightly touches your lower chest, keeping the elbows tucked at a moderate angle rather than flaring fully out.
Pause for one second at the bottom without bouncing the bar, keeping the wrists stacked over the elbows.
Exhale and drive the bar back up using your lower chest muscles until your arms are fully locked out, then squeeze the chest hard at the top for a moment.
Use a controlled tempo with the descent taking at least twice as long as the press, emphasizing the lower-pec contraction the decline targets.
Keep your hips and back in contact with the bench and never let the wide grip cause the elbows to splay straight out, which stresses the shoulders.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then re-rack the bar carefully with help if needed.

name: Wide-Grip Decline Barbell Pullover
instructions: Lie back on a decline bench and secure both legs under the foot pads at the high end so your body stays anchored on the incline.
Reach back behind your head and grasp a barbell with a pronated grip set wider than shoulder width, then lift it up off the floor.
Bring the bar up until your arms are fully extended and roughly perpendicular to the floor over your chest, keeping a slight, fixed bend in the elbows. This is your starting position.
Inhale and lower the bar back in a smooth semicircular arc over and behind your head as if reaching toward the floor, moving only at the shoulder joint.
Stop when your arms reach about parallel to the floor and you feel a strong stretch across the chest and lats, keeping the elbows locked in their fixed slight bend the whole time.
Exhale and pull the bar back up along the same arc until you return to the starting position over your chest, squeezing the chest as you finish.
Keep the movement slow and controlled with no jerking, and do not bend or straighten the elbows during the rep; the arms act as a fixed lever rotating at the shoulder.
Maintain full control of the bar at all times, especially in the deep stretched position behind your head where the shoulders are vulnerable.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then carefully lower the bar to the level of your head and release it safely.

name: Wide-Grip Lat Pulldown
instructions: Attach a long wide bar to the top pulley of a lat pulldown machine and adjust the thigh pad so it sits snugly across your legs to keep you anchored against the resistance.
Stand up and grasp the bar with a pronated (palms-forward) grip set wider than shoulder width, then sit down and tuck your thighs under the pad with feet flat on the floor.
With both arms fully extended overhead holding the bar, lean your torso back about 30 degrees, arch your lower back slightly, and stick your chest out toward the bar. This is your starting position.
Exhale and pull the bar down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back and drawing your shoulder blades down, leading the movement with the elbows.
Continue until the bar reaches your upper chest, then squeeze your shoulder blades together and contract the lats hard at the bottom for a one-second pause.
Keep your torso stationary and avoid swinging or leaning back further to heave the weight; only your arms should move while the back does the work.
Let your forearms act only as hooks holding the bar, not as the primary movers; think of pulling with the elbows and lats rather than the hands.
Inhale and slowly raise the bar back up under control until your arms are fully extended and you feel a complete stretch in the lats.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, keeping the eccentric controlled rather than letting the stack pull your arms up.

name: Wide-Grip Pull-Up
instructions: Reach up and grasp a fixed pull-up bar with an overhand (pronated) grip set noticeably wider than shoulder width, palms facing away from you.
Hang from the bar with your arms fully extended in a dead hang, ankles crossed or legs slightly bent, and your core braced so your body does not swing. This is your starting position.
Set your shoulders by depressing them down away from your ears, then exhale and begin pulling by driving your elbows down and back toward your sides.
Lead with your chest toward the bar, continuing to pull until your chin clears the bar or your upper chest approaches it, focusing on squeezing the lats.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top and hold the contracted position for a brief moment, keeping the torso from swinging.
Inhale and lower yourself under control over two to three seconds until you return to a full dead hang with arms completely straight and lats stretched.
Avoid kipping, swinging, or using momentum; keep the movement strict so the lats and upper back do the work rather than jerking up.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, maintaining a smooth controlled tempo on both the pull and the descent.

name: Wide-Grip Pulldown Behind The Neck
instructions: Attach a long wide bar to the top pulley of a lat pulldown machine and adjust the thigh pad so it holds your legs firmly against the seat.
Stand and grasp the bar with a pronated (palms-forward) grip set wider than shoulder width, then sit down and lock your thighs under the pad with feet flat.
With both arms fully extended overhead, tilt your head and torso slightly forward so there is an imaginary straight line from the bar down to the back of your neck. This is your starting position.
Exhale and pull the bar straight down behind your head by driving your elbows down and back and drawing your shoulder blades together, until the bar gently approaches the base of your neck.
Pause for one second in the contracted position and squeeze your upper-back muscles and shoulder blades together.
Keep your torso stationary and avoid yanking the bar onto your neck; control the depth so the bar stops at the back of the neck without impact.
Let only your arms move while your forearms simply hold the bar; pull with the elbows and lats rather than gripping hard with the hands.
Inhale and raise the bar slowly back to the starting position until your arms are fully extended and the lats are fully stretched.
Use a controlled, moderate load on this variation since the behind-the-neck path stresses the shoulders, and stop immediately if you feel impingement. Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Wide-Grip Rear Pull-Up
instructions: Reach up and grasp the pull-up bar with a wide, pronated (palms-forward) grip set well beyond shoulder width.

Hang with both arms fully extended, then tilt your head and torso slightly forward so there is an imaginary line from the bar down to the back of your neck, and brace your core to prevent swinging. This is your starting position.
Exhale and pull your torso up by driving your elbows down and back and drawing your shoulder blades together, leaning your head slightly forward as you rise.
Continue until the bar is near the back of your neck, focusing on squeezing the upper-back and lat muscles hard at the top of the movement.
Hold the fully contracted position for one second, keeping your upper torso stable as it travels rather than swinging through space.
Inhale and lower yourself slowly and under control until your arms are fully extended and the lats are completely stretched.
Keep the forearms passive, acting only as hooks holding the bar, and avoid any kipping or momentum so the back does all the work.
Because pulling behind the neck places the shoulders in a vulnerable position, keep the range comfortable and stop if you feel any pinching. Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Wide-Grip Standing Barbell Curl
instructions: Stand upright with your feet about shoulder-width apart and your torso tall, holding a barbell at the wide outer portion of the bar with a supinated (palms-up) grip wider than shoulder width.
Pin your upper arms and elbows close to the sides of your torso and let your arms hang straight so the bar rests against your thighs. This is your starting position.
Brace your core and keep your upper arms stationary throughout, since only the forearms should move during the curl.
Exhale and curl the bar upward by contracting the biceps, keeping the elbows fixed at your sides as the forearms rotate the bar toward your shoulders.
Continue until your biceps are fully contracted and the bar is at about shoulder level, then hold the top for one second and squeeze the biceps hard.
The wide grip biases the inner (short head) of the biceps, so focus on feeling that contraction rather than swinging the weight up.
Inhale and lower the bar slowly and under control over two to three seconds back to the fully extended starting position.
Avoid leaning back, swinging the torso, or letting the elbows drift forward to cheat the weight up; keep the movement strict.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Wind Sprints
instructions: Reach up and hang from a pull-up bar using a pronated (palms-forward) grip with your hands about shoulder-width apart.
Let your arms and legs extend fully so you are in a straight hanging position, and brace your core to keep your body from swinging. This is your starting position.
Exhale and quickly drive one knee up toward your chest as high as you can, flexing the abdominals to lift the leg rather than swinging it.
Immediately reverse that leg back toward the start while simultaneously driving the opposite knee up as high as possible, mimicking a fast sprinting motion.
Continue alternating knees in a rapid, rhythmic running cadence, keeping the pace quick but controlled and the core engaged.
Keep your torso stable and avoid swinging your body or letting the legs flail; all the drive should come from the hip flexors and abs.
Breathe in a steady rhythm with the leg cadence rather than holding your breath, since this is a higher-rep dynamic movement.
Continue alternating legs at a brisk pace until the set or time interval is complete.

name: Windmills
instructions: Lie flat on your back on the floor with your arms extended straight out to the sides at shoulder level, palms down, and your legs straight together.
Press your arms, shoulders, and upper back firmly into the floor to anchor your torso. This is your starting position.
Inhale to brace, then lift one straight leg and sweep it up and across your body, rotating at the hip and reaching the foot toward the opposite hand.
Lower the foot toward the floor near that opposite hand as far as your flexibility allows while keeping both shoulders pressed flat on the ground.
Exhale as you control the leg back up and over, returning it to the starting position alongside the other leg.
Repeat the same motion with the opposite leg, sweeping it across to the other hand, and continue alternating sides smoothly.
Move in a controlled manner rather than throwing the leg; the goal is to rotate through the hips and abductors while the upper body stays grounded.
Keep both shoulder blades in contact with the floor throughout to protect the lower back and maximize the stretch through the hips and obliques.
Continue alternating legs for 10 to 20 total repetitions.

name: World's Greatest Stretch
instructions: Begin standing, then step one foot forward into a long lunge so your front foot is planted flat on the ground and you are on the toes of your trailing back foot.
Bend both knees and sink down into the lunge until your back knee almost touches the floor, keeping your torso upright and tall. Hold this first position for 10 to 20 seconds, breathing steadily.

Next, place the hand on the same side as your front leg onto the floor with the elbow dropping down toward the inside of your front foot, while the other hand rests on the ground parallel to the lead leg for support, deepening the hip-flexor and groin stretch.
From there, rotate the inside arm and reach it up toward the ceiling, opening your chest and following the hand with your eyes to add a thoracic-spine rotation, then return the hand to the floor.

After 10 to 20 seconds, place both hands on either side of your front foot, lift the toes of the front foot off the ground, and straighten the front leg, repositioning your back leg as needed to hinge into a hamstring stretch.
Hold this straight-leg hamstring stretch for 10 to 20 seconds, feeling the lengthening through the hamstring, calf, and glute of the front leg while breathing slowly and deeply.
Keep all movements smooth and controlled, never bouncing into the stretches, and breathe continuously to help the muscles relax into each position.
Repeat the entire three-part sequence on the opposite side by lunging forward with the other leg.

name: Wrist Circles
instructions: Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, chest up, and core lightly braced to keep your torso stable throughout.
Raise both arms out to the sides until they are fully extended and parallel to the floor, level with your shoulders, so your body forms a T shape. Rotate your palms to face down.
Make loose fists or keep your fingers extended, whichever is more comfortable; this is your starting position.

Keeping your shoulders, elbows, and the rest of your body completely still, begin rotating both wrists in slow, controlled circles, imagining you are drawing small circles in the air with your knuckles.
Move through the fullest pain-free range of motion at each wrist, flexing, abducting, extending, and adducting so the hands trace a complete circle.
Breathe normally and rhythmically throughout; do not hold your breath since this is a low-intensity mobility drill.
Use a steady, even tempo of roughly one circle per second, never snapping or forcing the joint.
After completing the prescribed number of circles in one direction, reverse and rotate the wrists the opposite way for an equal count.
Keep the arms parallel to the floor the entire time; if they begin to drift down, reset to shoulder height rather than letting the shoulders compensate.
Focus on feeling the movement isolated in the wrist and forearm, not the shoulders, to truly mobilize and warm the joint.

name: Wrist Extensor Stretch
instructions: Stand or sit tall with relaxed shoulders and a neutral spine; this stretch can be done anywhere with no equipment.
Extend one arm straight out in front of you at shoulder height with the elbow fully straight and the palm facing down toward the floor.
Let the wrist relax so the fingers point downward, allowing the hand to drop naturally at the wrist.
With your opposite hand, gently grasp the back of the extended hand near the knuckles.
Slowly and smoothly pull the back of the hand toward your body, drawing the fingers and palm in toward you to deepen the bend at the wrist.
Continue until you feel a comfortable, moderate stretch along the top of the forearm and the wrist extensor muscles; never pull into sharp pain.
Exhale as you ease into the stretch and breathe slowly and deeply while you hold, letting the muscles release with each breath.
Hold the stretched position statically for 20 to 30 seconds without bouncing.
Keep the working arm fully extended and the shoulder down and relaxed; avoid shrugging or bending the elbow to cheat the angle.
Gently release, shake out the hand, then repeat on the opposite arm for the same duration.

name: Wrist Flexor Stretch
instructions: Stand or sit upright with your shoulders relaxed and spine neutral; no equipment is required for this stretch.
Extend one arm straight out in front of you at shoulder height with the elbow fully locked and rotate the forearm so the palm faces up toward the ceiling.
Let the fingers relax and point slightly downward as the wrist begins to extend.
Reach across with your opposite hand and gently grasp the fingers of the extended hand.
Slowly pull the fingers back and down toward the floor, drawing them in toward your body to increase the extension at the wrist.
Progress until you feel a comfortable stretch along the underside of the forearm and the wrist flexors; stop short of any sharp or pinching pain.
Exhale as you sink into the stretch and continue breathing slowly and steadily throughout the hold.
Hold the position statically for 20 to 30 seconds without bouncing or jerking.
Keep the stretching arm fully straight with the palm up; if the elbow bends the stretch loses its effectiveness on the flexors.
Ease out of the stretch gently, then switch and repeat on the other arm for an equal hold.

name: Wrist Roller
instructions: Load a light to moderate weight on the rope of the wrist roller and stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, core braced and chest up.
Grip the roller bar with both hands using a pronated grip, palms facing down, hands roughly shoulder-width apart.

Raise both arms straight out in front of you until they are fully extended and parallel to the floor at shoulder height, making sure the rope hangs freely and is not yet wrapped around the bar. This is your starting position.
Keep your entire body stationary except for the forearms and wrists; the upper arms and shoulders should not swing or rise.
Begin winding the weight upward by alternately rotating one wrist at a time, curling each hand over the top to roll the rope around the bar and draw the weight toward you.
Continue the alternating rolling motion in a controlled rhythm until the weight reaches the bar at the top.
Then reverse the action, slowly unrolling the rope by rotating the wrists in the opposite downward direction to lower the weight under control rather than letting it drop.
Breathe steadily throughout, exhaling on the effort of winding up and inhaling as you lower the weight back down.
Use a deliberate, controlled tempo in both directions; resisting the weight on the way down trains the forearms just as much as winding it up.
Keep the arms parallel to the floor the whole set; if they fatigue and drop, lower the weight rather than letting the shoulders compensate, and feel the burn isolate in the forearms.
Repeat for the prescribed number of full up-and-down cycles in your program.

name: Wrist Rotations with Straight Bar
instructions: Select a lightly loaded barbell or use an empty bar, and stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart and core braced.
Grasp the bar with both hands in a pronated grip, palms facing down, hands spaced about shoulder-width apart.
Hold the bar in front of your thighs with the elbows tucked close to your sides; keep the upper arms and shoulders fixed throughout. This is your starting position.
Keeping everything stationary except the wrists, begin extending the wrists one at a time in an alternating fashion, as if you were rolling up a newspaper away from you.
Continue the alternating extension motion back and forth in a smooth controlled rhythm until your wrist extensors reach failure.
Then reverse the direction, alternately flexing the wrists to roll the bar the opposite way toward you, working the wrist flexors.
Continue this alternating flexion motion until those muscles reach failure as well.
Breathe rhythmically and continuously throughout; do not hold your breath during the small repeated movements.
Use a controlled, moderate tempo and avoid swinging the bar with your arms; the only movement should come from the wrists.
Keep the elbows pinned to your sides the entire set so the forearms do the work and stay under constant tension.

name: Yoke Walk
instructions: Set the yoke apparatus to an appropriate height and load it with your working weight; position yourself centered under the crossbar inside the frame.
Step under the yoke and rack the padded crossbar firmly across the meat of your upper traps and rear shoulders, just as you would for a high-bar squat.
Set your feet roughly hip- to shoulder-width apart, grip the side posts or uprights of the frame to steady it, brace your core hard, arch your back, and fix your gaze straight ahead.
Take a big breath, brace your abdominals, and lift the yoke off its supports by driving powerfully through your heels until your hips and knees are fully extended.
Once standing tall and stable, begin walking forward immediately using short, quick, choppy steps to keep the load from swaying or rocking.
Keep your torso upright, chest up, and the load balanced directly over your midfoot; avoid leaning excessively forward or letting the back round.
Hold your breath and brace during each burst of steps, taking quick breaths only as needed to maintain intra-abdominal pressure and a rigid trunk.
Move as fast as you can safely control for the prescribed distance, typically 75 to 100 feet, keeping the steps small and rapid the whole way.
Use your grip on the side posts to dampen any side-to-side oscillation of the frame and keep the path straight.
At the finish line, slow under control and set the yoke down by bending the hips and knees together, keeping the back braced and flat throughout the descent.

name: Zercher Squats
instructions: For safety, set up inside a squat rack and position the bar on the pins at a height above your waist but below your chest, then load it with your working weight.
Step in close and crook your elbows under the bar so it rests in the crooks of your arms between the forearms and upper arms, then clasp your hands together in front of your chest.
Lift the bar off the pins so it sits cradled on top of your forearms; from the front it should look like your arms are crossed with the bar running across them.
Step back from the rack and set your feet in a shoulder-width stance with toes turned slightly outward, chest up, elbows tight, and a tall, neutral spine. This is your starting position.
Take a deep breath and brace your core, then begin descending by bending at the hips and knees together, keeping your torso as upright as possible and your head up.
Continue lowering under control until your hip crease drops just below the top of your knees, with the angle between thigh and calf slightly less than 90 degrees; inhale through this phase.
Keep your elbows pointed down and tucked inside your knees at the bottom so the bar stays close to your body and your back stays rigid.
Drive back up by pushing through the whole foot, extending the knees and hips together, and exhale as you ascend to the starting position.
Use a controlled two- to three-second eccentric, a brief pause at the bottom if desired, and a strong but controlled drive up.
Track your knees out over your toes and do not let them cave inward or shoot far past the toes, which would overstress the knees.
Resist the bar pulling you forward by keeping your chest tall and upper back braced throughout; the elbows should not droop.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, re-racking carefully onto the pins when finished.

name: Zottman Curl
instructions: Stand tall with your feet hip- to shoulder-width apart, torso upright, core braced, and a dumbbell in each hand held at arm's length by your sides.
Keep your elbows tucked close to your torso and rotate your forearms so your palms face each other in a neutral grip. This is your starting position.
Holding your upper arms stationary, curl both dumbbells upward while rotating your wrists so that by the top your palms face up in a fully supinated grip; exhale as you lift and squeeze the biceps.
Continue curling until the dumbbells reach shoulder level and the biceps are fully contracted.
Hold the top position for a one-second count, consciously squeezing the biceps hard.
At the top, rotate your wrists to flip into a pronated grip so the palms now face down with the thumbs higher than the pinkies.
Slowly lower the dumbbells back down using that pronated grip, taking two to three seconds on the descent to maximize tension on the forearm extensors; inhale as you lower.
As the dumbbells approach your thighs, rotate the wrists back to the neutral starting grip to begin the next repetition smoothly.
Keep your elbows pinned to your sides the entire set and avoid swinging the torso or using momentum; only the forearms should move.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, keeping the rotation deliberate so the lift trains the biceps and the controlled lowering trains the forearms.

name: Zottman Preacher Curl
instructions: Set up at a preacher bench or incline bench and select a dumbbell in each hand, then seat yourself so your upper arms rest flat on the angled pad.
Position your upper arms and the backs of your arms firmly against the pad with the dumbbells held up at shoulder height and the elbows flexed.
Rotate your forearms so the palms of your hands face down in a pronated grip. This is your starting position.
As you inhale, slowly lower the dumbbells under control, keeping the palms facing down, until your upper arms are extended and your biceps and forearms are fully stretched at the bottom.
Once at the bottom, rotate your wrists so that the palms now face up into a supinated grip.
As you exhale, drive the dumbbells back up using your biceps until they are fully contracted at shoulder height, bringing the pinky side slightly higher than the thumb to ensure peak contraction.
Squeeze the biceps hard for a one-second count at the top, then rotate your wrists back so the palms face down again, ready to lower.
Use a slow two- to three-second eccentric on the pronated lowering phase, since the back of the hand facing the floor heavily loads the forearm extensors.
Keep your upper arms glued to the pad the entire time and avoid lifting your elbows or rocking your torso to cheat the weight up.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions, keeping the wrist rotations crisp at the top and bottom of each rep.
